CONCLUSION: mNGS is a useful diagnostic tool with good performance for the diagnosis of PJP and the detection of co-pathogens. mNGS of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and/or blood samples is suggested in patients with presumptive diagnosis of PJP. Blood samples may be a good alternative to bronchoalveolar lavage fluid for mNGS when bronchoscopic examination is not feasible.

title: Fecal Microbiota Transplantation from Overweight or Obese Donors in Cachectic Patients with Advanced Gastroesophageal Cancer: A Randomized, Double-blind, Placebo-Controlled, Phase II Study.
journal: Clinical cancer research : an official journal of the American Association for Cancer Research
authors: de Clercq Nicolien C; van den Ende Tom; Prodan Andrei; Hemke Robert; Davids Mark et al.
summary_zh: 研究对晚期胃食管癌恶病质患者行肥胖供体粪菌移植，发现未改善恶病质但可能提高疗效和生存。
innovation: 使用健康肥胖供体粪菌移植干预癌症恶病质 | 结合宏基因组测序和代谢组学探索粪菌移植对肠道菌群及代谢物的影响
limitation: 样本量小（n=24） | 生存获益未达统计学显著性
study_object: 胃食管癌患者/粪便/粪菌移植及宏基因组测序
disease: 晚期胃食管癌伴恶病质
abstract:
PURPOSE: Cachexia is a multifactorial syndrome, associated with poor survival in patients with cancer, and is influenced by the gut microbiota. We investigated the effects of fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) on cachexia and treatment response in patients with advanced gastroesophageal cancer.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN: In a double-blind randomized placebo-controlled trial performed in the Amsterdam University Medical Center, we assigned 24 cachectic patients with metastatic HER2-negative gastroesophageal cancer to either allogenic FMT (healthy obese donor) or autologous FMT, prior to palliative chemotherapy (capecitabine and oxaliplatin). Primary objective was to assess the effect of allogenic FMT on satiety. Secondary outcomes were other features of cachexia, along with disease control rate (DCR), overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS), and toxicity. Finally, exploratory analyses were performed on the effect of FMT on gut microbiota composition (metagenomic sequencing) and metabolites (untargeted metabolomics).
RESULTS: Allogenic FMT did not improve any of the cachexia outcomes. Patients in the allogenic group (n = 12) had a higher DCR at 12 weeks (P = 0.035) compared with the autologous group (n = 12), longer median OS of 365 versus 227 days [HR = 0.38; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.14-1.05; P = 0.057] and PFS of 204 versus 93 days (HR = 0.50; 95% CI, 0.21-1.20; P = 0.092). Patients in the allogenic group showed a significant shift in fecal microbiota composition after FMT (P = 0.010) indicating proper engraftment of the donor microbiota.
CONCLUSIONS: FMT from a healthy obese donor prior to first-line chemotherapy did not affect cachexia, but may have improved response and survival in patients with metastatic gastroesophageal cancer. These results provide a rational for larger FMT trials.

title: ODFM, an omics data resource from microorganisms associated with fermented foods.
authors: Whon Tae Woong; Ahn Seung Woo; Yang Sungjin; Kim Joon Yong; Kim Yeon Bee et al.
summary_zh: ODFM整合发酵食品相关微生物的多组学数据，提供基因组、宏基因组等序列及比对分析功能，助力发酵剂筛选。
innovation: 整合发酵食品相关微生物的基因组、宏基因组、宏分类组和（宏）转录组序列 | 提供BLAST搜索和基于平均核苷酸相似性的遗传相关性测量 | 覆盖特定食品生态系统中整个微生物组的基因组
study_object: 发酵食品相关微生物（细菌、古菌、真核微生物、病毒）的基因组、宏基因组、宏分类组和（宏）转录组序列
abstract: ODFM is a data management system that integrates comprehensive omics information for microorganisms associated with various fermented foods, additive ingredients, and seasonings (e.g. kimchi, Korean fermented vegetables, fermented seafood, solar salt, soybean paste, vinegar, beer, cheese, sake, and yogurt). The ODFM archives genome, metagenome, metataxonome, and (meta)transcriptome sequences of fermented food-associated bacteria, archaea, eukaryotic microorganisms, and viruses; 131 bacterial, 38 archaeal, and 28 eukaryotic genomes are now available to users. The ODFM provides both the Basic Local Alignment Search Tool search-based local alignment function as well as average nucleotide identity-based genetic relatedness measurement, enabling gene diversity and taxonomic analyses of an input query against the database. Genome sequences and annotation results of microorganisms are directly downloadable, and the microbial strains registered in the archive library will be available from our culture collection of fermented food-associated microorganisms. The ODFM is a comprehensive database that covers the genomes of an entire microbiome within a specific food ecosystem, providing basic information to evaluate microbial isolates as candidate fermentation starters for fermented food production.

title: MicroPhenoDB Associates Metagenomic Data with Pathogenic Microbes, Microbial Core Genes, and Human Disease Phenotypes.
authors: Yao Guocai; Zhang Wenliang; Yang Minglei; Yang Huan; Wang Jianbo et al.
summary_zh: 构建MicroPhenoDB数据库，整合微生物与疾病表型及核心基因关联，支持宏基因组数据快速分析。
innovation: 首个详细描述病原微生物、核心基因与疾病表型关系的数据库平台 | 提供无需常规宏基因组数据处理和组装的序列搜索功能 | 基于证据指标开发了优先排序关联的评分模型
study_object: 人类多个身体部位/微生物组/宏基因组数据
abstract: Microbes play important roles in human health and disease. The interaction between microbes and hosts is a reciprocal relationship, which remains largely under-explored. Current computational resources lack manually and consistently curated data to connect metagenomic data to pathogenic microbes, microbial core genes, and disease phenotypes. We developed the MicroPhenoDB database by manually curating and consistently integrating microbe-disease association data. MicroPhenoDB provides 5677 non-redundant associations between 1781 microbes and 542 human disease phenotypes across more than 22 human body sites. MicroPhenoDB also provides 696,934 relationships between 27,277 unique clade-specific core genes and 685 microbes. Disease phenotypes are classified and described using the Experimental Factor Ontology (EFO). A refined score model was developed to prioritize the associations based on evidential metrics. The sequence search option in MicroPhenoDB enables rapid identification of existing pathogenic microbes in samples without running the usual metagenomic data processing and assembly. MicroPhenoDB offers data browsing, searching, and visualization through user-friendly web interfaces and web service application programming interfaces. MicroPhenoDB is the first database platform to detail the relationships between pathogenic microbes, core genes, and disease phenotypes. It will accelerate metagenomic data analysis and assist studies in decoding microbes related to human diseases. MicroPhenoDB is available through http://www.liwzlab.cn/microphenodb and http://lilab2.sysu.edu.cn/microphenodb.

title: Intestinal Virome Signature Associated With Severity of Nonalcoholic Fatty Liver Disease.
authors: Lang Sonja; Demir Münevver; Martin Anna; Jiang Lu; Zhang Xinlian et al.
summary_zh: 研究NAFLD患者粪便病毒组变化，发现病毒多样性降低与疾病严重程度相关，并构建了预测模型。
innovation: 首次研究NAFLD患者肠道病毒组变化 | 构建了基于病毒多样性指数和临床变量的预测模型，AUC达0.95 | 病毒多样性数据显著改善仅基于临床或细菌多样性的模型
study_object: 人类/肠道/粪便病毒组，鸟枪法宏基因组测序
disease: 非酒精性脂肪性肝病（NAFLD），包括肝硬化和纤维化
sample_size: n=73例NAFLD患者，9例无肝病对照，13例轻度原发性胆汁性胆管炎患者
abstract:
BACKGROUND & AIMS: Alterations in the gut microbiome have been associated with the severity of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). Previous studies focused exclusively on the bacteria in the microbiome; we investigated changes in the viral microbiome (virome) in patients with NAFLD.
METHODS: In a prospective, cross-sectional, observational study, we extracted RNA and DNA virus-like particles from fecal samples from 73 patients with NAFLD: 29 patients had an NAFLD Activity Score (NAS) of 0-4, 44 patients had an NAS of 5-8 or liver cirrhosis (LCI), 37 patients had F0-F1 fibrosis, and 36 patients had F2-F4 fibrosis. As controls, 9 individuals without liver disease and 13 patients with mild primary biliary cholangitis were included in the analysis. We performed shotgun metagenomic sequencing of virus-like particles.
RESULTS: Patients with NAFLD and NAS 5-8/LCI had a significant decrease in intestinal viral diversity compared with patients with NAFLD and NAS 0-4 or control individuals. The presence of more advanced NAFLD was associated with a significant reduction in the proportion of bacteriophages compared with other intestinal viruses. Using multivariate logistic regression analysis with leave-1-out cross validation, we developed a model, including a viral diversity index and simple clinical variables, that identified patients with NAS 5-8/LCI with an area under the curve of 0.95 (95% confidence interval, 0.91-0.99) and F2-F4 fibrosis with an area under the curve of 0.88 (95% confidence interval, 0.80-0.95). Addition of data on viral diversity significantly improved multivariate models, including those based on only clinical parameters or bacterial diversity.
CONCLUSIONS: In a study of fecal viromes from patients with NAFLD and control individuals, we associated histologic markers of NAFLD severity with significant decreases in viral diversity and proportion of bacteriophages. We developed a model based on fecal viral diversity and clinical data that identifies patients with severe NAFLD and fibrosis more accurately than models based only on clinical or bacterial data.

title: Identification of Cartilage Microbial DNA Signatures and Associations With Knee and Hip Osteoarthritis.
authors: Dunn Christopher M; Velasco Cassandra; Rivas Alexander; Andrews Madison; Garman Cassandra et al.
summary_zh: 对膝髋骨关节炎患者及对照软骨进行16S rRNA测序，发现微生物DNA特征改变与骨关节炎相关。
innovation: 首次刻画关节软骨微生物DNA图谱 | 发现人软骨微生物特征与小鼠品系特异性特征一致 | 重建宏基因组功能谱并关联代谢通路变化
limitation: 需要进一步研究这些DNA特征的建立及潜在致病作用
study_object: 人类及小鼠关节软骨样本，16S rRNA基因深度测序
disease: 膝骨关节炎、髋骨关节炎
sample_size: 人类：膝OA 21例侵蚀和21例完整样本，髋OA 34例侵蚀和33例完整样本，尸体对照10例膝和10例髋样本；小鼠：B6和MRL品系及无菌B6对照
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Alterations of the gut microbiota have been implicated in many forms of arthritis, but an examination of cartilage microbial patterns has not been performed. This study was undertaken to characterize the microbial DNA profile of articular cartilage and determine changes associated with osteoarthritis (OA).
METHODS: We performed 16S ribosomal RNA gene deep sequencing on eroded and intact cartilage samples from knee OA patients (n = 21 eroded and 21 intact samples) and hip OA patients (n = 34 eroded and 33 intact samples) and cadaver controls (n = 10 knee samples and 10 hip samples). Microbial DNA diversity was assessed, groups were compared, and metagenomic profiles were reconstructed. Confirmation was performed in an independent cohort by clade-specific quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Findings in human cartilage were compared to those in cartilage from OA-susceptible C57BL/6 (B6) mice and OA-resistant MRL/MpJ (MRL) mice. Germ-free B6 mouse cartilage was analyzed as a methodologic control.
RESULTS: Alpha diversity was reduced in human OA versus control samples (P < 0.0001), and in hip versus knee samples (P < 0.0001). Numerous clades were different in human OA versus control samples, and similar findings were noted in comparisons of murine B6 versus MRL mice. Hip samples were microbiologically distinct from knee samples. OA microbial DNA demonstrated increased gram-negative constituents (P = 0.02). Functional analysis demonstrated increases in lipopolysaccharide production (P = 9.9 × 10-3 ), phosphatidylinositol signaling (P = 4.2 × 10-4 ), and nitrogen metabolism (P = 8 × 10-3 ) and decreases in sphingolipid metabolism (P = 7.7 × 10-4 ) associated with OA.
CONCLUSION: Our study reveals a microbial DNA signature in human and mouse cartilage. Alterations in this signature, including increases in gram-negative constituents, occur during the development and progression of human OA. Furthermore, our findings indicate that strain-specific signatures exist within mouse cartilage that mirror human patterns. Further study of the establishment and potential pathogenic role of these DNA signatures is needed.

title: Alterations in Fecal Microbiomes and Serum Metabolomes of Fatigued Patients With Quiescent Inflammatory Bowel Diseases.
journal: Clinical gastroenterology and hepatology : the official clinical practice journal of the American Gastroenterological Association
authors: Borren Nienke Z; Plichta Damian; Joshi Amit D; Bonilla Gracia; Peng Vincent et al.
summary_zh: 研究静息期IBD患者疲劳相关的粪便微生物组和血清代谢组变化，发现疲劳者微生物多样性降低、产丁酸菌减少及血清代谢物改变。
innovation: 同时整合粪便宏基因组和血清代谢组/蛋白质组分析疲劳相关改变 | 发现疲劳相关微生物组与血清代谢物耗竭的关联
limitation: 仅50例患者提供粪便样本进行宏基因组测序 | 未描述
study_object: IBD患者/粪便和血清/宏基因组测序和代谢组学
disease: 静息期炎症性肠病（克罗恩病和溃疡性结肠炎）伴疲劳
abstract:
BACKGROUND & AIMS: Fatigue is frequent and disabling in patients with inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD) but its mechanisms are poorly understood. We investigated alterations in fecal microbiomes and serum metabolomes and proteomes in patients with quiescent IBD, with vs without fatigue.
METHODS: We performed a prospective observational study of patients (44% women; mean age, 39.8 y) with clinically and endoscopically quiescent Crohn's disease (n = 106) or ulcerative colitis (n = 60) at a tertiary hospital, from March 2016 through December 2018. Fatigue was assessed using the functional assessment of chronic illness therapy-fatigue scoring system and defined as a score of 43 or less. We performed metabolomic analysis of serum samples using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry methods and proteomic analysis using multiplex proximity extension assay (PEA) technology. Stool samples were obtained from 50 patients and analyzed by shotgun metagenomic sequencing on Illumina HiSeq platform.
RESULTS: Of the 166 study participants, 91 (55%) were fatigued. Serum samples from patients with fatigue (n = 59) did not have significant increases in levels of inflammatory cytokines compared with serum samples from nonfatigued patients (n = 72). We found a statistically significant difference in a cluster of 18 serum metabolites between patients with fatigue (n = 84) vs without fatigue (n = 72) (P = .033); serum samples from patients with fatigue had significant reductions in levels of methionine (P = .020), tryptophan (P = .042), proline (P = .017), and sarcosine (P = .047). Fecal samples from patients with fatigue had a less diverse gut microbiome, with significant reductions in butyrate-producing bacteria, including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii (P = .0002, q =.007) and Roseburia hominis (P = .0079, q = 0.105). This fatigue-like microbiome was associated with fatigue scales and correlated with progressive depletion of metabolites from serum samples.
CONCLUSIONS: In an analysis of fecal and serum samples from 166 patients with IBD, we found alterations in serum metabolites and fecal microbes that were associated with fatigue.

title: Genomic and serologic characterization of enterovirus A71 brainstem encephalitis.
authors: Leon Kristoffer E; Schubert Ryan D; Casas-Alba Didac; Hawes Isobel A; Ramachandran Prashanth S et al.
summary_zh: 利用mNGS和VirScan检测儿童脑干脑炎患者样本，提高肠道病毒A71中枢神经系统检出率并分析其基因组特征。
innovation: 联合mNGS与CSF泛病毒血清学(VirScan)显著提高EV中枢检测率 | 发现VP1蛋白S241P替换仅存在于一名患者的中枢神经系统 | 基因组分析确认 outbreak EV-A71与神经侵袭性德国EV-A71株密切关联
study_object: 儿童脑干脑炎/脑膜炎患者 + 脑脊液、血浆、粪便、鼻咽样本 + mNGS和VirScan
sample_size: n=20脑脊液、n=9血浆、n=15粪便、n=16鼻咽样本（来自10例脑干脑炎和10例脑膜炎/脑炎儿童）；n=12病例脑脊液和n=54对照脑脊液用于VirScan
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: In 2016, Catalonia experienced a pediatric brainstem encephalitis outbreak caused by enterovirus A71 (EV-A71). Conventional testing identified EV in the periphery but rarely in CSF. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) and CSF pan-viral serology (VirScan) were deployed to enhance viral detection and characterization.
METHODS: RNA was extracted from the CSF (n = 20), plasma (n = 9), stool (n = 15), and nasopharyngeal samples (n = 16) from 10 children with brainstem encephalitis and 10 children with meningitis or encephalitis. Pathogens were identified using mNGS. Available CSF from cases (n = 12) and pediatric other neurologic disease controls (n = 54) were analyzed with VirScan with a subset (n = 9 and n = 50) validated by ELISA.
RESULTS: mNGS detected EV in all samples positive by quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) (n = 25). In qRT-PCR-negative samples (n = 35), mNGS found virus in 23% (n = 8, 3 CSF samples). Overall, mNGS enhanced EV detection from 42% (25/60) to 57% (33/60) (p-value = 0.013). VirScan and ELISA increased detection to 92% (11/12) compared with 46% (4/12) for CSF mNGS and qRT-PCR (p-value = 0.023). Phylogenetic analysis confirmed the EV-A71 strain clustered with a neurovirulent German EV-A71. A single amino acid substitution (S241P) in the EVA71 VP1 protein was exclusive to the CNS in one subject.
CONCLUSION: mNGS with VirScan significantly increased the CNS detection of EVs relative to qRT-PCR, and the latter generated an antigenic profile of the acute EV-A71 immune response. Genomic analysis confirmed the close relation of the outbreak EV-A71 and neuroinvasive German EV-A71. A S241P substitution in VP1 was found exclusively in the CSF.

title: GMrepo: a database of curated and consistently annotated human gut metagenomes.
authors: Wu Sicheng; Sun Chuqing; Li Yanze; Wang Teng; Jia Longhao et al.
summary_zh: GMrepo数据库通过统一注释和人工管理人类肠道宏基因组数据，支持按表型查询和访问，以促进数据再利用。
innovation: 使用先进工具集一致注释微生物内容并人工管理宿主元数据 | 提供图形化查询构建器支持定制复杂查询 | 预计算物种/属相对丰度、流行率和共现信息并通过可编程接口访问
study_object: 人类肠道宏基因组和扩增子
sample_size: 58,903个人类肠道样本/运行（包括17,618个宏基因组和41,285个扩增子），来自253个项目，涉及92种表型
abstract: GMrepo (data repository for Gut Microbiota) is a database of curated and consistently annotated human gut metagenomes. Its main purpose is to facilitate the reusability and accessibility of the rapidly growing human metagenomic data. This is achieved by consistently annotating the microbial contents of collected samples using state-of-art toolsets and by manual curation of the meta-data of the corresponding human hosts. GMrepo organizes the collected samples according to their associated phenotypes and includes all possible related meta-data such as age, sex, country, body-mass-index (BMI) and recent antibiotics usage. To make relevant information easier to access, GMrepo is equipped with a graphical query builder, enabling users to make customized, complex and biologically relevant queries. For example, to find (1) samples from healthy individuals of 18 to 25 years old with BMIs between 18.5 and 24.9, or (2) projects that are related to colorectal neoplasms, with each containing >100 samples and both patients and healthy controls. Precomputed species/genus relative abundances, prevalence within and across phenotypes, and pairwise co-occurrence information are all available at the website and accessible through programmable interfaces. So far, GMrepo contains 58 903 human gut samples/runs (including 17 618 metagenomes and 41 285 amplicons) from 253 projects concerning 92 phenotypes. GMrepo is freely available at: https://gmrepo.humangut.info.

title: A novel faecal Lachnoclostridium marker for the non-invasive diagnosis of colorectal adenoma and cancer.
authors: Liang Jessie Qiaoyi; Li Tong; Nakatsu Geicho; Chen Ying-Xuan; Yau Tung On et al.
summary_zh: 研究通过宏基因组学发现粪便Lachnoclostridium菌属m3标志物，并在两个亚洲队列中验证其对结直肠腺癌和腺瘤的无创诊断价值。
innovation: 发现粪便Lachnoclostridium菌属m3作为结直肠腺瘤无创诊断的新型细菌标志物 | 在独立亚洲队列中验证m3对腺瘤的诊断性能优于粪便免疫化学试验（FIT） | 联合m3、Fn、Ch、Bacteroides clarus和FIT对结直肠癌诊断性能最佳
study_object: 人类粪便样本，宏基因组学和靶向定量PCR
disease: 结直肠腺瘤和结直肠癌
sample_size: n=1012（274例结直肠癌、353例腺瘤、385例对照）
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: There is a need for early detection of colorectal cancer (CRC) at precancerous-stage adenoma. Here, we identified novel faecal bacterial markers for diagnosing adenoma.
DESIGN: This study included 1012 subjects (274 CRC, 353 adenoma and 385 controls) from two independent Asian groups. Candidate markers were identified by metagenomics and validated by targeted quantitative PCR.
RESULTS: Metagenomic analysis identified 'm3' from a Lachnoclostridium sp., Fusobacterium nucleatum (Fn) and Clostridium hathewayi (Ch) to be significantly enriched in adenoma. Faecal m3 and Fn were significantly increased from normal to adenoma to CRC (p<0.0001, linear trend by one-way ANOVA) in group I (n=698), which was further confirmed in group II (n=313; p<0.0001). Faecal m3 may perform better than Fn in distinguishing adenoma from controls (areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) m3=0.675 vs Fn=0.620, p=0.09), while Fn performed better in diagnosing CRC (AUROCs Fn=0.862 vs m3=0.741, p<0.0001). At 78.5% specificity, m3 and Fn showed sensitivities of 48.3% and 33.8% for adenoma, and 62.1% and 77.8% for CRC, respectively. In a subgroup tested with faecal immunochemical test (FIT; n=642), m3 performed better than FIT in detecting adenoma (sensitivities for non-advanced and advanced adenomas of 44.2% and 50.8% by m3 (specificity=79.6%) vs 0% and 16.1% by FIT (specificity=98.5%)). Combining with FIT improved sensitivity of m3 for advanced adenoma to 56.8%. The combination of m3 with Fn, Ch, Bacteroides clarus and FIT performed best for diagnosing CRC (specificity=81.2% and sensitivity=93.8%).
CONCLUSION: This study identifies a novel bacterial marker m3 for the non-invasive diagnosis of colorectal adenoma.

title: Gut microbiome patterns in a multi-ethnic Asian population within a shared urban environment
authors: Zhou R; Shen X; Mina TH; Agrawal KR; Low DY et al.
abstract: The gut microbiome composition varies across human populations, but its characteristics and determinants in a multi-ethnic setting remain incompletely understood. Singapore, a multicultural city-state, provides a context in which culturally diverse groups share a broadly similar built environment. Using the Health for Life in Singapore (HELIOS) cohort, we profiled the gut microbiome of ethnic Chinese, Indian, and Malay participants (n = 861) residing in the country. These ethnicity-diet-microbiome relationships were further evaluated using data from two independent Malaysian cohorts (n = 544), a cohort from the United States (n = 210), and an in vitro microbial culture model. Each group displayed ethnicity-associated microbial patterns that paralleled culturally rooted dietary habits. Specifically, ethnic Indian participants showed enrichment of multiple Bifidobacterium species associated with greater intake of traditional grain-based staples such as idli and thosai; ethnic Malay participants exhibited higher abundance of Ruminococcaceae associated with coconut- and rice-based dishes; and ethnic Chinese participants had greater levels of Bacteroides associated with seafood- and meat-rich diets. These ethnicity-diet-microbiome relationships showed directionally consistent genus-level Bifidobacterium patterns in the Malaysian and US cohorts, as well as experimental support from an in vitro microbial culture model. Analysis of fecal microbiome-based risk scores revealed signature-dependent ethnic patterns in colorectal neoplasia scores. Together, these findings characterize gut microbiome variations across major Asian ethnicities residing in a shared urban environment, and provide a reference for precision health strategies in multi-ethnic Asian populations and other urban settings where culturally diverse communities share similar built environments.

title: Gut microbiome-based interventions to prevent ICU-acquired infections: A systematic review and meta-analysis
authors: Townsend EC; Fisch SA; Yip NH; Freedberg DE.
abstract: Gut microbiome colonization with potential pathogens is common and often precedes clinical infection in the intensive care unit (ICU). Two key gut microbiome-based interventions seek to prevent infections yet use opposite approaches: selective digestive decontamination (SDD) utilizes antibiotics to eliminate potential pathogens, whereas biotic supplementation (prebiotics, probiotics, or synbiotics) aims to enrich beneficial microbes. In the absence of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) directly comparing these two interventions, this systematic review and meta-analysis sought to compare the effect sizes of SDD versus biotic interventions for mortality and infection-related outcomes. We searched PubMed for RCTs published between 2000 and 2025. Eligible studies recruited adult ICU patients, assessed SDD or biotics against a comparator (standard care or placebo), and reported on mortality and/or acquired infection-related outcomes. Pooled relative risks (RR) were calculated using random-effects models. Nine SDD trials involving 19,907 subjects and 29 biotic supplementation trials involving 5,483 subjects were included. When compared versus standard care or placebo, neither intervention significantly reduced overall mortality (SDD: RR = 0.96 [95%CI: 0.88-1.05]; biotics: RR = 0.93 [95%CI: 0.87-1.00]).SDD was associated with modestly lower observed risk for ICU acquired all-cause infections compared to biotics (SDD: RR = 0.76 [95%CI: 0.60-0.98]; biotics: RR = 0.82 [95%CI: 0.64-1.05], no statistically significant difference) and specifically lower risk for pneumonia (SDD: RR = 0.50 [95%CI: 0.26-0.96]; prebiotics and synbiotics: RR = 0.70 [95%CI: 0.54-0.90]). In conclusion, neither SDD nor biotics was significantly protective for mortality, but both types of interventions showed similarly promising protective associations with infections, especially pneumonia. The studies selected were heterogeneous, especially those testing biotic interventions.

title: Gut Holdemania filiformis raises brain isoallopregnanolone in progesterone-treated female mice
authors: Brandon-Mong GJ; Chou CH; Hsiao TH; Wu TY; Wang PH et al.
abstract: Neuroactive 5α-steroids modulate γ-aminobutyric acid type A (GABAA) receptor signaling and are of growing therapeutic interest: allopregnanolone (3α,5α) is a positive allosteric modulator, whereas its 3β-epimer isoallopregnanolone antagonizes this action and is itself in clinical development. Their formation has been attributed to host enzymes in the liver, gastrointestinal tract, and central nervous system, whereas a contribution from any individual gut bacterium has not been demonstrated. Steroid 5α-reduction is an unusual microbial activity: among sequenced bacterial genomes, only 18 encode a recognizable steroid 5α-reductase. All available Holdemania genomes encode one of these (BaiJ-like, type 2), forming a clade distinct from the characterized Clostridium scindens BaiJ (type 1), together with a 3β-hydroxysteroid oxidoreductase. We therefore asked whether colonization with a single defined bacterium can measurably add to the host 5α-steroid pool. Consistent with this gene pair, anaerobic H. filiformis cultures converted progesterone principally to isoallopregnanolone, accumulating the intermediate 5α-dihydroprogesterone under sub-optimal conditions. In antibiotic-treated female C57BL/6 mice receiving oral progesterone, colonization with H. filiformis significantly increased isoallopregnanolone in cecal contents and brain, whereas hepatic allopregnanolone and isoallopregnanolone were unchanged. Brain isoallopregnanolone rose only in mice given both progesterone and H. filiformis, and [3,4-13C₂]progesterone tracing showed that the brain pool derived from the orally administered substrate rather than from endogenous progesterone. These findings identify Holdemania as a gut microbial source of isoallopregnanolone acting alongside host intestinal, hepatic, and cerebral steroidogenesis, and nominate H. filiformis as a candidate for microbiome-based modulation of host neuroactive 5α-steroid levels.

title: Modulation of neuroimmunity by early-life microbiota colonization
authors: Chao Gong; Xiaojun Tao; Daiyin Tian
abstract: Early life (fetal period to 2-3 y postnatally) is a critical window for the coordinated development of the intestine, lungs, and brain. As core pathways mediating microbe-immune-neuron crosstalk, the gut-brain and lung-brain axes drive cross-organ communication via early-life microbiota colonization, profoundly shaping immune maturation and neurodevelopmental trajectories. During fetal development, maternal microbial metabolites cross the placenta to prime in utero immune and neural development. After birth, rapid microbial colonization occurs in the intestine and lungs. Through signaling molecules including short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), tryptophan metabolites, and bacterial extracellular vesicles (BEVs), coupled with vagal nerve and mucosal immune pathways, the microbiota maintains intestinal and pulmonary immune homeostasis, preserves blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, and modulates microglial activation, thereby regulating neurogenesis, synaptic pruning, and brain functional programming. Early-life dysbiosis is commonly associated with preterm birth, cesarean delivery, infection, and antibiotic exposure. In human observational studies, it accompanies disrupted organ homeostasis and neuroinflammatory signatures, and is linked to an increased long-term risk of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and intellectual disability; in neonatal animal models, it aggravates hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) and encephalopathy of prematurity. Because dysbiosis frequently co-occurs with prematurity, infection, and other confounders, these associations do not by themselves establish causality. This review summarizes early-life colonization patterns of intestinal and pulmonary microbiota and their underlying neuroimmune mechanisms, analyzes the impacts of dysbiosis on neuroimmunity and related diseases, and proposes intervention strategies, aiming to provide a theoretical basis for neonatal health protection and neurodevelopmental disorder prevention.

title: Dysregulated microbiota-gut-brain axis induced by intermittent access to palatable food is associated with binge-like eating regardless of obesity development
authors: Aeschlimann L; Nassirnia S; Bouzourene N; Clavien C; Bangerter M et al.
abstract: Recurrent consumption of energy dense palatable foods contributes to the rising prevalence of obesity and can also promote loss-of-control eating in a subset of individuals. Obesity is commonly associated with peripheral inflammation, impaired sensitivity to appetite-regulating hormones, and alterations in gut microbiota composition, all of which may exacerbate binge-eating behaviors. However, emerging evidence suggests that repeated exposure to palatable foods alone can induce maladaptive eating patterns even prior to the development of obesity. In this study, intermittent access to palatable food (e.g., cheesecake) induced binge-like eating behavior in non-obese female rats, accompanied by hypothalamic microglial reactivity and altered leptin signaling pathway. Additionally, even sporadic exposure to palatable food was sufficient to alter gut microbiota composition, increasing microbial diversity and promoting taxa adapted to high fat and sugar availability, including potential pathobionts (e.g., Escherichia, Streptococcus, and Clostridium spp.) as well as carbohydrate-fermenting bacteria such as Bifidobacterium and Roseburia. Notably, increased microbial diversity was associated with both hyperphagic behavior and reduced hypothalamic leptin pathway responsiveness. Overall, these findings suggest that gut microbiota imbalance and central neuroimmune adaptations occurred in the absence of significant weight gain. This highlights the potential value of early interventions which may represent promising candidate strategies for future investigation.

title: Mapping the genetic landscape of microbial lipid transformation in the intestinal microbiome
authors: Valk LC; Ruigrok RAAA; Timmerman H; Björk JR; Li Q et al.
abstract: Dietary lipids are a key component in our diet, and fats and their derivatives have been associated with both beneficial as well as adverse effects on host health. However, the contribution of the gut microbiome to lipid metabolism remains understudied. Recognizing the importance of this interplay, we conducted extensive literature reviews to identify key bacterial genes involved in lipid metabolism, and created 88 Hidden Markov Models to allow rapid and accurate identification of these genes in genome and metagenome data. We applied these models to over 1000 metagenomes representative of the small intestine and colon, from both population-based and disease cohorts (LLDeep, MetaCardis and 1000IBD) to determine their lipolytic capacity. We observed that microbiome community types (enterotypes) carry different lipolytic potential. Serum levels of conjugated and sulfonated secondary bile acids were significantly associated with increased abundance of sterol-sulfonation genes (cysC, cysD and BtSULT). Small-intestinal communities were enriched in lipid genes compared to the colonic microbiota, underscoring the importance of microbial lipid metabolism in the small intestine compared to the colon. Overall, we demonstrate the value of our lipid metabolism models for functional microbiome profiling. Additionally, our study suggests that microbial activity in the upper gut might play a direct role in shaping host lipid metabolism, with potential implications for cardiometabolic health.

title: Microbiome changes following immigration: Rethinking "Westernization" as an explanatory concept
authors: Sharma R; Holcomb LE; Ishaq SL; O'Doherty KC.
abstract: An emerging focus in microbiome science is on changes to people's microbiomes following immigration, particularly to so-called Western countries, such as the USA, Canada, and Australia. Moving to these regions has been linked to microbiome changes that may increase immigrants' susceptibility to health problems, including obesity and Inflammatory Bowel Disease. The term "Westernization" (and adjacent terminology) is frequently used to describe changes in diet, lifestyle, and built environment - and the consequent microbiome shifts - associated with immigration. However, what Westernization means in this context, and whether it is an appropriate descriptor, is often unclear. The purpose of this article is to provide a review of the diverse meanings associated with the terms "West", "Western", "Westernization" (and similar) across microbiome-related research and broader uses. We argue that these terms can obscure the specific structural, environmental, and cultural factors shaping microbiome changes. We discuss the consequences of this imprecision and provide recommendations for future research. Avoiding oversimplified conclusions about what impacts immigrants' microbiome and health can contribute to more accurate targets for public health interventions for these groups in the long term.

title: Human cognitive performance-associated gut microbiota influences learning and memory in mice through arginine and pterin metabolism
authors: Tracey H; Antolín A; Teichenne J; Jones OAH; Van TTH et al.
abstract: The human gut microbiome undergoes changes across the lifespan and has been implicated in age-related decline. The symbol digit modalities test (SDMT) is a measure of information processing speed and is sensitive to mild cognitive impairment. Here, we assessed SDMT scores and fecal shotgun metagenomics in older individuals from the Imageomics cohort (n = 867) and performed fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) from human donors to male C57BL/6 mouse recipients. In mice, we evaluated cognitive performance using the Morris water maze (MWM) and measured neurone density, fecal shotgun metagenomics, hippocampal metabolomics, and cortical gene expression to identify microbial-derived functional properties related to cognitive performance. In humans, both microbial species composition and functional profiles were associated with cognitive performance. FMT from high-SDMT donors improved cognitive performance and increased neuronal density in recipient mice compared with FMT from low-SDMT donors. In both humans and mice, higher cognitive performance was associated with arginine and proline metabolism and pterin-related pathways. In mice receiving microbiota from high-SDMT donors, cortical gene expression showed enrichment of dopamine receptor pathways and reduced dopamine reuptake and catecholamine biosynthesis. Our findings highlight the potential role of the gut microbiome in cognitive performance among older individuals, particularly information processing speed, and identify potential mechanisms involving alterations in arginine and pterin metabolism. Integrating human and mouse data supports a model in which microbiota-associated metabolic remodeling influences cognitive performance.

title: Impact of Ruminococcus gnavus on lipid metabolism via isoCDCA
authors: Peng YL; Xiao YY; Yin SJ; Zhou HH; Zhang W et al.
abstract: The gut microbiota is increasingly recognized as a regulator of host lipid metabolism, yet the specific strains and effector metabolites driving hyperlipidemia remain poorly defined. Here, we identified Ruminococcus gnavus (R. gnavus) as a candidate contributor to cholesterol-related dyslipidemia and delineated its metabolic mechanism. Comparing individuals with high versus normal TC/LDL-C (HTL vs NTL) in both normal-weight and overweight populations, we found that fecal R. gnavus was enriched in HTL individuals regardless of BMI stratum, a finding validated by species-specific qPCR in an independent cohort (n = 488). Administering R. gnavus to mice fed a normal or high-fat diet induced alterations in circulating lipids and liver function markers, accompanied by hepatic steatosis. Hepatic transcriptomics and targeted bile acid profiling converged on bile acid metabolism: R. gnavus downregulated key hepatic genes (Cyp7a1, Cyp8b1, Ldlr, and Ppara) and elevated isochenodeoxycholic acid (isoCDCA) levels both in vivo and in vitro. In vitro, R. gnavus directly converted chenodeoxycholic acid (CDCA) to isoCDCA. Clinically, serum isoCDCA was elevated in HTL individuals in an independent cohort (n = 1,137) and was positively associated with TC, TG, and LDL-C. Functionally, oral isoCDCA supplementation reproduced key lipid disturbances in mice, and isoCDCA downregulated lipid metabolism genes and promoted lipid accumulation in hepatocytes; heterologous expression of R. gnavus hydroxysteroid dehydrogenases conferred isoCDCA-producing capacity on E. coli and elevated circulating TC and LDL-C in colonized mice. These findings nominate isoCDCA as a microbial effector metabolite linking R. gnavus to hepatic lipid dysregulation and identify the R. gnavus-isoCDCA axis as a potential target for the prevention and treatment of hyperlipidemia.

title: Colonoscopy-based Clostridioides difficile screening for inflammatory bowel disease patients
authors: Allegretti JR; Carlin A; McClure E; Delaney M; Bry L.
abstract: Patients with IBD have an increased risk for Clostridioides difficile infection, and the significance of asymptomatic colonization is poorly understood. Overlapping symptoms often complicate diagnosis, and there is a lack of validated screening methods. Colonic wash aspirates collected during routine colonoscopies may offer a convenient screening option. We aimed to evaluate culture methods for detecting C. difficile colonization in IBD patients using colonic wash samples. Patients with Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis undergoing outpatient colonoscopy were enrolled. Clinical characteristics, IBD activity indices, and endoscopic scores were recorded. Colonic wash aspirates were centrifuged and cultured on selective CHROMID® media with and without broth enrichment. Isolates were confirmed by Gram stain and MALDI-TOF. PCR/qPCR identified tcdB gene carriage. Whole-genome sequencing was performed on selected isolates, and associations between clinical factors and colonization were assessed. Of the 121 patients enrolled, 10.7% (13/121) were colonized. Crohn's patients were colonized more frequently than ulcerative colitis patients (13.3% CD, 8.2% UC). Among colonized patients, 53.8% (7/13) had C. difficile with detectable tcdB. Enrichment increased detection compared to direct plating. No clinical predictors of colonization were identified, but wash samples yielded sufficient DNA for sequencing with comparable depth to whole stool. Colonoscopy wash aspirates allow for the detection of asymptomatic C. difficile colonization in IBD. This screening method may provide a useful tool for investigating the prevalence, persistence, and clinical significance of C. difficile colonization in IBD and for informing future studies of CDI prevention.

title: Bacteroides uniformis-generated ornithine alleviates alcohol-associated liver disease via Sirt4-mediated mitochondrial regulation
authors: Shu H; Zhang M; Zhou H; Ji J; Hu P et al.
abstract: Gut microbiota plays a pivotal role in alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD), yet the contributions of individual bacterial strains and their metabolites remain poorly defined. Here, we analyzed 16S rDNA sequencing data from an ALD patient cohort and validated the findings using the NIAAA mouse model combined with multi-omics approaches. Bacteroides uniformis was significantly depleted in ALD patients, and supplementation with live B. uniformis alleviated ALD in mice by reducing hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and oxidative stress. Metabolomic analysis identified ornithine as a key metabolite produced by B. uniformis, and direct ornithine administration largely recapitulated the protective effects. Mechanistically, ornithine upregulated hepatic Sirt4, thereby restoring mitochondrial homeostasis, whereas pharmacological inhibition of Sirt4 abolished these effects. Dietary flaxseed oil increased intestinal B. uniformis abundance and hepatic Sirt4 expression, ameliorating ALD outcomes. These findings reveal a B. uniformis-ornithine-Sirt4 axis that modulates ALD via mitochondrial regulation and highlight potential microbial and metabolic therapeutic targets.

title: β-glucan mitigates necrotizing enterocolitis-induced long-term cognitive impairment by remodeling gut microbiota and restoring tryptophan metabolite IAA-mediated gut-brain signaling
authors: Zhang X; Cao H; Zhang Y; Shi Y.
abstract: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is a life-threatening gastrointestinal disorder prevalent in preterm infants, and most NEC survivors suffer from persistent cognitive deficits and neurodevelopmental disorders, with no targeted therapeutic approaches available to date. β-glucan has been documented to regulate gut microbiota, suppress inflammation, and exert neuroprotective effects, yet its efficacy and molecular mechanisms against NEC-associated cognitive dysfunction remain unclear. In this study, we established a mouse NEC model with β-glucan intervention to explore its gut-brain axis protective effects. Behavioral assessments verified that β-glucan significantly rescued NEC-induced cognitive impairments, with comparable therapeutic effects between low and high doses. Multi-omics analyses demonstrated that β-glucan effectively reversed NEC-triggered gut microbiota dysbiosis and restored disrupted tryptophan metabolism, notably elevating the level of indole-3-acetic acid (IAA). Fecal microbiota transplantation and exogenous IAA supplementation recapitulated the neuroprotective phenotypes of β-glucan, which inhibited excessive hippocampal microglial activation and neuroinflammation, and repaired impaired synaptic ultrastructure and plasticity. Further mechanistic validation confirmed that IAA mediated neuroprotection via activating the AHR/MAP2K3/p38 signaling cascade. Collectively, β-glucan alleviates NEC-related cognitive injury through modulating the gut microbiota-tryptophan metabolism-IAA axis and subsequent AHR/MAP2K3/p38 signaling activation. This study elucidates a novel gut‒brain axis regulatory mechanism of β-glucan, providing reliable preclinical evidence for the clinical prevention and treatment of long-term neurodevelopmental complications in NEC survivors.

title: Fecal neuraminidase correlates with inflammatory signatures and microbiome shifts in preclinical Crohn's disease
authors: Mu K; Dang CP; Xue M; Li Q; Huynh HQ et al.
abstract: The mucus layer, rich in mucin glycoproteins, serves as a critical barrier to microbial invasion. Neuraminidases cleave terminal sialic acids from mucin glycans, a process that may influence mucus integrity, epithelial exposure to microbial antigens, and mucosal immune responses, making fecal neuraminidase activity a biologically relevant functional readout of host-microbe interactions in the context of Crohn's disease (CD) pathogenesis. We evaluated whether fecal neuraminidase activity is associated with future CD risk and examine its relationships with inflammatory and microbial signatures relevant to early disease development. Within the prospective GEM cohort, 69 individuals who later developed CD were matched to 69 healthy first-degree relative controls. Fecal neuraminidase activity was measured using a fluorometric assay. Conditional logistic regression assessed its association with future CD risk. Partial Spearman correlations evaluated relationships with 446 serum proteins (OLINK), followed by pathway enrichment analysis, and with fecal calprotectin (FCP) and gut microbial composition (16S rRNA sequencing). Fecal neuraminidase activity was positively associated with future CD (OR = 1.541; 95% CI: 1.05-2.25; p = 0.026). Proteins correlated with neuraminidase activity were enriched in immune and inflammatory pathways. Neuraminidase activity was positively correlated positively with FCP (p ≤ 0.05), and its association with future CD was attenuated after adjustment for FCP. Fourteen microbial taxa were significantly correlated with neuraminidase activity (q ≤ 0.05). Fecal neuraminidase activity's relationships with inflammatory markers and microbial taxa support its potential relevance as a functional marker of host-microbe alterations during preclinical CD.

title: Gut‒liver‒brain axis signature of cirrhosis-related cognitive impairment is consistent across multi-national cohorts
authors: Sommer AJ; Kiudeliene E; Lauridsen M; Torre A; Fagan A et al.
abstract: Cognitive impairment in cirrhosis is associated with an altered gut‒liver‒brain axis, but geographic variations in diet and clinical practices may limit generalizability. We investigated consistency of microbial signatures for cirrhosis-related cognitive impairment across four countries. We enrolled outpatients with cirrhosis from USA, Denmark, Lithuania, and Mexico who underwent Psychometric Hepatic Encephalopathy Score (PHES) testing for covert hepatic encephalopathy (CHE), and stool shotgun metagenomic sequencing. Taxonomic and functional associations with PHES were evaluated after adjustment for MELD, country, demographics, sex, proton pump inhibitor (PPI), lactulose, and rifaximin use. We enrolled 221 patients (median age 58 y, 57.9% men, median MELD 12). Cognitive performance varied by country despite adjustment for clinical covariates. Lithuania demonstrated greater microbial richness and better cognition despite higher MELD, accompanied by distinct dietary patterns including greater yogurt and tea consumption. In the entire cohort, increasing MELD was associated with reduced microbial richness and depletion of commensals. Worse PHES performance, however, showed a distinct microbiome signature with increased Streptococcus abundance independent of MELD, country, PPI use, and HE therapies. Twenty-two microbial pathways were associated with PHES, mostly related to amino-acid biosynthesis and nitrogen metabolism. Of these, ornithine degradation and heme B biosynthesis II were uniquely enriched with worse PHES and CHE, which mapped onto Enterobacteriaceae. We conclude that across four geographically and culturally disparate countries, cirrhosis-related cognitive impairment was associated with consistent microbial compositional and functional alterations distinct from advancing liver disease. These findings support a consistent gut‒liver‒brain axis signature involving oral-gut translocation and altered nitrogen metabolism.

title: Lactylated MOESIN links gut metabolism to TGF-β-driven immune remodeling and bone protection in diabetic osteoporosis
authors: Lu J; Wang X; Zhou S; Zhang J; Fu Q et al.
abstract: Diabetic osteoporosis is characterized by impaired bone homeostasis and immune dysregulation. We investigated how fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) modulates microbial metabolism, immune signaling, and bone remodeling using a pilot clinical cohort and diabetic mouse models. The clinical component was treated as a safety/feasibility study with exploratory longitudinal BMD and serum biomarker endpoints. In experimental DOP models, FMT improved bone microarchitecture and reduced inflammatory and bone-resorption markers. Descriptive analysis of external PBMC scRNA-seq data (GSE274561) provided immune-cell context, while an independently replicated external splenic CD4+ T-cell dataset (GSE267853; CONT n = 3, DM n = 3) provided disease-context support for Treg/Th17 and TGF-β/SMAD dysregulation. Replicated flow cytometry, RT-qPCR, Western blot, and functional perturbation experiments supported FMT-associated restoration of the Treg/Th17 balance and activation of lactate-MOESIN-TGF-β signaling in the experimental models.

title: Surface-functionalized Bifidobacterium bifidum alleviates Clostridioides difficile infection by coordinating host immune modulation and gut microbiota restoration☆
authors: Yang H; Wu W; Wang L; Zhang R; Villafuerte Gálvez JA et al.
abstract: Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) is a major ecological disruption of the gut ecosystem, characterized by loss of colonization resistance, persistent inflammatory feedback and incomplete microbial recovery. Meta-analysis of clinical cohorts identified Bifidobacterium depletion as a conserved feature of CDI-associated dysbiosis, suggesting that restoring this genus may promote recovery from CDI. Comparative in vitro assays identified B. bifidum as the most protective strain. This effect was not attributable to direct inhibition of C. difficile growth, but instead was associated with strong adhesion to intestinal mucus and epithelial cells and direct competition for epithelial attachment sites. However, B. bifidum alone was insufficient to counteract host inflammation and showed limited survival during gastrointestinal transit. To address these constraints, we integrated B. bifidum with β-hydroxybutyrate (BHB) to mitigate inflammation-associated habitat filtering and applied an outer hyaluronic-acid (HA) coating to protect B. bifidum viability and confer preferential targeting to the colon and inflamed mucosa. This sequential strategy, termed BB@PCB-HA, markedly alleviated inflammation and restored epithelial barrier integrity, microbial community structure and metabolic function in both CDI and recurrent CDI mouse models. These findings advance probiotic therapy from strain supplementation to programmable functionalized microecological intervention, providing a new paradigm for treating CDI and other gastrointestinal diseases.

title: Microbial metabolites and MAMPs: orchestrators of intestinal stem cell function
authors: Shekhar S; Šrůtková D; Schwarzer M.
abstract: Intestinal stem cells (ISCs) are essential for maintaining and regenerating the intestinal epithelium. Recent studies have highlighted the critical role of the gut microbiota in regulating ISC function through diverse molecular signals, particularly microbial metabolites and microbe-associated molecular patterns (MAMPs). Microbial metabolites, such as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) and indoles, modulate ISC activities by influencing proliferation, differentiation, and overall epithelial renewal. MAMPs, such as lipopolysaccharide (LPS) and peptidoglycan-derived muramyl dipeptide (MDP), interact with pattern recognition receptors (PRRs), including Toll-like receptors (TLRs) and nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain (NOD)-like receptors (NLRs), affecting ISC proliferation and epithelial regeneration. In this review, we discuss emerging evidence on how these microbial signals regulate ISC function and elucidate the mechanisms underlying epithelial renewal and tissue repair. A comprehensive understanding of these host-microbe interactions holds therapeutic potential for enhancing epithelial regeneration and restoring gut homeostasis, paving the way for novel regenerative medicine strategies.

title: Integrated multi-omics analysis reveals distinct metabolic signatures and gut microbiome alterations across the pediatric obesity spectrum
authors: Arredondo-Hernandez R; Orduña P; Schcolnik-Cabrera A; Castillo-Rojas G; López-Filloy M et al.
abstract: Pediatric obesity drives extensive metabolic remodeling across gut and systemic compartments, yet integrated multi-omics characterization across the full obesity spectrum remains incomplete. We studied 57 Mexican children stratified by BMI into normal weight (NW, n = 15), overweight (Ow, n = 8), and obese (Ob, n = 34) groups using liver enzyme profiling, untargeted fecal and serum metabolomics, 16S rRNA gut microbiome sequencing, and antimicrobial resistance assessment. Demographic parameters were comparable across groups (p = 0.632), minimizing confounding. Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) showed the strongest obesity association (25.5 ± 6.0 vs. 15.0 ± 3.0 U/L in NW; p < 0.001), outperforming ALT and AST as an early hepatic stress biomarker. Metabolomic profiling identified 1088 altered fecal and 1041 altered serum metabolites (Ob vs. NW), with enriched pathways spanning aromatic amino acid metabolism, one-carbon metabolism, glycolysis/TCA cycle, and nucleotide biosynthesis. Key perturbations included upregulation of kynurenine and 3-nitrotyrosine alongside downregulation of bile acids and purine metabolites. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed 78, 95, and 28 differentially abundant taxa in Ow vs. NW, Ob vs. Ow, and Ob vs. NW comparisons, with elevated beta-diversity dispersion in obesity. Co-abundance network analysis uncovered disrupted metabolite-metabolite and taxon‒taxon interactions, including loss of beneficial SCFA-producing consortia, bile acid dysregulation, and altered amino acid-microbiome coupling. Integration of microbiome and metabolome data revealed high-magnitude genus-metabolite correlations-including Lachnospiraceae with acetate (ρ = 0.92) and Tyzzerella with vulpecholate (ρ = 0.94)-mapping to mechanistic pathways linking SCFAs, bile acids, tryptophan-indole derivatives, and aromatic amino acids to obesity pathogenesis. These findings identify GGT as a sensitive pediatric metabolic biomarker and provide mechanistic insights and therapeutic targets for early intervention.

title: A microbiota-metabolite-glial axis drives white matter repair via isorhamnetin-PSAP-GPR37 signaling after ischemic stroke
authors: Zhang Y; Qiu L; Wu J; Shi Y; Niu S et al.
abstract: Ischemic stroke (IS) induces persistent neuroinflammation and white matter injury that limit neurological recovery, yet effective repair-oriented therapies remain lacking. Although microbiota influences stroke outcomes, how microbial activity drives central nervous system repair is unclear. Here, we integrate clinical microbiome profiling, experimental stroke models, multi-omics analyses, and mechanistic validation to define a microbiota-metabolite-glial signaling axis that promotes post-stroke recovery. Akkermansia muciniphila (Akk) is associated with favorable outcomes in patients and improves recovery in mice without altering infarct size, supporting a repair-promoting rather than neuroprotective mechanism. Mechanistically, Akk increases circulating isorhamnetin (Iso), a key systemic mediator that suppresses lipid-laden, pro-inflammatory microglia and promotes oligodendrocyte maturation and white matter repair. Iso reprograms microglia to secrete PSAP, and conditioned medium-but not direct Iso-activates GPR37-ERK signaling in oligodendrocytes. In vitro knockdown of Psap or Gpr37 markedly attenuates these effects, demonstrating a microglia-dependent mechanism. In vivo adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated Gpr37 knockdown abolishes the beneficial effects of Akk and Iso on functional recovery and white matter repair, establishing the necessity of PSAP-GPR37 signaling. These findings identify a microbiota-driven metabolic pathway linking gut activity to white matter repair after IS.

title: Human milk oligosaccharides are distinctly processed by early life gut microbial sialidases
authors: Plisko OL; Chapel VS; Sekela JJ; Talbert JA; Townsend SD et al.
abstract: The infant gut microbiome in early life is shaped by numerous factors, including feeding method. Exclusively breastfed and formula-fed infants exhibit distinct microbiome compositions. While these effects are well-established, the underlying mechanisms that drive these differences are not fully understood. Here, we examine the removal of sialic acid from human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) influenced by human microbial sialidases in early life. We identify 351 and 214 unique sialidase sequences from adult and infant microbiome metagenomes, respectively, and characterize a diverse, representative set in vitro using sialylated HMOs normally present in human breastmilk. We find these proteins exhibit distinct abilities to metabolize 3'- and 6'-sialyllactose, which are the most abundant sialylated HMOs in breastmilk, and distinctly process other more complex substrates, as well. We provide structural insights into these functional differences by pinpointing active site features uniquely present in efficient enzymes and show that these results extend to activities on complex mixtures of sialylated HMOs purified from human breastmilk. Finally, we demonstrate in human clinical data that distinct profiles of sialidase-encoding bacterial taxa are observed in breastfed and formula-fed infants at 1 and 4 months of age, prior to the introduction of solid foods. Together, these findings show that specific bacterial sialidases are influential in shaping the early gut microbiome, data that may improve the supplementation of infant formulas for enhanced developmental outcomes.

title: Disease-specific gut microbiota-metabolite-immune networks in hematologic disorders: mechanisms, causal support, and translational strategies
authors: Yi L; Yuan Y; Ma X; Li C; Hao Y et al.
abstract: The gut microbiota is increasingly recognized as a systemic regulator of host immunity, host metabolism, epithelial barrier integrity, and distal tissue homeostasis. Hematologic disorders provide an important setting in which these host-microbe interactions converge on immune remodeling, marrow-niche function, hematopoietic recovery, treatment response, and transplant-related complications. This narrative review synthesizes mechanistic, clinical, and translational evidence linking gut microbial dysbiosis to benign and malignant hematologic diseases, clonal and premalignant states, and hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT)-related outcomes. Rather than treating microbiome associations as a single evidence category, we distinguish five complementary evidence strata: Mendelian randomization, experimental models, prospective human cohorts, randomized human interventions, and cross-sectional studies. These study designs address different causal questions and are interpreted as complementary rather than as a single linear hierarchy. We also separate microbial composition from microbial function: taxon-level enrichment or depletion is treated primarily as context-dependent and hypothesis-generating, whereas conserved functional pathways-including short-chain fatty acids, bile-acid transformation, tryptophan metabolism, microbial translocation and barrier dysfunction, and innate immune activation-provide the principal cross-disease mechanistic framework. We integrate disease-specific microbial features, functional mediators, immune and marrow consequences, and clinical outcomes into an author-constructed evidence map, while explicitly addressing bidirectionality, reverse causality, and translational readiness. Emerging applications include microbiota-based biomarkers, treatment-response prediction, fecal microbiota transplantation, probiotics and postbiotics, antibiotic stewardship, and microbiota-dependent modulation of drug metabolism.

title: A host-directed virulence factor of Clostridium perfringens is modulated by gut commensal strains
authors: Schumacher J; Stincone P; Rapp J; Lucas TN; Llaca-Bautista C et al.
abstract: In a healthy host, the residential microbes help regulate the growth of pathobionts, which are common members of the human gut microbiome, preventing them from causing diseases, including infections, under certain conditions. In cases of dysbiosis, this protection may be compromised. Targeted microbiome modulation offers a promising approach to restore healthy conditions in a disrupted community and consequently prevent infections using the natural colonization resistance of the microbiome. Elucidating the interaction mechanisms between microbial species within a microbiome is crucial for understanding how a microbiome can be modulated precisely and effectively to benefit the host's well-being. Here, we investigated the interactions between the pathobiont C. perfringens and human gut commensals by combining relative abundance measurements in co-culture versus monoculture with proteome and metabolome profiling of all mono- and co-cultures. We found that commensal strains affect C. perfringens growth by competing for substrates such as amino acids or a carbon source other than glucose. We further observed that Bacteroidaceae strains altered the levels of C. perfringens proteins, among others, the host-directed θ-toxin. Our findings reinforce the notion that modulating the composition of the gut microbiome is an effective strategy to prevent infections.

title: Population-scale identification of gut commensals that antagonize antibiotic-resistant pathogens
authors: Zhang Q; Chen B; Zhang Z; Ni Y; Xu N et al.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance poses a global threat, yet microbiome-encoded defenses against antibiotic resistance gene (ARG)-associated pathogens remain poorly defined. Here, we analyze 12,238 human gut metagenomes and prioritize 159 commensal species ("coexcluders") that show inverse associations with ARG-associated pathogenic taxa. These taxa carry low ARG burdens and encode candidate antimicrobial peptide repertoires. For Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, deep learning-guided mining of 2,053 genomes reveals 6,737 peptides prevalent in the human gut that inversely associate with ARG-associated pathogens. In antibiotic-perturbed mice, F. prausnitzii reduces the resistance burden and restores ecological stability, with peptide enrichment. These peptides show preferential activity against antibiotic-resistant E. coli derivatives while sparing commensals, which is consistent with a kill-the-winner dynamic. Anaerobic coculture reveals resistance-dependent peptide induction, linking the resistance phenotype to competitive suppression. This work establishes a scalable, resistance-guided framework that links population-level ecological signatures to strain-resolved microbial and molecular candidates, providing a basis for mechanistic and therapeutic development.

title: Genomic surveillance reveals age-structured SARS-CoV-2 transmission across settings
authors: Moreno GK; Brock-Fisher T; Krasilnikova LA; Schaffner SF; Burns M et al.
abstract: Understanding respiratory virus transmission requires integrating pathogen genomic data with detailed epidemiological context. We analyzed >85,000 SARS-CoV-2 genomes linked to epidemiological data collected in Massachusetts from November 2021 to January 2023. Collected in 666 settings, including schools, colleges, and skilled nursing facilities, this dataset enabled direct comparison of within-setting transmission to community-wide risk. Elevated transmission was concentrated in specific age-defined subpopulations-older adolescents in schools, undergraduates in colleges, and residents in nursing facilities-with little additional risk among other groups, notably including staff. Young adults, particularly in colleges, played a disproportionate role in spread, and new viral lineages consistently expanded first within this group. Viral spread followed reproducible urban-to-rural gradients, and vaccination was associated with reduced onward transmission. We further estimated sequencing thresholds required for timely detection of emerging variants. Together, these findings reveal consistent demographic and spatial structure in SARS-CoV-2 transmission that can inform viral respiratory pathogen genomic surveillance.

title: Closest relatives of poxviruses prevail in human and animal guts worldwide
authors: Gaïa M; Guyet U; Ruscheweyh HJ; Eren AM; Sunagawa S et al.
abstract: Large and giant double-stranded DNA viruses substantially affect eukaryotic ecology and evolution<sup>1-4</sup>. They prevail in the environment but are rarely found in the digestive system of animals<sup>5,6</sup>. Here we present the discovery of a diversified group of DNA viruses with large linear genomes, dubbed egoviruses, that comprise a putative viral order most closely related to animal-infecting poxviruses. Egoviruses are found worldwide, almost exclusively in the digestive system of humans, livestock and wild animals. The most prevalent human-specific egovirus is spread across continents, demonstrating a long-term association between egoviruses and the human gut microbiome. Eukaryotic homologues of egovirus core genes suggest that these viruses primarily infect Trichostomatia (ciliates), which assist ruminant digestive processes<sup>7</sup>, and Parabasalia (Metamonada), which influence animal immunity and gut microbiome ecology<sup>8</sup>. Egoviruses also contributed to the genetic makeup of polintons, endogenous viruses that proliferated in genomes of Trichomonas vaginalis<sup>9</sup> and its close Parabasalia relatives. Unlike poxviruses that form brick-shaped virions, egoviruses are predicted to form multilayered icosahedral capsids resembling those of asfuviruses and probably representing the ancestral virion structure. Egoviruses are the only known clade of double-stranded DNA viruses of eukaryotes prevailing in the animal digestive system. Phylogenomic analysis suggests an evolutionary scenario whereby egovirus-like ancestors of poxviruses infected anaerobic unicellular eukaryotes inside the gut of ancestral animals, before transitioning to animal cell infection, which was accompanied by the virion metamorphosis.

title: Population-level characterisation of the human gut phageome and its association with microbial metabolites
authors: Louca P; Khan Mirzaei M; Kouraki A; Khamespanah E; Lin Y et al.
abstract: Bacteriophages, viruses infecting bacteria, are abundant in the human gut, but their population-level structure and metabolic associations remain unclear Here we present a foundational characterisation of the gut phageome using deep shotgun metagenomic data in a large population-based cohort (n = 1,069: TwinsUK). We assembled 116,740 non-redundant vOTUs of which 52.9% were predicted to be temperate and 47.0% virulent. Individuals harboured an average of 3,370 vOTUs, mostly at low abundances, exhibiting structured population-level co-abundance patterns with bacterial species including Faecalibacterium prausnitzii and Blautia wexlerae. Phageome diversity was mostly driven by environmental factors, with modest heritable components. We detected 4 significant vOTU diet associations. Additionally, 6,572 phages were associated with short-chain fatty acids and secondary bile acids, identifying extensive population-level associations between phage-associated genomic variation and microbial metabolites. Over 100 vOTUs encoded auxiliary metabolic genes, while a distinct subset of phages encoded virulence-associated genes, including vacuolating autotransporter toxin (vat) and LPS glucosyltransferases (gtrA, gtrB, gtr) implicated in O-antigen modification and immune invasion, and showed consistent co-abundance patterns with bacterial species previously associated with opportunistic or pathobiont features. These results identify structured population-level associations between phage-associated genomic elements, bacterial communities, and microbial metabolites, motivating future experimental and mechanistic studies.

title: Echidna: a Bayesian framework for integrative inference of copy number alterations impacting phenotypic plasticity
authors: Fan JL; Zhang M; O'Brien W; Myers JD; Chatterjee S et al.
abstract: The ability of cells to adapt their behavior in response to genetic or environmental changes is a fundamental biological process that drives cellular diversity in both normal and pathological contexts, including in tumor evolution. Copy number alterations (CNAs), which can include large-scale changes in genomic ploidy, play a key role in creating adaptive advantages in evolving cell populations. However, tracing these populations across experiments and disentangling the role of CNAs from other sources of transcriptional variability remains challenging and expensive. Here we present Echidna, a Bayesian hierarchical model that integrates single-cell RNA sequencing and bulk whole-genome sequencing data to enable robust integrative inference of CNAs, jointly across samples and treatment time points, to better understand the impact of genomic events on cellular phenotype. Applying Echidna to patient tumor specimens, we demonstrate its superior performance in clonal reconstruction and derive insights into therapy resistance mechanisms.

title: Candidalysin: a decade of discovery
authors: Richardson JP; Griffiths JS; Moyes DL; Wilson D; Hube B et al.
abstract: Candida albicans is a globally prevalent commensal fungus and a major pathogen of humans that causes both superficial infections and lethal disease. Identifying the biological mechanisms that advance our understanding of C. albicans colonization and pathogenicity, and that may lead to disease prevention, is of critical importance. A decade ago, C. albicans was found to secrete a peptide toxin called candidalysin, the first of its kind produced by a human fungal pathogen. Here we review the first decade of candidalysin research and focus on the critical function that candidalysin plays in commensalism, infection and disease. Specifically, we discuss its role as a classical virulence factor, how it activates host immune responses in different disease models and its emerging role as a commensal factor in the gut microbiota. We outline how this decade of discovery is facilitating the development of therapeutics and what research questions are waiting to be answered.

title: Altered IgA-associated gut microbiota and serum IgA are associated with disease severity in alcohol-associated liver disease
authors: Schöler D; Hsu CL; Miwa T; Brol MJ; Freund L et al.
abstract: Background Alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD) is characterised by dysbiosis, impaired gut barrier function and microbial translocation driving hepatic inflammation. IgA, the dominant mucosal antibody, maintains intestinal homeostasis by coating bacteria. While serum IgA is elevated in advanced ALD, intestinal IgA responses and IgA-bound microbiota remain incompletely defined. Objective To define faecal and serum IgA responses and characterise IgA-bound bacterial communities across the spectrum of ALD. Design Stool and serum IgA were measured in 107 healthy controls (HCs), 191 individuals with alcohol use disorder (AUD) and 360 individuals with alcohol-associated hepatitis (AH). IgA-bound bacteria were isolated using magnetic-activated cell sorting and analysed by 16S ribosomal RNA sequencing. Results Faecal IgA increased with disease severity (AH > AUD > HC) and was associated with distinct microbial compositions. IgA-bound bacterial diversity was reduced in AH and partially recovered after abstinence. Beta diversity demonstrated separation by disease, with enrichment of pathobionts (eg, Streptococcus, Enterococcus, Escherichia/Shigella) and depletion of beneficial taxa (eg, Lachnospiraceae, Ruminococcaceae). IgA-bound taxa correlated with disease severity, with commensals showing inverse and Campylobacteraceae positive associations with Model for End-stage Liver Disease-sodium (MELD-Na). Serum IgA was elevated in AH, decreased after abstinence and did not correlate with faecal IgA. While faecal IgA was not associated with survival, higher serum IgA independently predicted reduced 6-month survival. Conclusion ALD is characterised by altered mucosal IgA responses and IgA-associated microbial alterations. The lack of correlation between faecal and serum IgA suggests regulation of mucosal and systemic IgA responses. Serum IgA may serve as a prognostic biomarker in ALD.

title: GPNMB+ fibroblasts crosstalk with gastric epithelium to activate a pro-stemness niche in gastric cancer through IGF1R/SRC/FOSL1 feedback loop
authors: Lin Z; Li Y; Li Y; Liu Z; Chen J et al.
abstract: Background Cancer stemness, characterised by SOX9 expression, drives therapeutic resistance and relapse in gastric cancer (GC), yet the mechanisms by which the tumour microenvironment (TME) regulates GC stemness remain poorly defined. Objective To compare regulatory networks associated with SOX9 expression in GC. Design We performed an integrative multi-omics analysis combining single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, bulk RNA sequencing, imaging mass cytometry and proteomics. Mechanistic validation was conducted using multiplex immunofluorescence, co-immunoprecipitation, xenograft models and fibroblast-specific Fosl1 conditional knockout (CKO) mice. Results We identified a novel subset of GPNMB+ cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), which was enriched in SOX9high GC and correlated with poor prognosis, promoted stemness via IGF1-IGF1R signalling. CAF-derived IGF1 activated IGF1R on malignant cells, inducing SRCY419 and YAP1Y357 phosphorylation, which facilitated IGF1R-SRC-YAP1 complex formation and SOX9 expression. FOSL1 transcriptionally regulated GPNMB and IGF1 expression in CAFs. Reciprocally, IGF1-stimulated malignant cells secreted AREG, activating CAF-expressed EGFR signalling. EGFR-GPNMB synergy triggered NF-κB-mediated FOSL1 upregulation, reinforcing the GPNMB+ CAF phenotype and establishing a self-reinforcing cancer stem cell niche loop. Fibroblast-specific Fosl1 CKO suppressed GC growth and stemness. Targeting IGF1 or SRC sensitised tumours to chemotherapy in vivo. Conclusions Our findings unravel the pivotal role of GPNMB+ CAFs in driving GC stemness via the IGF1R-SRC-YAP1-SOX9 signalling axis. Disrupting this axis or its upstream regulator FOSL1 offers a therapeutic strategy to ablate TME-supported stemness and overcome chemoresistance.

title: Identification and selective inhibition of patient-specific pathobionts in inflammatory bowel disease
authors: Sabachvili M; Abbott S; Thomson C; Davoli Ferreira M; Ohland C et al.
abstract: Background The microbiome has been linked to various chronic diseases. However, the congruency of proposed bacterial taxa between studies is low and identifying inflammation-driving pathobionts for personalised therapy is hampered by a complex microbiota, heterogeneous patient risk factors and technical challenges to sort and maintain viable bacteria. Objective Development of an approach that enables patient-specific identification of bacterial triggers of inflammation and their selective elimination. Design Faecal samples were collected from individual inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) patients during inflammation and remission and transferred into germ-free (GF) mice. Comparing microbiomes collected at different times from the same individual uncoupled the inflammatory capacity of the microbiome from other factors, such as genetic or environmental risk factors. Results We show that inflammatory states of patients with IBD were recapitulated on faecal microbiota transplantation and identified putative disease-driving bacterial taxa by sorting and culture of immunoglobulin-coated intestinal bacteria. Colonisation of GF mice identified Sarcina perfringens and Hathewaya massiliensis as pathobionts promoting inflammation. Mechanistically, innate immune cells required TLR1/2-MyD88 signalling to sense both pathobionts. Compared with healthy individuals, S. perfringens and H. massiliensis were enriched in ~25%–30% and ~5% of patients with IBD, respectively, across diverse populations. S. perfringens abundance was also correlated with mucosal inflammatory transcripts. Both pathobionts increased IL-8 production or reduced ZO-1 expression in IBD patient-derived organoids. Screening >1500-approved compounds revealed five molecules, including oxolinic acid, that selectively inhibited pathobiont growth and protected from intestinal inflammation. Conclusions Collectively, we developed an approach for identifying disease-driving pathobionts and selecting compounds for targeted therapy.

title: Shigella flexneri activates the mature DC-Tfh axis to drive tertiary lymphoid structure neogenesis and maturation in colorectal tumour microenvironments
authors: Zheng F; Jia W; Wang C; Weng R; Chen M et al.
abstract: Background Tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) serve as critical antitumour immune mediators within the tumour microenvironment and are associated with favourable immunotherapy outcomes and prognosis. Therefore, inducing intratumoural TLS formation represents a promising therapeutic approach. However, the mechanisms underlying their formation in colorectal cancer (CRC) remain unclear. Objective This study aims to characterise the immune landscape of TLS-enriched CRC and to identify TLS-associated microbes along with their mechanisms of action as TLS inducers. Design 16S rRNA sequencing identified TLS-associated microbial signatures. Immunocompetent mouse models validated microbial effects on TLS formation and tumour growth. Single-cell RNA sequencing, multiplex immunofluorescence and flow cytometry characterised the immune landscape. In vitro infection models assessed microbial effects on immune cells. Results Microbiome sequencing identified Escherichia coli and Shigella as TLS-correlated intratumoural microbes in CRC. In vivo models demonstrated that only Shigella flexneri (S. flexneri) colonisation promoted the formation of TLSs and significantly suppressed tumour growth. Core TLS-associated immune subsets were identified: T follicular helper cells (Tfh), germinal centre B cells and mature dendritic cells (mature DCs). Mechanistically, S. flexneri activated type I interferon signalling to drive DC maturation. Mature DCs recruit T cells via CCL19 and CXCL10, and Tfh cells further recruit B cells through CXCL13, thereby establishing structured TLSs. Conclusion This study is the first to demonstrate that S. flexneri promotes the organised formation of TLSs in CRC via a mature DC-Tfh axis-mediated chemokine network. Therapeutic strategies targeting this bacterium represent a novel paradigm for TLS induction and may contribute to immunotherapy in CRC.
