title: Degradation of mucin O-glycans by a human gut symbiont requires a complex enzyme repertoire and promotes colonization
authors: Schaus SR; Jin C; Raba G; Pereira GV; Bains R et al.
abstract: Secreted mucins are the major component of the mucus layer that protects intestinal epithelial surfaces. Mucins are complex glycoproteins decorated with over 100 different O-glycans. Some bacteria degrade mucins, contributing to disruption of the mucus barrier and inflammation. However, the enzymatic pathways by which gut bacteria degrade colonic mucin O-glycans and the impact of this process on gut colonization are unknown. Here, we identified >100 genes that are expressed by the symbiont Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron during growth on different O-glycan substrates, revealing the effects of specific glycan structures on gene expression. The characterization of 33 Bacteroides glycoside hydrolase enzymes revealed the pathway for colonic O-glycan degradation, uncovering 13 collective enzymes sufficient for mucin degradation. In vivo competition experiments showed that multiple exo-acting enzymes targeting mucin capping structures are central to gut colonization. This repertoire of Bacteroides enzymes illuminates complex mucin degradation pathways and potential targets to inhibit bacterial mucin degradation.

title: Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA
authors: Donaldson GP; Lima Dos Reis G; Saad M; Wichmann C; Mamede I et al.
abstract: Immunoglobulin A (IgA) is the most abundant antibody isotype produced by mammals, and has a specialized role in mucosal homeostasis<sup>1</sup>. IgA is constantly secreted into the intestinal lumen and binds to commensal microorganisms to regulate their colonization and function<sup>2,3</sup>, with unclear implications for health. IgA deficiency is common in humans, but difficult to study, because of its complex aetiology and comorbidities<sup>4-8</sup>. Here we use genetically and environmentally controlled mice to show that various models of IgA deficiency result in increased susceptibility to several models of endogenous colorectal cancer. Cellular and molecular analyses revealed that, in the absence of IgA, colonic epithelial cells induce antibacterial factors and accelerate cell cycling in response to the microbiota. Oral treatment with IgA was sufficient to reduce steady-state proliferation and protect mice from tumours; however, this function was due to the structure of the antibody rather than to binding specificity. In a reductionist culture system, IgA directly suppressed epithelial growth. Co-immunoprecipitation mass spectrometry and targeted CRISPR screening identified DMBT1 as an IgA-binding epithelial surface protein that is required for IgA-mediated suppression of proliferation. Together, IgA and DMBT1 tune the normal cycling of absorptive colonocyte progenitors. In IgA-knockout mice, deleting the transmembrane and cytoplasmic signalling portions of DMBT1 was sufficient to reverse both the increased epithelial cell proliferation and the increased tumour susceptibility seen in these mice. These experiments establish a homeostatic function for IgA in tempering physiological epithelial responses to the microbiota to maintain mucosal health.

abstract: The relationship between industrialization and the gut microbiome remains incompletely understood due to limitations in cohort design involving host physiology and bacterial isolates. title: In situ profiling of plasma cell clonality with image-based single-cell transcriptomics
authors: Yang E; Aceves-Salvador J; Castrillon C; Herrmann US; Akama-Garren EH et al.
abstract: Image-based single-cell transcriptomics can identify diverse cell types in intact tissues. However, in adaptive immunity, V(D)J recombination generates unique immune receptors in cells of the same type, leading to important functional variation that is not yet defined by these methods. Here we introduce B cell receptor multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (BCR-MERFISH), which measures plasma cell clonality based on V gene usage in combination with transcriptome profiling. We demonstrate that BCR-MERFISH accurately identifies V gene usage in cell culture and in mice with restricted or native plasma cell diversity. We then use BCR-MERFISH to elucidate the microbiota-dependent changes in plasma cell abundance, clonal diversity, and public clonotype usage in the mouse gut and the non-uniform distribution of plasma cell clones along the mouse ileum. Given that tissue context is an essential modulator of plasma cell dynamics, we anticipate that BCR-MERFISH may offer new insights into a wide range of immunological questions.

title: Microbial metabolism of methotrexate produces a STAT3 signaling molecule that alleviates gut inflammation
authors: Cho J; Danner R; Kim WS; Lopez L; Williams J et al.
abstract: Methotrexate (MTX) is a gold standard therapy for inflammatory diseases but has mixed therapeutic success in inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The gut microbiota impact MTX efficacy and toxicity by metabolizing MTX and altering its bioavailability, yet how inflammation alters this metabolism, and how the resulting metabolites act on the host, remain poorly understood. Here, we find that gut microbes, notably Clostridium asparagiforme, metabolize MTX via carboxypeptidase G2 (CPDG2) to produce deoxyaminopteroic acid (DAMPA). In intestinal epithelial cells, DAMPA preserves mitochondrial health through mitochondrial signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) signaling and enhances mitophagy. DAMPA administration attenuates intestinal inflammation in vivo, and remodels colonic mitochondrial pathways. IBD mouse models show reduced microbial CPDG2 and DAMPA, while patients with IBD show reduced CPDG2 gene abundance and suppressed DAMPA-enriched mitochondrial pathways, potentially explaining MTX outcomes in IBD. Together, these findings reframe microbial MTX metabolism from passive drug detoxification to active regulation of host mitochondrial and inflammatory homeostasis.

title: Targeting hormone conversion through dietary fiber improves polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome
authors: Qi X; Chen H; Nie Q; Niu H; Ding Y et al.
abstract: Excessive androgens serve as a primary driver for many phenotypic features of polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). Although dietary fiber has been shown to alleviate PMOS, its effects on androgen concentrations and the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. In a clinical trial, we demonstrated that a dietary fiber combination consisting of inulin, resistant starch, and β-glucan reduces androgen concentrations in patients' plasma. Mechanistically, dietary fiber increased the abundance of Bacteroides xylanisolvens, which converts androstenedione into a nonandrogenic secondary hormone metabolite we named coproandrosterone, which is further metabolized by gut microbiota into dihydro-coproandrosterone. This metabolic pathway was validated in a mouse model. These findings highlight the potential of dietary fiber to alleviate PMOS by modulating androgen homeostasis through gut microbiota, offering insights for prebiotic and probiotic therapies.

title: Microbiome-wide PheWAS links gut microbial SNVs to health and exposures
authors: Wang D; Goumagias A; Andreu-Sánchez S; Peng H; Ruiz-Moreno AJ et al.
abstract: Alterations in the microbial composition of the human gut have been associated with a wide range of chronic diseases<sup>1,2</sup>. Yet species-level composition alone can obscure extensive within-species genetic diversity and functional variation. This has driven a shift towards strain-resolved, genetic-level analysis of the microbiome, leveraging microbial genetic variation to identify disease-relevant genes and pathways<sup>3-6</sup>. Here we conducted a phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) analysing 12.8 million gut microbial single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) with 244 host health phenotypes and environmental exposures in 10,781 individuals from 6 independent cohorts. We identify 940 independent associations across 69 host factors, including age, sex and cardiovascular and metabolic parameters. Structural analyses identified host-phenotype-associated SNVs in functionally important regions of proteins, findings that inform mechanistic hypotheses about how microbial genetic changes relate to environmental and host physiological factors. For example, we identified an age-associated SNV in Faecalibacterium prausnitzii that affects an amino acid within the protein pocket that binds glutathione. To support future efforts, all study summary statistics are provided in an online catalogue ( https://fulab.web.rug.nl/SNV-MWAS/ ). Together, these results identify new biological connections between the human host and microbial genetic variants at base pair resolution and provide a resource for hypothesis generation that will aid future understanding of the strain-level functionality of the gut microbiota.

title: Engineering commensal Lachnospiraceae for programmable therapeutic delivery in the mouse gut
authors: Arnold J; McClure S; Glazier J; Shakya S; Jansen Z et al.
abstract: Engineered native gut bacteria could offer persistent, programmable therapeutic delivery in the gut, but many dominant taxa remain genetically intractable. Members of one such family of obligate anaerobic Clostridia, Lachnospiraceae, are prevalent in the human gut microbiome and produce metabolites linked to intestinal and metabolic health. Here we report a modular toolkit for engineering Lachnospiraceae, including constitutive and inducible expression, chromosomal integration and secretion systems. Applying this toolkit to gut native Coprococcus comes, we programmed the secretion of cytokine interleukin-22 (IL-22) in the mouse intestinal tract, where it induces epithelial defence transcriptional programmes. In a mouse model of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, IL-22-secreting C. comes improved glucose homeostasis, reduced systemic endotoxemia and attenuated hepatic steatosis. This work demonstrates that native Lachnospiraceae can be genetically programmed to modulate host metabolic and immune physiology. The toolkit provides a foundation for the development of Lachnospiraceae-derived engineered therapeutics and for dissecting causal relationships between commensal gene programmes and host physiology.

title: Overconsumption of low-digestible sugars can increase susceptibility to Salmonella Typhimurium infection
authors: Nguyen BD; Wotzka SY; Maier L; Fetz C; Steiger Y et al.
abstract: Low-digestible carbohydrates (LDCs), including dietary fibers and sugars that resist absorption, are generally considered beneficial for the gut microbiota. However, we show that acute overconsumption of certain LDCs, particularly low-digestible sugars (LDSs), such as arabinose, lactulose, and polyols commonly used as sugar substitutes, can compromise colonization resistance against the common foodborne pathogen Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium. LDS overconsumption results in elevated fecal pathogen loads, systemic dissemination, and colitis in infected mice. Mechanistic analysis of arabinose overconsumption revealed that rapid fermentation acidifies the intestinal environment, perturbs the microbiota, alters gut-luminal short-chain fatty acid levels and elevated amino acid availability, which can support pathogen growth. Additionally, this perturbation impacts virulence by broadening tissue tropism (e.g. expansion to small intestine) and selecting for invasive Salmonella. Unlike antibiotic perturbations, Salmonella colonization requires SPI-1 and SPI-2 Type-III-secretion systems, linking virulence to pathogen fitness. These findings reveal how dietary perturbations can impact the gut ecosystem in ways that not only compromise colonization resistance but also enhance pathogen virulence.

title: Metabolic specialization in the gut microbiome of aquatic mammalian herbivores
authors: Persinoti GF; Martins MP; Silva CBC; Streit RSA; Paixão DAA et al.
abstract: Sirenians, such as manatees, are the only extant mammals fully adapted to aquatic herbivory. Through specialized hindgut fermentation, they play a role in modulating nutrient fluxes and carbon cycling across tropical coastal and riverine ecosystems. However, our understanding of their gut microbiome and its metabolic potential remains elusive. Here we present an ultradeep genomic atlas of the gut microbiome from 47 freshwater and marine manatees spanning distinct developmental stages, comprising 1,215 non-redundant prokaryotic metagenome-assembled genomes and their associated virome. The manatee microbiome encodes a multilayered enzymatic repertoire for plant cell wall deconstruction, including free enzymes, cellulosomes and CAZyme-enriched outer membrane vesicles, alongside diverse pathways for aromatic catabolism. Combining biochemical and structural approaches, we characterize a previously unrecognized enzymatic pathway involving epilactase, which enables a specific Bacillota species to exploit a carbohydrate inaccessible to most microbial life, defining a specialized biochemical strategy for nutrient niche partitioning. Together, these findings uncover the microbial and metabolic basis of aquatic mammalian herbivory.

title: Convergent genomic evolution of human gut bacteria along an industrialization gradient
authors: Rühlemann M; Ma Y; Szánthó LL; Waschina S; Moitinho-Silva L et al.
abstract: Whether human-associated environments drive adaptive genome evolution in gut commensal bacteria remains largely unknown. Here, we investigate how genomic adaptation in gut bacteria differs between industrialized and non-industrialized human populations. We generated a collection of isolate genomes spanning diverse host geographies, lifestyles, species, and strains. We first found that, compared with metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), paired isolate genomes recover more functional elements and signals of horizontal gene transfer (HGT). Leveraging isolate genomes from multiple species, we find that strains from industrialized hosts experience an expansion of proteome size and harbor greater pangenome fluidity, driven by recent HGT events. Gene- and variant-level analyses reveal convergent patterns of lifestyle-specific adaptation in functions that are critical for ecological adaptation, such as the stress response, cell-envelope remodeling, and central metabolism. Our results demonstrate that industrialization drives convergent genome evolution in gut bacteria, providing a framework for understanding the mechanisms of microbial adaptation to rapidly changing human environments.

title: Industrialization drives convergent microbiome and host physiological shifts in the human metaorganism
authors: Poyet M; Rühlemann M; Schaan AP; Ma Y; Moitinho-Silva L et al.
abstract: Understanding how industrialization reshapes the human metaorganism requires integrating microbiome ecology with host physiology across globally diverse populations. Here, we generate multivariate data from the Global Microbiome Conservancy cohort, including gut microbiome, immunoglobulin A (IgA) sequencing, host genotyping, diet, lifestyle, and fecal biomarker profiles, to investigate host-microbiome interactions across gradients of industrialization and geography. We show that industrialization is associated with homogenized microbial compositions, reduced microbial diversity, and lower community stability, independent of host confounders. We further show that industrialization is linked to elevated markers of gut stress, increased IgA secretion, and altered patterns of IgA-bacteria interactions. Finally, we show that microbiome-based disease predictors trained on industrialized populations are uninformative in less industrialized cohorts, highlighting limited cross-population transferability. Together, our results reveal coordinated restructuring of the microbial ecosystem and host physiology and emphasize the need for inclusive, globally representative data to improve translational microbiome applications across diverse human populations.

title: A haplotype reference panel constructed from 490,319 UK Biobank genomes improves genotype imputation for global populations
authors: Wienbrandt L; Prieß C; Schmöhl M; Neff V; Gretsova M et al.
abstract: Here we constructed a genotype imputation reference panel from whole-genome sequencing data from 490,319 UK Biobank (UKB) participants<sup>1</sup> and enabled both standalone and cloud-based phasing and imputation through EagleImp<sup>2</sup> and EagleImp-RAP within the UK Biobank Research Analysis Platform. The UKB reference panel achieves lower phasing switch error rates than the widely used TOPMed r3 panel (133,597 individuals) for all global superpopulations except AMR and for 25 of 26 1000 Genomes Project subpopulations. Imputation accuracy, measured by MAE, improved for 4 of 5 superpopulations and 12 subpopulations for variants with minor allele frequencies down to 0.01%. Estimated squared correlation further improved across all 5 superpopulations and 22 subpopulations, with the largest gains in East and South Asian populations. Reimputation of COVID-19 genome-wide association study datasets from Italy, Germany, Spain and Norway<sup>3,4</sup> demonstrated that common-variant imputation remains unsaturated, enhancing the discovery of genome-wide significant loci and improving fine-mapping resolution.

title: Planetary-scale metagenomic analysis reveals CRISPR targeting dynamics across ecosystems
authors: Roux S; Neri U; Bushnell B; Fremin BJ; George NA et al.
abstract: Interactions between microorganisms and their mobile genetic elements (MGEs), including viruses and plasmids, impact microbiome dynamics. CRISPR-Cas systems are important regulators of these host-MGE interactions, but a global understanding of the diversity, activity and roles of CRISPR spacers across Earth's biomes is still lacking. Here we develop a computational approach to search short-read data and collect 794 million CRISPR spacers across 367,609 public metagenomes, from which we identified 1.18 billion hits between 41 million spacers and 2.5 million viruses and plasmids. While spacers were highly variable across samples, those matching known viruses were more prevalent and conserved, consistent with a positive selection pressure associated with phage targeting. Among these, however, we find evidence suggestive of recurrent entry of phage genomes into non-host microbial cells, further blurring the line between CRISPR targeting and virus-host interactions. These results highlight key drivers of CRISPR targeting patterns likely to influence strain-level diversification and selection processes in microbiomes.

title: Rare and common genetic variants shape single-cell immune gene expression
authors: Cuomo ASE; Spenceley E; Tanudisastro HA; Bowen B; Henry A et al.
abstract: Understanding the genetic basis of gene expression can shed light on the regulatory mechanisms underlying complex traits and diseases<sup>1,2</sup>. Single-cell-resolved measures of RNA levels and single-cell expression quantitative trait loci have revealed genetic regulation that drives cell states and types across diverse tissues<sup>3</sup>. Here we describe phase 1 of TenK10K, which leverages single-cell RNA sequencing data from more than 5 million cells across 28 immune cell types, along with matched whole-genome sequencing data from 1,925 individuals. This provides power to detect associations for rare and low-frequency genetic variants that have largely been uncharacterized in their impact on cell-specific gene expression. We map the effects of both common and rare variants in a cell-type-specific manner using a recent method that increases power by modelling single cells directly rather than aggregated 'pseudobulk' counts. We identify putative common regulatory variants for 83% of all 21,404 genes tested and cumulative rare-variant signals for 47% of those genes. We explore how genetic effects vary across cell types and states, develop a framework to determine the degree of single-cell expression quantitative trait loci cell-type specificity and show that about half of the effects are observed only in one or a few cell types. By integrating our results with functional annotations and disease information, we further characterize the likely molecular modes of action for many disease-variant associations. Finally, we explore the effects that genetic variants have on gene expression across continuous cell states, and effects that vary cell-state abundance directly.

title: Genetic variants shape single-cell chromatin accessibility and disease risk
authors: Xue A; Fan J; Dong OA; Huang HL; Chen L et al.
abstract: Understanding how genetic variation shapes gene regulation at single-cell resolution is crucial for elucidating complex disease mechanisms<sup>1</sup>, but has been limited by the lack of large-scale single-cell multi-omics data<sup>2-4</sup>. Here we present single-cell assay for transposase-accessible chromatin with sequencing of 3.5 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells from 1,042 donors with matched whole-genome sequencing. Across 28 immune cell types, we tested 440,996 chromatin accessibility peaks and identified 243,225 chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTLs) at 100,483 peaks, 60% of them cell-type specific. Rare variant analysis identified 38,161 associated peaks, with predicted transcription factor-binding disruption implicated at individual loci. Colocalization with expression QTLs (eQTLs) from single-cell RNA sequencing data (5.4 million peripheral blood mononuclear cells)<sup>5</sup> defined 28,834 candidate cis-regulatory elements. Across genome-wide association studies for 16 diseases and 44 blood traits, caQTLs colocalized 4.5-22.6% more signals than eQTLs alone. Cell-type-specific and tissue-specific context, distal effects and multi-causal-variant models raised genome-wide association study-eQTL concordance from approximately 16% to approximately 65%. Cell state further modulates genetic effects, with 27% of over 200,000 caQTL-cell-state interactions lacking a main effect. At the inflammatory bowel disease risk gene ADCY7, accessibility effects varied with genotype and G protein-mediated pathway activity in CD4<sup>+</sup> T cells. A graph neural network trained on both eQTL and caQTL layers inferred peak-gene links in unpaired multiome data with up to 17.2% higher accuracy than QTL-agnostic data, uncovering 128 additional transcription factor-target pairs (22% increase). Together, these results show that genetic variants shape chromatin accessibility in a cell-type-specific and cell-state-specific manner, influencing immune function and disease risk.

title: Gastric microbiota-mediated immune remodelling in gastric cancer
authors: Gao J; Lau HC; Fuhler GM; Yu J.
abstract: Increasing evidence indicates that the gastric microbiota plays crucial roles in regulating the tumour microenvironment (TME), influencing gastric tumourigenesis and progression. Several bacteria, including Streptococcus, Lactobacillus and Bacteroides, have shown robust immunomodulatory effects on TME. In this review, we summarise current understanding of the crosstalk between the gastric microbiota and TME in gastric cancer (GC). Functional alterations of the gastric microbiota from healthy mucosa to malignancy are delineated, with emphasis on the impacts of bacteria on different immune cell populations in gastric tumours, such as CD8+ T cells, macrophages, dendritic cells and regulatory T cells. The immunomodulatory roles of microbial metabolites and pathogen-associated molecular patterns in shaping immune cell infiltration, cytokine profiles and checkpoint molecule expression are also explored. While immune checkpoint blockade (ICB) has emerged as a promising treatment of various cancers, its efficacy in GC remains unsatisfactory due to the immunosuppressive gastric TME. We therefore evaluate the intricate interplays between the gastric microbiota and immunotherapy, and suggest potential microbiota-targeting strategies (eg, microbiota modulation, probiotics supplementation and combination therapies) to enhance antitumour immune response and boost ICB efficacy. We conclude by highlighting current challenges and providing future directions for microbiota research in GC. Overall, a deeper understanding of host-microbe interactions can provide promising avenues for precision medicine and the development of microbiota-targeting interventions against GC.

title: Stage-dependent gut microbiome and functional signatures across the liver disease spectrum: an integrative multicohort study
authors: Vázquez-Castellanos JF; Yoon SJ; Won SM; Raes J; Kwon HC et al.
abstract: BACKGROUND: The gut-liver axis plays a critical role in liver disease progression; however, how gut microbial ecology and function vary across disease stages remains unclear. OBJECTIVE: To define stage-specific microbial and functional signatures and evaluate their diagnostic potential. DESIGN: We analysed faecal samples from 1168 individuals spanning healthy controls, fatty liver, hepatitis, cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma by 16S rRNA sequencing, with a subset (n=141) profiled by shotgun metagenomics. To increase statistical power and enable external validation, 2376 publicly available metagenomic datasets, including 734 liver-related, were integrated. Machine learning-based multicohort analysis was used to identify microbial biomarkers, assess risk factors and classify disease stages. RESULTS: Microbial diversity declined and a low-richness enterotype expanded with disease severity. Machine learning revealed a discordance in hepatitis, which lacked taxonomic markers but was defined by a conserved functional signature of biosynthetic upregulation. In contrast, advanced stages featured consistent markers like Ligilactobacillus and Veillonella, with strain-level evidence confirming oral-gut transmission. Functional profiling delineated a metabolic continuum from anabolic precursor synthesis in hepatitis to virulence factor production in cirrhosis and putrefactive metabolism in carcinoma. Comparative analysis confirmed that these signatures were distinct from those in non-liver metabolic and oncologic disorders. Importantly, the expansion of oral-derived Veillonella spp and the low-richness enterotype were significantly associated with increased mortality. CONCLUSION: This large-scale study delineates stage-dependent ecological and functional remodelling of the gut microbiome across liver diseases. These findings highlight the potential of microbiome-based markers for non-invasive diagnosis and prognostic risk stratification in liver diseases.

title: Genomic surveillance meets clinical practice: rule-based individualized treatment prediction for gonorrhoea using SensiTyper
authors: Golparian D; Sánchez-Busó L; Unemo M.
abstract: Extensively drug-resistant (XDR) Neisseria gonorrhoeae strains threaten the current empirical gonorrhoea treatment. We designed and analytically validated SensiTyper, a rule-based framework that predicts antimicrobial susceptibility from whole-genome sequencing data and generates susceptibility-guided individualized treatment recommendations. SensiTyper was applied to 13,701 gonococcal genomes from 68 countries in 1928-2024, including cultured isolates and clinical molecular samples, and benchmarked predictions against previous genomic and phenotypic data. Susceptibility predictions for ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin, spectinomycin, and zoliflodacin had 98.9-100% sensitivity and specificity. Azithromycin susceptibility predictions had 92.5% sensitivity and 97.1% specificity, and gepotidacin susceptibility prediction 100% sensitivity, but 0% specificity, illustrating that low-level phenotypic gepotidacin resistance is not caused by the only known resistance determinants (GyrA A92T plus ParC D86N). The SensiTreat module integrates antimicrobial susceptibility profiles into sequential treatment logic, providing susceptibility-guided individualized treatment recommendations while also enabling alternative stewardship strategies prioritizing, e.g., ciprofloxacin. SensiTyper flags XDR isolates for expert follow-up, test-of-cure and comprehensive contact tracing. In conclusion, SensiTyper is a robust and adaptable approach for gonococcal antimicrobial susceptibility prediction, individualized gonorrhoea treatment and antimicrobial stewardship.

title: A human gut-associated picobirnavirus establishes the Picobirnaviridae as the third clade of RNA bacteriophages
authors: Gan T; Rosen AL; Wang L; Vernon S; Droit L et al.
abstract: Picobirnaviruses (PBVs) are commonly detected RNA viruses in human and animal guts and are associated with multiple human diseases. Although PBVs have been assumed to infect vertebrate hosts, there is neither direct evidence for this nor any culture system to propagate PBVs. Here we demonstrate that a PBV infects bacteria and is therefore an RNA phage. Two different PBVs from human faeces were propagated in germ-free mice after faecal microbiota transplantation, establishing a mouse model for PBV. One PBV could be cultured in vitro, in a community of anaerobic gut bacteria, and its growth could be inhibited by multiple antibiotics. RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization revealed PBV RNA within bacterial cells, and enrichment and sequencing of PBV RNA-containing cells identified a previously unidentified 'Candidatus Anaerotignum faecalis' as its host. Our findings define the family Picobirnaviridae as only the third clade of RNA phages in addition to leviviruses and cystoviruses.

title: Systemic exposure to typhoid toxin primes the murine vascular endothelium for intestinal perforation during Salmonella Typhi infection
authors: Zhao H; Hua C; Hur JI; Lara-Tejero M; Galán JE.
abstract: Intestinal perforation is a late complication and the leading cause of death in typhoid fever, but its mechanism has remained undefined. Here, using sequential exposure to the PltC form of typhoid toxin followed by oral Salmonella Typhi infection, we develop a mouse model of late-stage human typhoid, when circulating toxin precedes the onset of intestinal pathology. Systemic exposure to the toxin renders otherwise resistant mice susceptible to oral infection and establishes a transient vascular endothelial priming state, resulting in vascular injury, haemorrhage and lethal intestinal perforation localized to Peyer's patches. These lesions were accompanied by the appearance in blood of microbiota-derived taxa, consistent with translocation across a breached small-intestinal barrier. Lethality required the SPI-1 type-III secretion system (T3SS), which drives intestinal inflammation, but not the SPI-2 T3SS, which drives systemic infection, indicating that death results from intestinal rather than disseminated infection. Although PltC-typhoid toxin causes leucopaenia, loss of circulating white cells was not sufficient for sensitization. Endothelial-specific expression of CMAH, which masks the toxin's Neu5Ac receptors, prevented priming and disease. These findings define intestinal perforation as a typhoid toxin-dependent vascular-barrier disease.

title: Antimicrobial peptides derived from Nemuri induce ribosomal condensation to inhibit translation
authors: Nishinami S; Hasan M; Niwa T; Inui T; Yokoyama T et al.
abstract: Antibiotic resistance is a global health threat requiring antimicrobials with alternative modes of action. Growing evidence indicates that bacteria organize key intracellular processes through biomolecular condensates and other forms of spatial organization, yet whether such spatial organization can be exploited as an antimicrobial target remains unclear. Here, we identify intrinsically disordered antimicrobial peptides, generated from the Drosophila sleep-inducing protein Nemuri, that inhibit bacterial growth by targeting ribosomal organization. Mechanistically, these peptides enter bacterial cells without overt membrane disruption and accumulate in ribosome-rich regions, where they bind broadly to RNA and ribosomal surfaces through multivalent interactions. This engagement remodels ribosome-rich regions into condensates with reduced ribosomal mobility, thereby suppressing global protein synthesis and distinguishing these peptides from canonical site-specific ribosome-targeting antibiotics. Furthermore, Nemuri-derived peptides exhibit broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, including activity against drug-resistant pathogens, with low cytotoxicity toward Drosophila and mammalian cells. Together, our findings identify the organization and material dynamics of bacterial ribosomes as a biophysical vulnerability that can be exploited by antimicrobial peptides, revealing how a naturally evolved metazoan host-defense system turns intracellular organization itself into an antibacterial target.

title: Widespread selection of antibiotic resistance within hospital sewers
authors: Gray DA; Nhung NT; Coertze RD; Ekwanzala MD; Waters N et al.
abstract: Environmental microbiomes are sources of diverse antibiotic resistance determinants that can be mobilized and transferred to human pathogens under a selection pressure from antibiotics. Hospital sewers contain more antibiotics than most environments and are thus increasingly recognised as potential arenas for resistance evolution. However, it is unknown if resistance selection occurs there and what the drivers are. Here we show selection of antibiotic-resistant bacteria within Swedish hospital sewers. Evidence include; consistent selection of multiple resistances in Escherichia coli exposed to filtered wastewater from ten hospitals, but not to corresponding municipal wastewaters; in-situ enrichment of resistant over sensitive E. coli from wastewater to sewer biofilms at hospitals, but not at municipal sites; and higher resistance in bacteria collected from hospital sewers than from municipal sites as assessed by culturing and metagenomics. Evidence for drivers includes complete rescue of sensitive E. coli by addition of resistance genes to fluoroquinolones and β-lactams, and cellular effects typical for β-lactams. Measured concentrations by liquid-chromatography-tandem-mass-spectrometry compared to selective thresholds identify ciprofloxacin and cefotaxime as principal selective agents. Antibiotic concentrations and use data allow extrapolation of risks beyond Sweden. Given the absence of detectable selection at municipal sites, mitigations of risks in hospital sewers should be prioritized.

title: Microbial products trigger chemosensory dialogues through intestinal G protein-coupled receptors
authors: Kadoki M; Nanki K; Szamosvári D; Mohamed AMT; Stražar M et al.
abstract: Organismal reactions to changing environmental conditions require information relays that sense cues and elicit appropriate responses. G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), including olfactory receptors, comprise the largest receptor family that recognizes environmental cues, consisting of over 800 genes in the human genome. Here, by screening libraries of gut metabolites and natural products using a multiplexed GPCR reporter system, GPCR-seq, we reveal multiple intestinal chemosensory pathways. Among these, we determine that a cyclic fatty acid promotes serotonin production from enterochromaffin cells via olfactory receptor OR51E1. Two additional gut microbe-derived molecules, a β-carboline and 6-hydroxynicotinic acid (6-HNA), function as agonists for GPR35, a receptor linked to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The IBD-associated GPR35 risk variant, T108M, shows aberrant responses to 6-HNA, while Enterocloster bolteae, a species increased in IBD, generates high levels of 6-HNA. This approach provides an accelerated path to mapping critical chemosensory pathways and host physiological responses.

title: Perinatal elimination of genetically aberrant human cortical neurons
authors: Shao DD; Zhao Y; Brew J; Adla Y; Ghosh U et al.
abstract: Human neurons are postmitotic and long-lived, requiring precise genomic regulation. Normal neuronal function is highly dosage-sensitive, with copy number variants (CNVs) and heterozygous point mutations associated with a host of neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric conditions<sup>1-4</sup>. Here we investigated somatic CNVs arising in single neurons to understand the dynamic processes that shape the normal neuronal genetic landscape. Altogether, we sequenced 2,357 single neurons from human postmortem brain from fetal to postnatal life. Two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches-Tn5-transposase-based amplification (1,526 neurons, 16 individuals) and primary template amplification<sup>5</sup> (831 neurons, 12 individuals)-showed that an average of 25.9% [12.7-46%] of prenatal cortical neurons have highly aberrant genomes, that is, widespread CNVs involving multiple chromosomes. This proportion reduced by about 4.5-fold after birth across the two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches (Fisher meta-analysis P = 3.5 × 10<sup>-</sup><sup>6</sup>). Neurons with widespread CNVs were mainly eliminated perinatally, timed roughly parallel to periods of programmed cell death<sup>6</sup>, whereas neurons with smaller CNV burdens declined slowly in frequency with postnatal age. CNVs in surviving neurons were depleted for dosage-sensitive genes and genes involved in neurodevelopmental disorders (hypergeometric test P < 0.05), suggesting selective elimination of neurons with these CNVs. Analysis of 44,861 nuclei with single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (snATAC) and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) showed that neurons with high CNV burdens exhibited abnormal synaptic gene expression, suggesting that abnormal synaptic gene regulation contributes to neuronal elimination. Elimination of defective neuronal genomes might represent an important developmental genome quality-control process that may be vulnerable in neurodevelopmental disease, and suggests purifying selection during human neurodevelopment.

title: Clostridium perfringens Delta toxin targets CD9 to drive NEC and brain injury
authors: Zhang S; Gong X; Tian S; Yang Y; Tong X et al.
abstract: Necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC) is the most devastating gastrointestinal emergency in preterm infants, frequently causing mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental impairment<sup>1,2</sup>. Although the gut microbiota has been implicated in NEC pathogenesis<sup>3-5</sup>, the microbial factors driving NEC and the following brain pathology remain unclear. Here we identify Clostridium perfringens pathobionts containing Delta toxin in the gut microbiome of individuals with severe and fatal NEC. Clinically, infected infants show worse outcomes, including aberrant systemic inflammation, severe neurological damage and coagulopathy. We establish a mouse model in which Delta-toxin-positive C. perfringens infection, or Delta toxin exposure alone, recapitulates clinical features of NEC, including intestinal necrosis and acute cerebral injury. Mechanistically, Delta toxin preferentially targets macrophages, potently activating inflammasome signalling and pyroptosis, triggering a rapid inflammatory cascade that compromises blood-brain barrier integrity and drives neuroinflammation. Through a genome-wide CRISPR screen, we identify the tetraspanin CD9 as the host receptor for Delta toxin. Using systemic, myeloid-specific and intestinal-epithelial-specific Cd9-knockout mice, we show that systemic and myeloid Cd9 ablation protects mice against toxin-induced lethality, blood-brain barrier dysfunction and multiorgan injury, whereas epithelial Cd9 deletion shows partial protection, implicating macrophage targeting as a primary driver of C. perfringens CD9-dependent pathogenesis. Furthermore, a neutralizing anti-Delta toxin monoclonal antibody confers protection against disease progression. These findings suggest that a subset of NEC is a specific-toxin-mediated disorder and validate the Delta toxin-CD9 axis as a therapeutic target for this subset.

title: Gut microbiome profiles associated with simple liver steatosis in MASLD
authors: Pradhan M; Molinaro A; Ginanni Corradini S; Silecchia G; Ferri F et al.
abstract: Background Alterations in the gut microbiota have been linked to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). However, most studies have focused on advanced disease stages with limited consideration of the impact of medications such as proton pump inhibitors and metformin. Objective To characterise the gut microbiota signatures in individuals with simple steatosis, free from such confounders, across three European cohorts spanning a broad range of body mass index. Design Faecal samples from 134 participants were analysed by whole-genome metagenomic sequencing. Participants included biopsy-confirmed steatosis cases and controls from Austria (18 vs 18) and Italy (20 vs 12), and ultrasound-diagnosed steatosis from Sweden (33 vs 33). Results Simple steatosis was associated with a gut microbiota profile characterised by reduced microbial gene richness and decreased abundance of butyrate-producing species. These alterations appeared in the absence of histological steatohepatitis or significant fibrosis, indicating that microbial shifts occur before advanced disease and are not simply a consequence of disease progression. Across all cohorts, enrichment of oral-origin and small intestinal-origin bacteria, including opportunistic pathogens such as Fusobacterium nucleatum and Klebsiella oxytoca, was consistently observed in steatosis. Furthermore, gut microbiota profiles associated with steatosis exhibited increased genetic potential for lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis, suggesting an enhanced capacity for systemic inflammatory signalling. Conclusion Gut microbiota alterations occur early in MASLD before advanced inflammatory or fibrotic disease. The consistent enrichment of oral-origin and pro-inflammatory taxa across cohorts suggests that both oral-gut and gut-liver axes may contribute to steatosis pathogenesis, independent of common pharmacological confounders.

title: Early-life skin molecular signatures are predictive of atopic dermatitis risk in an Asian preconception birth cohort
authors: Le Duc Huy Ta; Stephen Wearne; Seong Soo Lim; Minghao Chia; Kaibo Duan et al.
abstract: Early identification of infants at risk of atopic dermatitis (AD) is critical for timely prevention, yet preclinical biomarkers remain elusive. In this nested study within the prospective Singapore Preconception Study of Long-Term Maternal and Child Outcomes (S-PRESTO) cohort (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03531658), we investigated whether early molecular signatures of infant skin could predict disease onset. The primary endpoint was physician-diagnosed AD by 18 months of age; secondary endpoints included AD severity and longitudinal trajectories of skin metagenomic, metabolomic, and proteomic profiles. Non-lesional skin tape strips were collected longitudinally from 119 infants (60 AD cases, 59 controls) at week 1 and months 3, 6, and 18. Here, we show that distinct microbial and host molecular alterations significantly precede clinical manifestation. Healthy infants exhibited progressive microbial diversity, transitioning from Staphylococcus epidermidis to lipophilic commensals, accompanied by butanoate fermentation and elevated natural moisturizing factors. Conversely, infants developing AD displayed early dysbiosis, driven by Pseudomonas stutzeri at week 1 and Staphylococcus aureus by month 3, alongside premature upregulation of antimicrobial peptides and uncoupled host-microbiome interactions. Predictive models showed strong performance in stratifying AD risk, shifting from microbial and peptide markers at week 1 to sustained inflammation at month 3. These preclinical signatures offer practical non-invasive tools for early infant risk stratification.

title: VHSeek: biology foundation model-based virus representations revealing virus host associations
authors: Wei Liu; Yuqiu Wang; Jed A. Fuhrman; Hui Li; Le Song et al.
abstract: Virus-host association prediction is fundamental to virus-related disease control and phage therapy, yet many existing tools require candidate-host genome sequences, which may be unavailable for some eukaryotic hosts or impractical to search at the scale of large virome studies. We present VHSeek, a supervised virus-host association predictor that integrates DNA- and protein-derived viral representations. VHSeek combines nucleotide representations from AIDO.DNA and protein representations from ESM2 to learn virus-host association patterns, and then transfers predictions through known host taxonomies from lower to higher ranks. During inference, VHSeek uses viral sequence data and known host taxonomies, without host sequence data. Compared with iPHoP, the state-of-the-art baseline evaluated in this study, VHSeek improves genus-level maximum F1 score (Fmax), Top-1 accuracy, and area under the precision–recall curve (AUPR) by 12%, 19%, and 27%, respectively. Confidence thresholding enables abstention and reduces false discoveries. On the processed IMG/VR v4.1 metagenomic collection, VHSeek expands effective host coverage from 36.5% to 64.5% using a validation-calibrated confidence threshold. VHSeek prioritizes candidate viruses and reservoir hosts with potential human health impacts, including multi-host hypotheses in which one virus may be associated with humans and additional hosts (e.g., Saboya virus with Homo sapiens and Culicidae) not currently captured in the dataset.

title: Linking human sources to antibiotic resistance genes in global surface waters
authors: Guangbin Zhong; Shuaiqi Li; Kevin C. Jones; Ying Bo Zhu
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a global public health threat driven by antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs). Yet global human ARG generation, environmental discharges and surface-water abundances remain poorly characterized, and their linkages remain unclear, particularly at gene-specific absolute abundances, given differences in antibiotic and pathogen associations among ARGs. Here, we compiled 464 absolute abundance measurement data of five key ARGs ( qnrS , ermB , tetA , tetM , and sul1 ) and intI1 in wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) influent covering 30 countries, and combined these data with machine learning, a WWTP removal framework and a spatially explicit dilution model to estimate these metrics. Per capita generation was highest in Africa, whereas total generation and discharges were greatest in Asia; surface-water hotspots clustered in water-scarce regions, highlighting hydrological constraints alongside discharge intensity. Raising WWTP coverage in below-average countries to the global mean and high-income standards could increase global removal from 12–29% to 53–60% and 72–76%, respectively. These findings quantitatively link human ARG sources to surface-water abundances, providing a foundation for surveillance and intervention to curb ARG dissemination.

title: The evolutionary plateau of efflux-mediated drug resistance in mycobacteria
authors: S.C. Sharma; Asis Kumar Khuntia; Vinay Kumar Nandicoori; Sarika Mehra
abstract: Multidrug efflux pumps are major drivers of antimicrobial resistance, but overlapping resistance mechanisms mask the physiological limits of efflux alone. Bacterial genomes encode a large repertoire of multidrug efflux pumps, which could theoretically combine to achieve exceptionally high levels of resistance. To delineate the extent of resistance achievable through efflux driven adaptation, we performed adaptive laboratory evolution of Mycobacterium smegmatis mc²155 wild-type and efflux-deleted ( ΔlfrA , ΔefpA ) strains against ethidium bromide, a broad-spectrum efflux substrate. Despite prolonged selection, resistance reproducibly plateaued at 8-16 fold increase in MIC under the tested conditions. This plateau emerged through distinct evolutionary trajectories characterized by non-overlapping efflux pump sets: from overexpression of the well-characterized lfrA to upregulation of multiple uncharacterized pumps, all conferring cross-resistance. Genetic reconstruction of mutations in a transcriptional regulator and a membrane protein, together with overexpression of efflux pumps, recapitulated the resistance phenotypes of the evolved strains. Sustained pump overexpression depleted membrane potential and drove metabolic suppression, suggesting that energetic exhaustion may constrain further increase in efflux-mediated resistance. Similar constraints were observed in Mycobacterium tuberculosis , indicating that they may extend to other mycobacterial species. Efflux-metabolic integration thus affects resistance evolution, revealing therapeutic vulnerabilities to combat multidrug resistance.

title: STMetaDB: an integrated spatial metatranscriptomics web server and database for microbiome and host-microbe interactions
authors: Hao Yu; Lu Zhou; Tingting Tan; Ke Sui; Hai Fang et al.
abstract: The mammalian body harbors trillions of microbes that interact dynamically with host tissues, shaping health and disease. However, methodological constraints limit spatial insights into these host-microbe interactions, a gap that hinders progress in understanding microbiota-driven biological processes. STMetaDB ( https://stmetadb.jflab.ac.cn:8084 ) is an integrated database and web server for spatial metatranscriptomics, enabling systematic exploration of microbiome composition and host–microbe molecular interactions within tissue microenvironments. It integrates 643 validated spatial transcriptomic datasets across multiple human and mouse tissues, identifying diverse microbial genera and their spatial links to host transcriptional programs. Key features include differential gene expression analysis in microbial-enriched regions, cross-tissue colonization pattern mapping, and knowledge graphs linking microbial-associated genes to protein mutations, pathways, and diseases. STMetaDB fills the spatial insight gap, providing a transformative platform to investigate microbiota-driven spatial heterogeneity in cancer progression, immune microenvironment modulation, and precision therapeutic strategies. title: Sugar alternatives shift the evolutionary trajectory of fluoride resistance in cariogenic and non-cariogenic dental bacteria
authors: Shay; M. R.; Eakin; M. A.; Stockbridge; R. B.; Tenuta; L. M.; Lin et al.
abstract: Dental caries result from acidogenic biofilms dissolving enamel while growing on fermentable dietary sugars. While fluoride from toothpastes and professional products is widely used for caries control, sugar alternatives with inhibitory effects on some dental microbiota (e.g., erythritol and xylitol) instead reduce the cariogenicity of foods and act as prebiotics, often in combination with of fluoride, to control caries progression. Despite their growing prevalence, we do not understand how frequent exposure to sugar alternatives impacts the evolutionary pressures faced by oral bacteria. Herein, we tested the effects of carbon source (glucose, sorbitol, erythritol, or xylitol) on the modes and effectiveness of evolving fluoride resistant cariogenic (S. mutans) and non-cariogenic (S. gordonii) populations. For S. gordonii, evolving in glucose resulted in significantly more non-synonymous mutations compared to populations evolving in sugar alternatives (erythritol, sorbitol, xylitol), but without a drastic increase in fluoride resistance. Contrastingly, for cariogenic S. mutans, evolving in the presence of fermentable sugars resulted in much greater fluoride resistance, but without higher numbers of substitutions relative to those found in isolates from populations evolved in the presence of non-fermentable sugars. We observed previously unreported fluoride resistance mutations across carbon conditions, including a case of parallel evolution in the histone-like binding protein (smu_589) in S. mutans isolates evolved in environments with fluoride and a variety of sugar alternatives. Together, these results demonstrate that commonly used sugar alternatives can shape the evolutionary trajectory of dental microbiota to a broad stressor, such as fluoride.

title: Machine Learning Prediction of Antibiotic Resistance Genes: Performance, Interpretability, and Cross-Database Redundancy
authors: Ruthbah; C. A.; Sadi; T. H.; Jahan; N. E. S.; Tanzim Adib; A. N. M.
abstract: Antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) classifiers are typically developed and evaluated within a single curated database, leaving open how much two independently curated databases agree and what that implies for apparent cross-database generalization. We trained an XGBoost classifier on amino acid trigram frequencies and physicochemical descriptors using the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD), the field's largest curated ARG resource. The model separated resistance genes from non-resistance proteins with near-ceiling accuracy (AUROC = 0.982, MCC = 0.886); a label-shuffling null baseline collapsed to chance (AUROC = 0.508) and bootstrap confidence intervals were narrow, confirming genuine signal rather than data leakage or overfitting. SHAP analysis attributed this performance to biologically interpretable features, notably the trigram KTG, isoelectric point, and aromaticity, each consistent with known catalytic motifs in resistance enzymes. Before testing the classifier against ResFinder, one of CARD's most widely used counterparts, we assessed database independence by clustering sequences with CD-HIT, finding that 96.8-98.7% of ResFinder sequences shared substantial protein identity with CARD even at a permissive 50% identity threshold, indicating the two databases largely represent the same sequence population, with direct implications for how cross-database generalization should be measured. On the small subset of ResFinder sequences genuinely non-redundant with CARD (40-100 sequences, depending on threshold), the classifier failed completely, never classifying any as resistance genes; SHAP traced this failure to sequence length, as non-redundant sequences are nearly three times longer than training proteins, and length is among the model's most influential features. The same pattern emerged by resistance mechanism: the model achieved perfect accuracy on beta-lactamases, compact single-domain enzymes well represented in training (100%, n = 351), but correctly identified only 38.5% of efflux pump components (n = 13), a mechanism built from large, multi-domain transporters rather than compact catalytic enzymes. Together, these results describe a capable, interpretable ARG classifier alongside a quantified methodological caution: cross-database redundancy must be measured rather than assumed, and when a sequence-composition classifier fails, the failure is often explained by protein architecture rather than database origin.

title: Infectious Disease Knowledge Graph (IDKG) for Antiviral and Antibacterial Drug Discovery
authors: Martin; H.-J.; Beasley; J.-M.; Kaneva; V.; Tieghi; R.; Causey et al.
abstract: Infectious diseases remain a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, while therapeutic discovery is hindered by fragmented biomedical data and antimicrobial resistance. To address this challenge, we developed the Infectious Disease Knowledge Graph (IDKG), a queryable platform that integrates curated chemical, biological, pharmacological, and clinical information relevant to infectious-disease drug discovery. Using a customized ORION pipeline, we integrated 20 data sources, including DrugCentral, SMACC, Heli-SMACC, NPASS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and host-virus interaction databases, into a Neo4j graph containing more than 4.6 million nodes and 26 million edges. IDKG supports graph-based reasoning through Clinical Outcome Pathways (COPs) and incorporates curation workflows for small molecules, biologics, and complex mixtures. Illustrative applications include reconstruction of a literature-supported remdesivir pathway for COVID-19 and graph-based mechanistic interpretation of experimentally observed quorum-sensing inhibitor-antibiotic synergies in multidrug-resistant bacteria. The platform provides an interoperable framework for drug repurposing, target prioritization, and mechanism-based hypothesis generation. IDKG is freely available at https://idkg.mml.unc.edu.

title: Striking Differences in Tetrabromobisphenol A (TBBPA) Deconjugation by Human Fecal Microbiota: The Pilot-10 Human Donor Study
authors: Rong; C.; Lim; J.; Liu; X.; Li; L.; Cui et al.
abstract: Tetrabromobisphenol A (TBBPA) is a widely used brominated flame retardant with multiple adverse health effects. Although TBBPA undergoes phase II conjugation to facilitate elimination, gut microbial deconjugation may regenerate unconjugated TBBPA, increasing intestinal re-exposure. However, the extent of interindividual variability and its underlying microbial determinants remain poorly understood. To address this critical knowledge gap, we hypothesized that human fecal microbiota exhibit donor-dependent differences in TBBPA-sulfate (S-TBBPA) deconjugation and potential downstream debromination to tribromobisphenol A (Tri-BBPA). In our Pilot-10 Human Donor Study (PM10), fecal microbiota from five healthy adult male and five female human donors were incubated anaerobically with S-TBBPA at 37 C for six hours. Heat-inactivated microbiota served as controls. S-TBBPA, unconjugated TBBPA, and Tri-BBPA were quantified using targeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Metagenomic shotgun sequencing (MGS) was performed followed by microbial taxonomic and gene-family profiling using MetaPhlAn v4.11 and HUMAnN v3.9, respectively. Unheated fecal microbiota from all donors regenerated TBBPA, whereas heat inactivation nearly abolished its formation, supporting microbial enzyme-dependent deconjugation of S-TBBPA. The proportion of regenerated TBBPA varied substantially among donors, accounting for approximately 10-50% of the combined detected S-TBBPA and TBBPA. No statistically significant sex-associated differences were detected. Tri-BBPA was undetectable or negligible across incubations. Notably, the cumulative sulfatase-maturation enzyme gene family abundance was positively associated with LC-MS-measured S-TBBPA deconjugation activity, whereas the cumulative arylsulfatase and other sulfatase gene abundances showed no significant associations. Furthermore, 12 taxonomically stratified microbial desulfation-related gene-family annotations exhibited nominally significant positive correlations with deconjugation activity, highlighting potential roles for specific microbial sulfatases and their maturation enzymes in TBBPA reactivation. Collectively, our PM10 pilot study revealed substantial interindividual variability in microbial TBBPA-sulfate deconjugation and identified sulfatase-maturation enzyme gene abundance as a potential indicator of activity. These findings highlighted an underexplored pathway of xenobiotic reactivation and support future personalized microbiome-directed strategies to reduce internal TBBPA exposure and associated health risks.

title: Intestinal epithelial differentiation factor HNF4α restrains homeostatic interferon signaling and is required for its full induction during Salmonella infection
authors: Rivet-Noor; C. R.; Lickwar; C. R.; Tillman; M. C.; Orr; L. M.; DeLoach et al.
abstract: Intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) must interpret microbial signals to transcriptionally adapt their identity and function. Which transcription factors (TFs) mediate those adaptations, and whether competing transcriptional pathways signal within the same or in different IEC subpopulations, remains unclear. We find that microbiota colonization shifts nearly all IECs toward an interferon-driven inflammatory program at the expense of genes involved in enterocyte differentiation and metabolism. These opposing gene expression programs are associated with different TF motifs and are inversely correlated within individual cells. We discover that HNF4, a TF central to enterocyte differentiation, acts as a brake on interferon signaling in vitro. In accord, loss of HNF4 in IECs in mice elevates baseline interferon-stimulated gene expression but prevents its full induction during infection with the bacterial pathogen Salmonella. Together our findings reveal a novel mechanism by which opposing intestinal epithelial differentiation and interferon signaling programs interact within the same cell to maintain proper transcriptional control and homeostasis.

title: Formate, hydrogen, and acetate shape the morphology, physiology and lifestyles of the host-associated methanogen Methanobrevibacter smithii
authors: Del Mazo-Monsalvo; I.; Poulter; A. N.; Ovando-Ovando; C. I.; Santiago-Martinez; M. G.
abstract: Methane-producing archaea (methanogens) are increasingly linked to gastrointestinal, neuropsychiatric, and neurodevelopmental disorders. These conditions are often associated with altered microbial metabolism that changes the availability of acetate, formate, hydrogen, carbon dioxide, and methane in the gut. However, the physiological importance of formate and acetate in host-associated methanogens remains poorly understood, limiting our ability to interpret microbiome data and infer functions and cross-domain interactions of methanogens in health and disease. Here, we investigated the physiological and metabolic capabilities of Methanobrevibacter smithii, the predominant methanogen of the human gut. Formate limitation altered growth, morphology, extracellular pH, gas metabolism, and cellular organization, and induced the formation of cell aggregates. Although acetate was consumed only in small quantities (nmol), its availability significantly influenced growth, gas metabolism, extracellular pH, and formate utilization, indicating functions that extend beyond its role as a biosynthetic precursor. Conversely, nutrient excess promoted a transition to a biofilm lifestyle, suggesting that biofilm formation may function as a carbon sink. We further developed Msm_MEP, an experimentally refined genome-scale metabolic model based on the AGORA2 reconstruction, which captures the metabolic capabilities of M. smithii, quantifies ATP allocation across cellular processes, and predicts the phenotypic consequences of gene deletions. Together, our findings identify formate, hydrogen, and acetate as interacting determinants of M. smithii physiology and suggest metabolite-dependent transitions between planktonic growth, cell aggregation, and biofilm formation. Our results establish a framework for interpreting microbiome data and understanding how environmental metabolites shape archaea physiology and cross-domain interactions within the human microbiome.

title: Identification and characterization of a Streptococcus strain isolated from the esophagus of an adult male heterozygous for the CF allele
authors: Abrahamson; E. A.; Surve; S. V.; OToole; G.
abstract: The genus Streptococcus consists of diverse bacteria that are integral components of the human microbiome, acting as both important commensals and opportunistic pathogens. In this study, one strain of an -hemolytic species of the genus Streptococcus, GP0011T, isolated from an esophageal aspirate collected during an endoscopy, was characterised phenotypically to establish its taxonomic status. The strain was isolated from an adult male heterozygous for a cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) mutation. The phylogenetic analysis indicates that the strain is a novel species within the mitis group, with Streptococcus oralis ATCC 35037T being the closest relative with 94.84% average nucleotide identity (ANI) and 58.3% digital DNA-DNA hybridization (dDDH). Phenotypic characterization and API20 Strep strips distinguished GP0011T from S. oralis by the absence of alkaline phosphatase activity, trehalose fermentation, and starch fermentation, and by superior growth on D-mannitol and D-sorbitol, consistent with genomic data. The strain is Gram-positive, catalase-negative, and the cells are ovoid with a mean cell diameter of 1.3 {micro}m. Growth occurred at 25-43 C, with an optimum at 30 C, with an optimum at pH 8.0. Antibiotic resistance genes msrD and mefA, conferring resistance to azithromycin and erythromycin, as well as pathways for mannitol and sorbitol metabolism, were found and phenotypically confirmed in the GP0011T genome but were absent from S. oralis. These findings indicate that GP0011T represents a novel species within the genus Streptococcus with the proposed name of Streptococcus ruoffae sp. nov. The type strain is GP0011T (ATCC TSD-627 and NCTC 15312).

title: An iron acquisition system promotes Bifidobacterium longum fitness in competitive early life gut communities
authors: Acton; L.; Soe; C. Z.; Kujawska; M.; Augustine; J.; Senoo et al.
abstract: Iron availability influences the composition of the gut microbiota, yet the mechanisms that enable beneficial bacteria to acquire iron and compete within iron-variable communities remain poorly understood. Here, we identify Fei (Fe import), an iron-responsive acquisition system that promotes the fitness of Bifidobacterium longum subsp. longum, a prevalent member of the early-life gut microbiota. Comparative profiling of 20 bifidobacterial strains revealed substantial inter- and intraspecies variation in growth under iron limitation, with multiple B. longum subsp. longum strains maintaining comparatively robust growth. Transcriptomic analysis identified a four-gene locus, feiMQOX, that was strongly induced during iron depletion and returned towards control expression following iron supplementation. The complete locus was highly conserved within B. longum subsp. longum but unevenly distributed across the wider genus. Disruption of individual Fei components impaired growth and reduced cell-associated iron under iron-restricted conditions, while metal-binding studies of purified FeiX demonstrated a physiological preference for Fe(II). FeiX also provided a pronounced fitness advantage during competition with an infant-derived Enterococcus faecalis isolate, particularly under iron limitation. Finally, analysis of longitudinal metagenomic data from Bangladeshi infants demonstrated that Fei is present within infant gut communities and that its abundance changes following iron supplementation. Together, these findings identify a lineage-associated iron-acquisition system that connects micronutrient availability with bifidobacterial physiology and competitive fitness. More broadly, our findings establish strain-level micronutrient acquisition as a potentially important determinant of beneficial bacterial fitness within the developing gut microbiota.

title: Illumina MiSeq, MiSeq i100, and Element AVITI yield concordant ecological patterns for universal 16S and 18S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing
authors: D'Agostino; E.; Needham; D.
abstract: Molecular microbiome analyses require high-resolution, comparable measurements, often obtained by sequencing marker genes such as the rRNA gene. Recently, new platforms and chemistries have promised to improve performance at lower cost relative to the commonly used Illumina MiSeq 2x300, but have not yet been systematically compared especially for rRNA gene amplicon studies. Here, we compared MiSeq 2x300, MiSeq 2x500, and AVITI 2x300 by sequencing mock communities and field samples via a 'universal' (16S + 18S) rRNA gene amplicons (V4-V5 region) approach. All platforms recovered similar community patterns (Mantel r > 0.93), with no major differences in recovered lineages. MiSeq 2x500 showed ~4.5-fold higher index hopping (5.9 +/- 3.8% vs. 1.3 +/- 1.5%). For 18S, MiSeq 2x500, despite longer reads overlapping the 18S V4-V5 region, only marginally improved taxonomic classification (+0.7% on average) and ASV resolution (+/-1.3%). Meanwhile, all platforms similarly biased against 18S due to its greater length, which we demonstrate can be offset by a gel-based size selection, with no apparent taxonomic bias. Overall the platforms yield ecologically similar results. We highlight platform-specific advantages to help guide decision-making and challenges that can be addressed through dedicated bioinformatic or wet-lab approaches.

title: Brain disorder mechanisms and therapeutic targets identified from developmental, cell-specific gene regulation
authors: Rohani; N.; Kovner; R.; Liu; Y.; Garcia Guerra; A.; Markati et al.
abstract: Genetic variation influences brain physiology and disease across cell types and development. We integrated whole-genome sequencing, bulk RNA sequencing, and single-nucleus multiome profiling from 231 human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex donors spanning six postconceptional weeks to 92 years. Across 24 brain-related traits, neurodevelopmental and psychiatric genetic risk was enriched in neuronal transcriptomic and chromatin profiles, whereas neurodegenerative risk was enriched in microglia. Thousands of expression, chromatin accessibility, and splicing quantitative trait loci revealed developmental and cell-type-specific regulatory effects. Colocalization linked multiple sclerosis risk to AHI1 expression in prenatal neurons and problematic alcohol use to GPX1 expression in postnatal glia. Leveraging dynamic cis-regulatory elements, we identified therapeutic candidates for haploinsufficient neurodevelopmental disorders, including a SOX5 enhancer whose CRISPR activation increased transcript and protein abundance. Together, these findings establish a publicly accessible genomic resource for resolving the developmental and cellular contexts of genetic risk and identifying therapeutic targets in the human brain.

title: Gut Microbial Butyrate Metabolism Generates an N-Acyl Amide that Regulates Host Transcriptional Programs
authors: Hamchand; R.; Chang; P. V.
abstract: Faecalibacterium prausnitzii is a prominent member of the human gut microbiota whose depletion is associated with various intestinal and metabolic disorders. While multiple mechanisms have been proposed to explain how F. prausnitzii promotes host health, the molecular determinants underlying these activities remain elusive. Here, we show that F. prausnitzii is a prolific producer of the human metabolite N-butyrylglycine, which we find accumulates to millimolar concentrations in bacterial culture and is readily detectable in the feces of conventional wildtype mice. We establish an enzymatic basis of N-butyrylglycine production by identifying and biochemically validating an F. prausnitzii N-acyltransferase that catalyzes the conjugation of butyryl-CoA and glycine. Despite being derived from butyrate, N-butyrylglycine exhibits distinct bioactivity from its precursor, including reduced histone deacetylase inhibitory activity, an altered inflammatory profile, and enhanced suppression of cellular proliferation across multiple cancer cell lines. Furthermore, transcriptomic profiling revealed N butyrylglycine coordinates repression of G2/M checkpoint-associated programs and downregulation of the colorectal cancer associated gene AOC1. Together, these findings suggest that specialized metabolites produced by F. prausnitzii contribute to its beneficial effects and may underlie its protective role in colorectal cancer.

title: Intestinal goblet cell loss induces microbiota-independent mucosal and systemic IgA dysregulation
authors: Vanhercke; S.; Thiran; A.; Blancke; G.; Ciers; M.; Petta et al.
abstract: Goblet cells are essential for establishing the intestinal mucus layer and exert diverse immunomodulatory functions. The mucus barrier cooperates with secretory immunoglobulin A (IgA) to regulate host-microbiota interactions and maintain intestinal immune homeostasis. The extent to which goblet cells directly regulate IgA responses remains unclear. Here, we show that depletion of Muc2-expressing intestinal secretory cells in mice caused barrier dysfunction and intestinal inflammation accompanied by profound mucosal and systemic IgA dysregulation, including hyper-IgA, circulating IgA-IgG immune complexes and renal IgA deposition. Selective Paneth cell depletion did not reproduce these IgA abnormalities, and Muc2-deficient mice showed an intermediate phenotype, implicating loss of goblet-cells rather than Paneth cells or of Muc2 loss in this phenotype. Germ-free rederivation markedly attenuated intestinal inflammation but did not prevent mucosal and systemic hyper-IgA or IgA-IgG immune-complex formation, demonstrating that goblet cell loss drives IgA dysregulation independently of live microbial colonisation. Goblet cell loss and IgA deficiency shaped the mucosa-associated microbiota largely independently, as goblet cell depletion promotes expansion of the genus Akkermansia, whereas IgA deficiency reduced Akkermansia but allowed expansion of Mucispirillum and aggravated colonic pathology, indicating that elevated IgA response is partially protective. These findings reveal goblet cells as critical regulators of mucosal and systemic IgA homeostasis beyond mucus production and point to epithelial-immune interactions as potential contributors to IgA-mediated diseases.

title: The intestinal microbiome shapes responses to the GD2/GD3 cancer vaccine in children with high-risk neuroblastoma
authors: Ma; L.; Argyropoulos; K.; Dhuri; K.; Waters; N.; Fei et al.
abstract: The intestinal microbiome influences vaccine responses, but its role in therapeutic cancer vaccination remains largely unexplored. We investigated the gut microbiome, vaccine immunogenicity and clinical outcomes in 137 children with high-risk neuroblastoma receiving GD2/GD3 vaccination with oral b-glucan. Microbiome-perturbing antibiotic exposure was associated with inferior progression-free survival (PFS). Among patients vaccinated in first remission, higher a-diversity and enrichment of Lachnospiraceae, including Blautia, were associated with higher anti-GD2 IgG1 responses, while higher Clostridia abundance was associated with superior PFS. Patients had microbiome profiles resembling those of chronologically younger healthy children, consistent with delayed microbiome maturation. A greater discrepancy between patients' chronological age and the age of microbiome-matched healthy children was associated with inferior PFS among patients in first remission. In a complementary mouse model, antibiotic treatment impaired vaccine-induced anti-GD2 IgG responses and accelerated tumor growth. Together, these findings support a role for the intestinal microbiome in therapeutic cancer vaccine responses and identify microbiome maturation as a clinically relevant feature in pediatrics.

title: Ventricular proximity associates with survival and immune remodelling in glioblastoma
authors: Gutierrez-Arroyo; J. L.; Chakraborty; C.; Gallego-Porcar; P.; Barcelo; J.; Guillou et al.
abstract: Glioblastoma is clinically and molecularly heterogeneous, yet whether its position relative to the lateral ventricles shapes tumour biology remains unclear. Here we measured tumour ventricle distance in 57 patients with IDH-wildtype glioblastoma and combined survival analysis with RNA sequencing, whole-genome sequencing, proteomics and multiplex immunofluorescence. Proximity to the ventricles was associated with shorter survival. Ventricle-proximal tumours lacked a distinct genomic driver but displayed an inflammatory yet immunoregulatory profile: antigen-presentation, leukocyte-activation and cytokine programmes coexisted with checkpoint and immunosuppressive transcripts, and proteomics revealed concordant complement and myeloid signals. In tissue, these tumours tended to show more Ki67-positive cells and proliferating SOX2-positive stem-like cells, suggesting increased plasticity of the stem-like compartment, without more CD4- or CD8a-positive lymphocytes. Ventricular proximity thus marks a clinically adverse context with a distinct immune-inflammatory profile, providing a framework for validation and patient stratification.

title: KORUS: probabilistic ancestry inference beyond variant calls
authors: Warren; R. L.; Coombe; L.; Birol; I.
abstract: Ancestry inference typically relies on variant calling and predefined population labels. We present KORUS, a probabilistic framework that infers ancestry from sequencing-derived k-mer representations constructed using ancestry-informative reference variants and encoded in Bloom filters, without requiring explicit variant calls for query genomes. KORUS separates genomic feature representation from ancestry decoding, enabling supervised classification, fractional ancestry inference, and unsupervised population structure discovery within a unified framework. Reference models were constructed from 643 genomes from the 1000 Genomes Project and the Simons Genome Diversity Project. Evaluation on an independent cohort of 22 whole-genome sequencing samples, with comparisons to ntRoot, SNVstory, and ADMIXTURE, showed recovery of continental-scale population structure, with supervised classification accuracy of 72.7-81.8% and ancestry-fraction concordance of R2 = 0.844-0.993 relative to ADMIXTURE and R2 = 0.665-0.983 relative to ntRoot. Ancestry estimates were consistent across alternative k-mer representations. Analyses of ancient human and archaic hominin genomes demonstrated that probabilistic projections quantify affinity to the learned feature space rather than necessarily indicating modern continental ancestry. KORUS provides a unified approach to ancestry inference directly from sequencing-derived representations and is freely available under the GPLv3 license at https://github.com/BirolLab/korus.

title: Generalist method to reconstruct metabolic networks from multi-omics data at large-scale
authors: Kumar S; P.; Sridhar; S.; Alsmadi; N.; Mahadevan; R.; Bhatt et al.
abstract: Metabolic network databases often suffer from inconsistent pathways with blocked reactions. Furthermore, current reconstruction methods lack scalable ways to integrate multi-omics data and cannot flexibly combine diverse modeling pipelines. We introduce SPECTRA, a unified platform that reconstructs metabolic networks across multiple biological scales. SPECTRA uses distinct optimization formulations and achieves a 56-fold speed improvement over existing algorithms for flux consistency based model reconstruction. We demonstrated SPECTRA across three applications. First, we gap-filled 7,302 microbial reconstructions from the AGORA2 database, reducing blocked reactions from an average of 482 to 169 per model. Second, we modeled synthetic gut microbiota at the community scale with superior performance in reaction inclusion. Third, we extracted models for 1,479 cancer cell lines, capturing more cancer hallmark reactions than current methods. This framework provides a scalable and flexible approach for modeling metabolic networks, and generates testable hypotheses for machine learning applications in biology.
