title: Daphniphyllum macropodum genome assembly and multiplexed screening unveils alkaloid modifying enzymes
authors: Swamidatta; S. H.; Radzikowska; B. A.; Taylor; D. J.; Smit; S. J.; Waddell et al.
abstract: Daphniphyllum macropodum, a small shrub or tree native to East Asia, produces bioactive polycyclic alkaloids of remarkable complexity and variety, making them long-standing, attractive targets for chemical synthesis. However, the biosynthetic origins of Daphniphyllum alkaloids remain unknown, and no pathway-associated enzymes have been identified to date. Here, we report the chromosome-level genome assembly of D. macropodum, representing the first genome assembly for the Daphniphyllaceae, a family in the Saxifragales woody clade. To discover alkaloid-modifying enzymes, we developed a highly combinatorial, multiplexed screening approach which enabled testing multiple enzyme candidates with multiple substrates in a single reaction. Deconvolution and characterisation identified two cytochrome P450 enzymes that catalyse the hydroxylation of the yuzurimine-type alkaloid daphhimalenine B. Specifically, CYP82C230 functions as a daphhimalenine B 2-hydroxylase to yield the natural product yuzurimine C, whereas its paralog, CYP82C231, acts as a daphhimalenine B 13-hydroxylase generating a novel alkaloid we have named yuzurimine F. These are the first reports of an enzymatic modification of a Daphniphyllum alkaloid. Collectively, this work advances our understanding of D. macropodum biology and represents the first steps towards elucidating the complex Daphniphyllum alkaloid biosynthetic pathway.

title: EvoRx: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Antibiotic Resistance in Escherichia coli Using Genomic Features
authors: Arora; A.; Natarajan; E.
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) complicates bacterial infection management, motivating genomic approaches to predicting antibiotic susceptibility. This study assessed the predictive performance and generalisability of machine-learning models using resistance-associated genomic features from Escherichia coli. Publicly available genomic and phenotypic records yielded 446 genomes, 252 binary genomic features and 1,935 susceptibility observations across nine antibiotics. Logistic Regression, Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers were compared using validation ROC-AUC, followed by evaluation on held-out test subsets. Additional analyses examined identical genomic feature profiles across partitions, performance across source publications and feature redundancy. Ampicillin and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole achieved held-out accuracies of 93.98% and 93.59%, ROC-AUC values of 0.912 and 0.954, and resistant-isolate recall of 95.16% and 94.55%, respectively. In contrast, ceftazidime achieved 88.52% accuracy and 0.940 ROC-AUC but identified only 22.22% of resistant isolates. Seventy-four held-out observations shared identical 252-feature profiles with training isolates; all were correctly classified. After excluding overlapping observations without retraining, ROC-AUC decreased from 0.912 to 0.848 for ampicillin and from 0.954 to 0.901 for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. Exploratory cross-publication evaluations showed variable performance, with shared multilocus sequence types in 16 of 18 comparisons. Reducing genomic features did not materially alter validation performance in the two antibiotics examined. These findings indicate that genomic predictors can discriminate resistance phenotypes, but aggregate accuracy may obscure poor resistant-isolate detection. The findings also distinguish performance on conventionally held-out isolates from performance on previously unseen resistance-feature profiles, an important consideration when bacterial population structure and correlated determinants substantially influence model evaluation. Independent phylogenetic and prospective validation remains necessary before clinical use.

title: Common early-life exposure of the colorectal epithelium to the microbiome-derived mutagen colibactin
authors: Marshall; H. N.; Pham; M. H.; Jung; H.; Humphreys; L.; Hooks et al.
abstract: Colibactin is a mutagen produced by bacterial strains in the colorectal microbiomes of some healthy people. It generates somatic mutations characterised by the mutational signatures SBS88 and ID18 in normal human colorectal epithelial cells in vivo. Increasing prevalence of colibactin mutagenesis during the 20th century is hypothesised to have caused recent international increases in early-onset colorectal cancer incidence. Here, we establish the early-life prevalence, timing, mutation burdens and distribution through the colon of colibactin mutagenesis by sequencing normal colorectal epithelial cell genomes to detect SBS88 and ID18 in 90 healthy and inflammatory bowel disease affected children and adolescents. Colibactin-induced mutagenesis was present in ~43%, with or without inflammatory bowel disease. It usually begins shortly after birth and ceases by age five years. Mutation burdens are higher in the left than right colon and show substantial variation, with some children displaying mutation burdens comparable to those of healthy non-exposed individuals greater than 60 years of age. The future public health implications of this common early life mutagen exposure will depend on clarification of its role in colorectal cancer causation.

title: Identifying disease-associated dysbiosis in image-based spatial microbiome via MiSA
authors: Liu; R.; Grodner; B.; Samorodnitsky; S.; Deng; D.; Roy et al.
abstract: Background: Extensive studies have revealed the associations of microbiome dysbiosis with disease through compositional analysis of 16S rRNA amplicon or shotgun metagenomic sequencing data. However, dysbiosis in spatial organization of microbiome inhabiting the body sites and its implication for diseases remain understudied. Recently developed high phylogenetic resolution fluorescence in situ hybridization (HiPR-FISH) is an image-based mapping technology that provides spatial microbiome data at single-cell resolution, which allows for visualizing and quantifying spatial arrangement of microbial cells. Despite the growing availability of such data, no methods have been tailored to studying spatial dysbiosis in image-based microbiome data. Results: Here we introduce MiSA (Microbiome Spatial Aberration), the first statistical framework for identifying disease-associated spatial dysbiosis and the individual taxa that may contribute to it, based on differing degrees of clustering or regularity, i.e., microbial cells being more aggregated or more evenly spaced than expected under complete spatial randomness, between diagnostic groups. In simulations based on a real dataset, MiSA was robust across diverse and noisy spatial configurations, achieving substantially higher statistical power than a method borrowed from spatial proteomics, while controlling type I error at both the individual-taxon and community levels. When applied to an oral biofilm study, MiSA detected peri-implant mucositis-associated spatial dysbiosis at the community level and identified five taxa as potential contributors, including Actinomyces, which showed increased clustering in mucositis. Conclusions: MiSA is a powerful and robust framework for identifying spatial dysbiosis and the contributing taxa in image-based microbiome data, offering new insights into the spatial organization of microbial communities in disease.

title: Resistome-based machine learning source attribution of a superbug
authors: Mendez; C.; Vargas-Peralta; D.; Rendon; L. A.; Castillo-Ramirez; S.
abstract: Many bacterial human pathogens infect not only humans but also other species, and source attribution has been very useful for studying transmission among the different sources. Yet, critical pathogens such as Acinetobacter baumannii have not been studied using source attribution approaches. Here, we conducted machine source attribution using the resistome of almost 1200 A. baumannii genomes from four sources: humans, companion animals , soil, and white storks. Of note, no other study has used the resistome as input data before. First, we selected the best model among 168 parameter combinations, which was Random Forest, with 5-fold cross-validation and chi2 for feature selection. The model shows a reasonably good accuracy with an F1 weighted score = 0.744, yet class accuracy was dependent on the source. Whereas for companion animals and humans, 93% and 86% of the predictions were correct, respectively; the other two categories (soil and white stork) show correct predictions below 50%. Yet, a core phylogeny and ST assignment reveal that the wrong predictions are associated with multi-host lineages. Finally, we identify the most important ARGs contributing to each class prediction and, in the case of companion animals, tetgenes, which confer resistance to tetracycline, were among the top contributors. Our study shows the resistome's potential for developing models to predict source associations. More broadly, this study shows how integrating machine learning and phylogenomics can help us understand multi-host transmission dynamics.

title: Hidden but Expanding Sampling Bias Distorts Prokaryotic Genome Collections
authors: Götsch; H.; Baumdicker; F.
abstract: Public genome collections underpin our understanding of bacterial diversity and the distribution of traits such as antibiotic resistance, and increasingly serve as training data for genomic foundation models. Their growing size promises an increasingly complete view of microbial genetic variation. However, these collections combine studies with different sampling priorities, often overrepresenting subgroups of closely related strains of particular interest. The resulting bias reduces effective information, and its consequences for diversity estimates and the value of further sequencing remain insufficiently quantified. Here we show that accounting for this escalating sampling bias is essential for accurate gene frequency estimates and hints at greater genomic diversity than current data suggest. We propose to detect and reduce sampling bias based on phylogenetic relationships compared to expectations under random sampling, which, in contrast to dereplication and data reduction methods, preserves fine-scale diversity in large samples. Applied to 402 prokaryotic species in the NCBI genome database, our method PhyloThin indicates that the effective number of samples is 41% lower than the actual number but retains more than twice as many genomes as dereplication. Sampling bias varies substantially among species, showing that genome counts alone provide an incomplete measure of how well a species has already been characterized. PhyloThin thus turns biased, expanding genome collections into more representative samples for studying genome evolution and population genetic inference with implications for training genomic foundation models, pathogen surveillance, and the discovery of novel genetic functions.

title: QuadSeq: A duplicated-duplex DNA-synthesis technology for high-fidelity nanopore sequencing of linear DNA amplicons
authors: Waneskog; M.; Nor Nielsen; K.; Julienne; A.; Acevedo-Rocha; C. G.; Ozdemir et al.
abstract: Long-read nanopore sequencing is a highly versatile technology that is currently constrained by high error-rates, which can impair accurate genotyping of complex DNA samples. Common mitigation strategies based on creating consensus sequences from tandem duplications synthesized by rolling-circle or multiple-displacement amplification are prone to create both chimeric DNA molecules and require an initial DNA-circularization. Here we present QuadSeq, a three-step DNA-synthesis technology that can convert linear DNA amplicons into duplicated DNA duplexes that encode two forward and two reverse strand copies of a sequence-of-interest. Intramolecular consensus sequences generated from QuadSeq duplicated DNA duplexes yielded a median single-amplicon accuracy of up to 0.9992 (Q31), without requiring a cumbersome DNA-circularization of the amplicon-of-interest. We can also show that the primary bottleneck for achieving accurate nanopore amplicon sequencing is not the mutation rate of the initial PCR-amplification, but the fidelity of the nanopore sequencing. QuadSeq consensus sequences generated from amplicons synthesized by a low-fidelity DNA polymerase (Taq) had a 6.6-fold lower median error-rate compared to amplicon simplex reads synthesized by a high-fidelity DNA polymerase (Phusion U). Going forward, we predict that the QuadSeq DNA-synthesis technology will enable the use of almost any low-fidelity DNA polymerase for high-fidelity nanopore amplicon sequencing.

title: TDP2 couples PKA-CREB signalling to genome stability in human cerebellar development
authors: Wang; W.-P.; Ma; G.; Wang; F.; Deng; Y.; Zheng et al.
abstract: Transcription and neuronal activity in the central nervous system generate abundant DNA damage, particularly DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), rendering neural cells - and cerebellar neurons especially - vulnerable to genome instability. Tyrosyl-DNA phosphodiesterase 2 (TDP2, also known as TTRAP) resolves topoisomerase-2-linked DSBs, and biallelic TDP2 mutations cause spinocerebellar ataxia autosomal recessive 23 (SCAR23), yet how DNA repair shapes human cerebellar development is unknown. Here we model SCAR23 in cerebellar organoids derived from patient induced pluripotent stem cells carrying TDP2 c.650del and from prime-edited isogenic TDP2 c.400C>T lines. TDP2 inactivation caused organoid hypoplasia during FGF8b-dependent cerebellar specification, which was reversed by TDP2 complementation. Single-nucleus transcriptomics across three developmental stages revealed early dysregulation of ribosome biogenesis, attenuated CREB1 regulon activity and a subsequent failure of Purkinje cell maturation. TDP2 inactivation upregulated PKIB, a cerebellum-enriched inhibitor of protein kinase A, lowering PKA and CREB phosphorylation. Whole-genome sequencing showed excess de novo deletions in mutant organoids, enriched at candidate cis-regulatory elements of neurodevelopmental genes. Pharmacological activation of the cAMP-PKA cascade restored CREB phosphorylation, reduced DNA damage and rescued organoid growth. These findings link developmental signalling to genome maintenance in the human cerebellum and identify the cAMP-PKA-CREB axis as a candidate therapeutic target in DNA-repair-deficient cerebellar disease.

title: De novo Genome Assembly and Annotation of the Seep Tubeworm Lamellibrachia satsuma using Oxford Nanopore Sequencing
authors: Patra; A. K. K.; Kwon; Y. M.; Won; Y.-J.; Yang; Y.
abstract: The tubeworm Lamelllibrachia satsuma inhabits seep region by forming a mutualistic symbiotic relationship with chemosynthetic bacteria residing in its trophosome. Genomic and symbiotic studies have been extensively conducted, primarily from a bacterial perspective. But rarely vice versa. Here we present a high-quality draft genome assembly of L. satsuma and its tissue-specific transcriptome data. This genome will be valuable for further understanding the mechanisms of adaptation in cold seep environments, host-microbe interactions, as well as genome variation among tubeworms. We generated ~103 Gb of genomic sequencing data using Illumina and Oxford Nanopore platforms, which assembled in a 665 Mb draft genome. The assembled genome consisted of 6,320 scaffolds with 95.7% genome completeness. Among 32,394 predicted protein-coding genes, 1,063 gene families have expanded, and 1,385 gene families were contracted. Among the expanded gene families, multiple copies of leukocyte elastase inhibitor, reverse transcriptase, arylesterase, and xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase genes were found. Molecular clock analysis based on the phylogenomic dataset revealed that L. sastuma and L. luymesi were diverged from their common ancestor during the Early Cenozoic era, approximately 13 million years ago.

title: Rapidly and reproducibly building a comprehensive catalogue of resistance-associated variants for M. tuberculosis surveillance
authors: Adlard; D.; Malone; K. M.; Westhead; J.; Hunt; M.; Thai et al.
abstract: Background: Catalogues of genetic variants associated with resistance underpin whole-genome sequencing (WGS)-based predictions of drug susceptibility in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and are essential for molecular diagnostics and surveillance. The current gold standard catalogues are those released by the WHO but the underlying data are not fully released and they are difficult to interpret. Open and reproducible methods would help address these problems, extending the important work already done. Methods: We have developed an automated method, catomatic, that uses a binomial test to associate informative isolates with resistance or susceptibility, and built a catalogue (catomatic-1) from the same 39,358 samples used to construct the first edition of the WHO catalogue (WHOv1). We performed a sensitivity analysis to optimise statistical and bioinformatic parameters for each drug, and benchmarked catomatic-1 against WHOv1 using an independent Validation Dataset of 14,380 isolates. Findings: By using simpler statistics, catomatic-1 algorithmically classified 1,329 genetic variants, ranging from five for linezolid to 440 for pyrazinamide. WHOv1 included generalisable rules added by a panel of experts, increasing its predictive coverage, but at the cost of reproducibility. Despite not including such expert rules, catomatic-1 achieves comparable performance for all drugs, with sensitivities for first-line agents above 88% on the independent Validation Dataset. The automated process allowed us to efficiently explore parameter space; for instance, detecting resistant variants with low read support improved the sensitivity for all drugs. Interpretation: Performant resistance catalogues for M. tuberculosis can be built automatically using transparent and reproducible statistical methods. As more data are collected, catalogue content and performance will evolve, highlighting the need for proper versioning, machine/human readability, and open access. This approach demonstrates resistance catalogues used in surveillance and diagnostics can be rapidly and reproducibily updated. Funding: The National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR), Engineering and Physics Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) and ORACLE Corporation.

title: Altered age-dependent somatic mutational trajectories in ALS motor cortex neurons
authors: Liu; L.; van Dijk; C.; Bonsall; S.; Kazu; R. S.; Zhang et al.
abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease in which disease onset is influenced by genetic, age-associated and environmental factors. Somatic mutations accumulate throughout life and may provide a molecular link between aging and neuronal vulnerability. Here, we investigated neuronal somatic mutational patterns in ALS and control motor cortex using three previously generated 10X single-nucleus RNA and ATAC sequencing datasets. Within the genomic regions accessible to 10X sequencing, variant calls showed established features of neuronal somatic mutagenesis, including neuronal enrichment, age-associated accumulation and recovery of the clock-like SBS5 mutational signature. ALS was associated with a disease-specific age-dependent trajectory of neuronal somatic mutation burden, with higher burden in younger ALS donors and a decreasing difference with age. SBS5 represented the largest fitted mutational component and showed a corresponding age-dependent difference. A similar pattern was observed in an independent single-cell whole-genome sequencing dataset. These findings support age-dependent alterations in neuronal somatic mutational patterns in ALS.

title: XAMPGen: An Interpretable Super Intelligence Pipeline For Novel Antimicrobial Peptide Discovery
authors: Mondal; K.; Padi; S.; Kaur; N.; Makambi; W.; Hoogerheide et al.
abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are short peptides with a broad spectrum of activity against bacterial pathogens, representing a promising avenue for combating the growing threat of antibiotic resistance. This study focuses on two main components: 1) generative super intelligence (GenSI) and 2) utilizing explainable super intelligence (XSI). We fine-tuned ProGen, a decoder-only protein language model, on known AMPs to generate novel peptide sequences with strong antimicrobial properties. Generated candidates were screened with an AMP classifier and filtered based on predicted minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), along with human insights into AMP structure and activity in bacterial membranes. A final set of peptides was selected for synthesis and experimental testing. Biological assays confirmed antimicrobial activity in all generated and tested peptides, while fluorescence and circular dichroism measurements characterized membrane binding and peptide structure. We then applied XSI techniques to interpret the generative model and derive biological insights. Specifically, layer probing was used to identify cornerstone layers that encode functionally critical information. Self-attention analysis within these layers revealed residue-level interdependencies and patterns underlying antimicrobial functions, which we evaluated against well-characterized AMPs from the literature. We further examined associations between amino acid sequence patterns and binding properties in bacterial membrane mimics, relating these observations to biological activities in cell-based assays. These analyses provide insight into the model's decision-making process. This builds confidence that the learned amino acid interdependencies have physico-chemical significance, as applied to AMPs, and may facilitate the discovery of novel AMPs with therapeutic potential. This work demonstrates that interpretable generative language models can support rational AMP discovery.

title: ARGeement: sequence-based, versioned mapping of antimicrobial resistance gene databases
authors: Vujic; V.; Helyes; G.; Toth; A. G.; Csabai; I.; Solymosi et al.
abstract: Genomic studies of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) rely on several independently curated reference databases, which describe the same genes under different names, in different structures and with different classifications. This makes results obtained with different databases difficult to compare. ARGeement maps the entries of AMRFinderPlus, the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD) and ResFinder/DisinFinder to each other by protein sequence, independently of their names. It characterises every link by its relation type, difference count and coverage, tracks the database versions, and produces a documented, immutable mapping for every release. The 17,920 entries of the release described here encode 17,959 protein sequences, corresponding to 9,337 unique proteins. For 64.4% of the cross-database entry pairs that encode the same protein, the names differ even when letter case is ignored, and 447 pairs show a genuine naming conflict. Conversely, 2.0% of the pairs with the same allele name do not encode the same protein. For synthetic variants created with known modifications, the original protein was among the best hits in 99.6% of the cases. In 100 complete RefSeq genomes annotated with AMRFinderPlus, the Resistance Gene Identifier (RGI) and ResFinder, the gene names agreed at 55.3%-75.6% of the loci called by both tools of a pair, whereas after mapping the two reference proteins were identical, near-identical or length variants at 89.6%-94.2%. These results show that name-based comparison is unreliable even for identical sequences, and that a sequence-based, versioned mapping is needed.

title: Genome assembly for Amanita muscaria var. muscaria
authors: Turley; L.; Larcombe; M.; Bryant; D.; Chen; A.; Lord et al.
abstract: Amanita muscaria is a charismatic and widely distributed mushroom-forming fungus. Amanita muscaria comprises a species complex, and genomic resources are unevenly distributed, which may bias genetic and genomic study of the species complex. This study produces a high quality hybrid genome assembly of a specimen from New Zealand. Phylogenetic analysis shows that this belongs to Amanita muscaria var. muscaria.

title: Aging remodels the neuronal activity-dependent transcriptome
authors: Um; J.; Lei; H. C.; Nakamura; K.; Tycksen; E.; Adelman et al.
abstract: Experience-driven neuronal activity induces coordinated transcriptional programs in neurons and glia that support plasticity and memory. How aging reshapes these activity-regulated gene (ARG) programs, and whether activity mitigates or exacerbates aging phenotypes, remain open questions with implications for cognitive decline. Here, we develop novel-environment and chemogenetic paradigms to characterize age-dependent remodeling of ARG transcriptomes in the mouse hippocampus at single-cell resolution. Aging contracts youthful ARG programs in both gene number and dynamic range, a contraction that persists under controlled chemogenetic stimulation independent of behavior. In parallel, novel experience in older mice reveals a latent transcriptional competence. First, distinct sets of genes respond to neuronal activity selectively in older cells. Second, enhancing activity in older animals partially reverses, or buffers, basal aging-associated changes across the transcriptome. Novel experience counteracts aging-associated changes in the target genes of the memory regulator CREB1 and the ER-stress sensor ATF6 across cell types. These data constitute a resource for neuronal activity-dependent transcription across the lifespan and identify a basis for the benefits of cognitive engagement: novel experience buffers age-related transcriptional drift.

title: Benchmarking Machine Learning Methods for Antimicrobial Peptide Prediction and Discovery in Ancient Microbiomes
authors: Zhao; Q.; Ma; Q.; Luo; J.; Chen; C.; Ke et al.
abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) offer a promising alternative to conventional antibiotics amid the growing global threat of antimicrobial resistance. Expanding AMP discovery requires both effective computational tools to accurately identify candidate peptides and access to underexplored biological resources that may harbor novel AMPs. However, the comparative performance of existing computational methods remains poorly understood, while ancient microbiomes have received limited attention as potential reservoirs of AMPs. Here, we systematically benchmarked six machine learning methods across with twelve feature configurations spanning sequence, structural, and protein language model features under a unified framework using eight curated AMP datasets. The best-performing methods were subsequently applied to three ancient metagenomic datasets representing the human gut (archaeological fecal sediments), human oral cavity (dental calculus), and mammoth-associated communities (teeth, skulls, and skin). In parallel, we employed reinforcement learning to select candidate peptides directly from ancient sequence pools without relying on modern AMP labels. Our benchmarking shows that protein language model embeddings provide the most informative features, and deep learning models, including convolutional, transformer-based, and recurrent architectures, outperform classical methods. Applying these models to ancient microbiomes identified candidates occupied the physicochemical space characteristic of AMPs but differed from those of candidates predicted from modern microbiome catalogs. We identified 111, 76, and 50 high-confidence candidate AMPs from the Neanderthal gut, ancient oral, and mammoth-associated communities, respectively. Reinforcement learning selected additional candidate AMPs with distinct properties compared with those predicted by models trained on modern AMP databases. Together, these findings establish a systematic benchmark for AMP prediction and highlight ancient microbiomes as an untapped source of antimicrobial peptide candidates. By integrating supervised machine learning with reinforcement learning, this study expands AMP discovery beyond modern microbiome catalogs and provides new opportunities to identify potentially novel AMPs.

title: MtbAIM: AI/ML-guided endpoint-specific prediction of small-molecule activity across drug-susceptible and drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis
authors: Singh; J.; Singh; K.
abstract: The emergence of drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb) presents a major challenge to drug discovery, as compounds active against drug-susceptible (DS) isolates may not retain comparable inhibitory activity against drug-resistant (DR) isolates. Here, we developed an AI/ML workflow to independently prioritize small molecules separately against DS and DR isolates of M.tb and predict MIC, MIC90, and MIC99 as distinct quantitative endpoints. Following curation of data retrieved from the ChEMBL repository, molecular-activity datasets comprised 25,645 and 3,749 compounds tested against whole cell DS and DR isolates respectively. Molecular representations were generated using RDKit descriptors and Morgan fingerprints, along with embeddings from ChemBERTa, MolCLR, and Uni-Mol, and evaluated for binary activity classification and endpoint-specific regression. The best-performing DS classifier combined RDKit/Morgan features with ExtraTrees (balanced accuracy 0.782; AUROC 0.864; AUPRC 0.870), while histogram gradient boosting using the same features performed best for DR classification (balanced accuracy 0.762; AUROC 0.836; AUPRC 0.880). Similarly, RDKit/Morgan features combined with tree-based regressors achieved the best overall performance across all six DS/DR regression endpoints, with pooled out-of-fold RMSE values ranging from 0.604 to 0.784 pMIC units. To facilitate broader application, we developed MtbAIM (https://github.com/jasdeep002/MtbAIM), a Google Colab-based prediction platform that enables users to assess and prioritize small molecules against DS and DR isolates of M.tb.

title: Doublecortin like kinase 1 (DCLK1) interacts with BRG1 chromatin remodeler and regulates neuronal activity-induced gene activation
authors: Luo; Y.; Kim; B.; Haghighinajafabadi; N.; Westover; K. D.; Wu et al.
abstract: SWI/SNF-like BAF ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complexes play important roles in neural development and plasticity by regulating neural gene expression, especially in response to neuronal stimulations. Previously, we have shown that BRG1, the core subunit of BAF, undergoes neuronal activity-induced phosphorylation, which is important for the expression of a group of activity regulated genes (ARGs). Proteomic analyses identified Doublecortin like kinase 1 (DCLK1) as a novel BRG1 interacting protein. Neuronal depolarization induces nuclear enrichment of DCLK1 and increases interactions between BRG1 and DCLK1. We showed that the DCLK1 kinase domain and BRG1 C-terminal fragments are sufficient to mediate their interaction. Thus, DCLK1 is a candidate kinase responsible for BRG1 phosphorylation in response to neuronal activation. Using DCLK1 specific inhibitors and kinase inactive mutations, we showed that DCLK1, in a kinase activity dependent manner, promotes BRG1 phosphorylation and ARG activation. Thus, we identified a novel interacting kinase of BAF chromatin remodeling complex that regulates ARG expression. Because abnormal expression and mutations of both BAF complexes and DCLK1 are associated with neural disorders and cancer, our study provides molecular insights into their functions in these diseases.

title: Persistence of Non-industrial Gut Microbiota Discriminates Health and Disease States in Industrial Populations
authors: Ibata; N. G. O.; Sarkar; A.; Brielle; E. S.; Penumarthi; L. R.; Moeller et al.
abstract: Industrialization has sharply reduced gut microbial diversity, possibly affecting human health. To isolate the effects of industrialization, we assembled 18,075 human metagenomes spanning hunter-gatherer, agro-pastoral, and industrial lifestyles. We confirmed individual-level diversity reductions in industrial populations, but also found that nearly all known human-associated microbes exhibit population-level persistence. Previously hypothesized 'vanishing' microbes are reduced from high prevalence in non-industrial populations to above-median prevalence in industrial populations. Species-level signatures in industrial case-control cohorts suggest that harboring 'vanishing' taxa can be associated with health or pathology, depending on the condition. Controlling for background prevalence, 'vanishing' microbes were more likely associated with cases than controls in obesity, both 'vanishing' microbes and those now 'blossoming' in industrialized populations were associated with glucose intolerance, while 'blossoming' taxa were associated with inflammatory bowel disease. We conclude that most microbes have not gone extinct under industrialization, and that the health effects of lifestyle-associated taxa are context-dependent.

title: Tracking the trajectory of individual conjugative plasmids in bacterial communities using CRISPR acquisition-based recording
authors: Fernandez-Gomez; A.; Guridi-Fernandez; P.; Guzman-Herrador; D. L.; Gonzalez-Fernandez; I.; Barrabes et al.
abstract: Horizontal gene transfer mediated by conjugative plasmids is a primary driver of bacterial evolution and the spread of adaptive traits, including antibiotic resistance determinants. Tracking how these plasmids disseminate through complex microbial communities remains a major challenge. Current methodologies often yield static, endpoint snapshots of host identity, overlooking transient transfer events and plasmid encounters with the co-resident mobilome. To overcome these limitations, we introduce SPacer Integration (SPI) plasmids, which turn the mobile element itself into a recorder of its own transfer history. We engineered conjugative and mobilizable plasmids to carry a CRISPR-Cas adaptation cassette (cas1-cas2 and a minimal CRISPR array) and maintain tight repression of cas1-cas2 expression in the donor cell, so that upon transfer they capture spacers from the chromosome and plasmids of new hosts and store them permanently in their own array. Subsequent PCR amplification and sequencing of these expanded arrays provide a molecular record of both the bacterial hosts and the co-resident plasmids encountered. We created SPI plasmids using the backbones of well-characterized mobilizable and conjugative plasmids RSF1010, RP4, F, and R100-1. We tested SPI plasmids in defined laboratory matings and in complex wastewater communities. The analysis of the acquired spacers successfully mapped permissive host ranges and profiled the co-resident plasmids in situ. Requiring only standard cloning, PCR and sequencing, this accessible and cost-effective strategy establishes a new framework for studying plasmid ecology. Because spacers are integrated chronologically, it further offers the potential to reconstruct multi-step transfer trajectories across natural microbial networks.
summary_zh: 开发SPI质粒，利用CRISPR适应盒记录接合质粒转移历史，在实验室和废水中追踪宿主范围和共存质粒。
innovation: 将移动元件自身改造为转移历史的记录器 | 通过CRISPR间隔序列捕获实现宿主和共存质粒的分子记录 | 仅需标准克隆、PCR和测序，成本低且易推广

title: VPHYL: A Web Application for Converting Emu and EPI2ME wf-16s Nanopore 16S rRNA Abundance Tables into phyloseq and BIOM Objects
authors: Ramireddy; V. S. R.; Srivastava; S. K.
abstract: Taxonomic abundance data derived from 16S rRNA gene sequencing data are fundamental in microbiome research. To perform downstream statistical analysis and visualization, raw abundance data must typically be converted into standardized data structures, such as phyloseq S4 objects or BIOM files. This conversion requires three input data files: an Operational Taxonomic Unit (OTU) table (count of specific taxa across samples), a Taxonomy table (hierarchical lineage from Kingdom to Species), and a Sample Data table (experimental metadata). For Oxford Nanopore (ONT) 16S data, the two commonly used classifiers, Emu and the EPI2ME wf-16s workflow (Minimap2/Kraken2), generate output files with different formats and column schemas. We found no web-based tool that accepts these classifier outputs directly. Experienced users can reshape them with a script. Researchers who do not program cannot, and for them, this step remains a hurdle. We introduce VPHYL(Versatile PHYLogenetic Standardizer), an R Shiny web application that accepts abundance outputs directly from Emu and EPI2ME wf-16s, splits the lineage into standard ranks, attaches sample metadata, and generates phyloseq objects or BIOM files. VPHYL integrates multi-file aggregation and produces automated HTML reports comprising read statistics, alpha diversity metrics, and taxonomic abundance visualizations. VPHYL output was identical to that of an independently written R script for all nine supported classifier-database combinations. We validated the framework by processing raw abundance datasets processed using the EPI2ME Labs 16S Workflow from a published respiratory microbiome study comprising both porcine and human microbiota composition samples. The published tables were processed by VPHYL without modification, and the resulting alpha diversity indices and taxonomic profiles were consistent with the reported findings; small differences reflect read filtering applied in the original study. The application is publicly available at https://venkat-247.shinyapps.io/VPHYL/.
summary_zh: 开发VPHYL网页应用，将Emu和EPI2ME wf-16s的16S丰度表转换为phyloseq或BIOM对象，并验证其输出与脚本一致。

title: Multireplicon plasmids show broad host distributions, high transfer potential, and are enriched in antimicrobial resistance genes
authors: de Quinto; I.; Ramiro Martinez; P.; Silva Rosa; R.; Herencias; C.; Lanza et al.
abstract: Plasmids are DNA molecules that replicate independently of the bacterial chromosome and are typically associated with the spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and virulence determinants, among other relevant traits. Complex genetic rearrangements (including plasmid fusion) can result in plasmids carrying two or more replication systems, known as multireplicon plasmids. Despite decades of study, we are still far from understanding how multireplicon plasmids arise, persist, and shape the evolution of AMR. Here, we analyzed 24,000 non-redundant plasmids across bacterial genera and found that more than 30% encoded multiple replicons. Compared with single-replicon plasmids, multireplicon plasmids were larger, enriched in antimicrobial, metal, and biocide resistance genes, virulence factors, and transfer-associated features, and observed across broader host taxonomic distributions. Some replicon pairs frequently co-occurred on multireplicon plasmids, whereas others were typically maintained on separate plasmids even when present within the same cell. Replicon pairs also showed non-random spatial organization, being preferentially located either in close proximity or at distant positions along the plasmid backbone. Their phylogenetic congruence varied substantially, suggesting that some replicon associations are evolutionarily transient, whereas others may be persistently co-inherited. Finally, we highlight the contribution of insertion sequences to multireplicon plasmid formation. Together, our work sheds light on the abundance, gene content, organization, and evolutionary dynamics of multireplicon plasmids and underscores their relevance to bacterial evolution and human health.

title: BGC Atlas v2: biosynthetic gene clusters with taxonomic and environmental context at scale
authors: Bagci; C.; Talamas-Tanner; A.; Ziemert; N.
abstract: Genomic and metagenomic studies have revealed that microbes have the capacity to produce an enormous diversity of secondary metabolites. These compounds play important roles in microbial interactions and are also a major source of medicines and other useful natural products, yet only a small fraction of this biosynthetic potential has been experimentally characterized. BGC Atlas was developed to explore this largely uncharacterized diversity by placing biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) into genomic and environmental context. Here, we present BGC Atlas v2, which expands the collection more than eightfold to more than 16 million predicted BGCs and extends it from metagenomic assemblies to metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), single-amplified genomes and isolate genomes. The new release provides taxonomic assignments for nearly all BGCs, harmonized environmental metadata, nested searches across biosynthetic, taxonomic, environmental and geographic properties, and protein-sequence searches against BGC-encoded genes. Its scale also reveals how much bacterial and archaeal biosynthetic diversity remains unexplored. By connecting pathways to related families, organisms and environments, BGC Atlas v2 supports natural-product discovery and investigations of prokaryotic biosynthetic diversity across taxa and ecosystems. BGC Atlas v2 is freely available at https://bgc-atlas.cs.uni-tuebingen.de.

title: Sparrowhawk: harnessing WebAssembly for private microbial genomics, and beyond
authors: Rodriguez-Bouza; V.; von Wachsmann; J. H.; Constantinides; B.; Andreoletti; A.; Odih et al.
abstract: Computational methods are a growing component of every scientific discipline, but the pace of training and expertise for using these methods has not kept up with their widening usage. Researchers expect state-of-the-art methods to be able to independently explore their results, and do so dynamically and interactively. Producing such an application which implements a new algorithm, even though it would access a much wider audience, is typically beyond the expertise and time constraints of computational method developers. Here, we show our Sparrowhawk framework can rapidly create an interactive web application to run interactive analysis on a user's machine, across a wide range of algorithms. Focusing first on genomic epidemiology, a domain with a specific need for such methods, we created novel lightweight methods for genome assembly, antimicrobial resistance gene annotation, and taxonomic identification. Our results exceed performance of previous lightweight methods, and produce results that reproduce or closely match previous analysis pipelines. By using WebAssembly, our framework benefits from not requiring installation, command line knowledge, or transferring sensitive data over an internet connection. We show how algorithms from other researchers, and spanning fields from machine learning to physics, can rapidly be ported to web tools using our framework. We demonstrate an immediate impact on microbial bioinformatics, but expect that uptake of Sparrowhawk by developers of other tools broadly will help other researchers, and create new tools for teaching and public engagement. Thanks to the broad availability and familiarity with web browser tools across society, Sparrowhawk has the potential to significantly lower the barrier to entry to advanced computational methods.

title: Synchronized Seasonal Shifts in the Climate, Diet, and Gut Microbiome of a Rainforest Lemur (Eulemur rufifrons)
authors: Stephens; J. N.; Weisrock; D. W.; Raheimanjato; J. P.; Wright; P. C.; Donohue et al.
abstract: Gut microbiome (GM) flexibility extends the adaptive potential of host species in the face of rapid ecological change. Madagascar's endemic primates offer a powerful natural system to study GM plasticity as the island experiences substantial environmental change throughout the year. This is especially true in the eastern rainforests, which experience marked variation in temperature, rainfall, and fruit availability between the wet and dry seasons. To elucidate interactions between climate, diet, and the GM, we conducted a 10-month study of the ecologically flexible red-fronted brown lemur (Eulemur rufifrons) in Ranomafana National Park. We detected significant shifts in gut microbial communities correlated with monthly rainfall, temperature, and dietary diversity. Trade-offs between abundances of carbohydrate- and fiber-metabolizing bacteria reflected shifts between frugivory and folivory, suggesting that the GM buffers energetic and/or nutritional imbalances when resources are scarce. Finally, we observed synchronized shifts in climate and the GM despite deviation from normal seasonal patterns, demonstrating the GM's rapid response to environmental cues. Our results suggest that the GM contributes to phenotypic plasticity across seasons, enabling endangered primates to better cope with environmental stressors like climate change.

title: Lipid nanoparticle-delivered Cas13b ribonucleoproteins targeting survivin overcome gemcitabine resistance in pancreatic cancer
authors: Castano-Esteban; D.; Lopez-Valls; M.; Santos; M.; Recuero; E.; Martin-Vallejo et al.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the deadliest cancers, largely due to its poor response to chemotherapy and the development of drug resistance. Survivin (BIRC5), an inhibitor of apoptosis frequently overexpressed in PDAC, contributes to tumor cell survival and gemcitabine resistance, making it an attractive therapeutic target. Here, we developed a lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based platform for the delivery of preassembled spCas13b ribonucleoproteins (RNPs) to achieve transient and sequence-specific RNA silencing in pancreatic cancer cells. We optimized ionizable lipid formulations for Cas13b RNP encapsulation and identified a formulation achieving approximately 80% encapsulation efficiency, with sustained colloidal stability and gene-silencing activity during seven days of storage at 4{degrees}C. LNP-delivered Cas13b RNPs efficiently silenced endogenous BIRC5 in three pancreatic cancer cell lines, reducing survivin protein levels and inducing apoptosis. In gemcitabine-resistant PANC-1 cells, BIRC5 silencing synergistically enhanced the cytotoxic effect of gemcitabine in vitro. This therapeutic combination was further evaluated in a PANC-1 xenograft model, where only the combined administration of BIRC5-targeting Cas13b RNP-LNPs and gemcitabine significantly inhibited tumor growth, without apparent systemic toxicity. Intratumoral administration also restricted nanoparticle distribution to the injected tumors. These findings establish LNP-mediated delivery of Cas13b RNPs as a new strategy for transient RNA-targeted therapy and provide proof of concept for combining survivin silencing by Cas13b with chemotherapy to address gemcitabine resistance in pancreatic cancer.

title: Not all plant-based diets are alike: intake of minimally processed plant foods is associated with gut microbial richness among vegetarians and vegans
authors: Mendez-Hurtado; A.; Coleto-Checa; D.; Alvarez; A.; Marcos-Pasero; H.; Calderon et al.
abstract: Plant-based diets are usually defined by what they exclude, overlooking which plant foods are eaten and how processed they are. Here we examine whether this overlooked dimension is related to the gut microbiome. In a cross-sectional study of 172 omnivorous, lacto-ovo-vegetarian and vegan adults profiled by shotgun metagenomics, vegetarians and vegans harboured fewer gut species than omnivores. Within this group, however, each standard deviation increase in minimally processed plant-food intake was associated with 27 additional species (p = 0.001), independently of fibre intake, and richness in participants with the highest intake approached that of omnivores. No such association was seen among omnivores. Higher intake was also linked to more species previously associated with favourable cardiometabolic health and to better health-related quality of life. Dietary labels alone may therefore conceal meaningful variation in the gut microbiome, and characterising how plant foods are processed may help in understanding how plant-based diets relate to health.

title: Body-wide microbial ecosystem reorganization across the cognitive impairment spectrum in Parkinsons disease
authors: Arıkan; M.; Delice; B.; Yıldız; Z.; Kahraman Demir; T.; H. Yılmaz et al.
abstract: Cognitive impairment (CI) is a major determinant of disability in Parkinsons disease (PD), yet how microbial alterations across multiple body sites accompany cognitive dysfunction remains poorly understood. We characterized microbial communities from five body sites (stool, saliva, tongue, nasal cavity, and axilla) in 150 participants spanning healthy controls, PD with mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI), and PD dementia (PDD), generating 616 samples for 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Multi-Omics Factor Analysis v2 (MOFA2) identified a multisite microbial signature with prominent oral and gut contributions that varied across clinical groups (Factor 8; {beta} = -0.58, p < 0.0001). MintTea analysis identified stable multisite microbial assemblies associated with cognitive status, including a module distinguishing PD-MCI from PDD (in-sample AUROC = 0.810). Core microbiome analysis revealed a net reduction of 45 genus-site core memberships across four anatomical sites in cognitively impaired participants, including reduced prevalence of the butyrate-associated genus Roseburia. Multivariable models incorporating microbial signatures and demographic covariates explained an average of 35.4% of cognitive-outcome variance, with microbial features contributing an additional 8.0 percentage points beyond age, sex, and education. Procrustes analysis revealed a pronounced, non-linear pattern of weakening cross-site microbial community correspondence at the dementia stage. The Global Body-wide Organization Index remained relatively stable between HC (0.335) and PD-MCI (0.341) but declined to 0.257 in PDD, representing a 23% reduction relative to HC. Together, these findings identify disease-associated multisite microbial signatures and altered core-community composition across the PD cognitive impairment spectrum, supporting further investigation of multisite microbiome profiling for cognitive stratification.

title: Pili-like proteins are essential for conjugation also in Gram-positive bacteria
authors: ter Beek; J.; Svedberg; D.; Deane-Alder; K.; Ibrahim; M. I. A.; Mateus et al.
abstract: Type IV secretion systems (T4SS) enable the spread of antibiotic resistance and other virulence factors. In Gram-positive bacteria, T4SSs have long been thought to lack VirB2-like proteins that form conjugative pili and instead rely on adhesins for cell-cell contacts. Yet, it has remained unclear how subsequent DNA transfer (conjugation) is mediated. Here we identify a VirB2-like protein, PrgFB2, from the clinically isolated plasmid pCF10 in Enterococcus faecalis and show that it is essential for conjugation. Structural modelling confidently predicts a pilus-like assembly for PrgFB2. This is in line with recently proposed models for conjugative pili in Gram-negative T4SSs. We validate the PrgFB2 pili prediction through mutagenesis, conjugation assays, and targeted chemical labelling. By combining various machine learning bioinformatic techniques, we analysed >1000 Gram-positive conjugative plasmids from diverse species, including major pathogens, and identified probable pili-forming VirB2-like proteins in a large majority. Our findings challenge the prevailing view that Gram-positive T4SSs lack pili and highlight critical targets for combating antimicrobial resistance and virulence in Gram-positive bacteria.

title: HIV-1 Mutational Bias Shapes the Supply of Drug Resistance Mutations
authors: Nitido; A. D.; Ömür; N.; Balazs; A. B.
abstract: The development of durable HIV-1 therapeutics requires understanding not only which mutations confer resistance, but also how readily those mutations arise. Prior work has characterized the effects of individual mutations on viral fitness and drug or immune escape; however, the contribution of mutational bias to HIV-1 evolutionary pathways remains largely unquantified. Here, we report and provide an interactive HIV-1 Mutation Rate Atlas (MRA), built on a dataset of empirical measurements of single-cycle HIV-1 mutation accumulation in the absence of selection pressure, using error-corrected long-read sequencing. The MRA estimates the mutation rate at every genomic position to each possible nucleotide, enabling evaluation of amino acid mutability across the genome. Using the MRA, we show that mutation rate biases predict HIV-1 drug resistance variant frequencies across patients. These results demonstrate that mutational biases shape HIV-1 evolutionary outcomes, providing a framework for predicting HIV-1 evolution and drug resistance.

title: SNP2Cluster-Py: A pathogen-agnostic, context-aware framework for Core SNP and transmission-cluster analysis
authors: Kwenda; S.; Christoffels; A.
abstract: Whole-genome sequencing enables high-resolution identification of genetically related pathogen isolates, but genomic similarity alone does not establish epidemiologically meaningful transmission. We developed SNP2Cluster-Py, an open-source Python framework that separates context-aware Core SNP clustering from the subsequent application of epidemiological and temporal criteria. The software accepts a precomputed pairwise Core SNP-distance matrix and user-configured metadata and supports analysis of all eligible isolates in a single context, as well as sequence-type, geographical, epidemiological and ordered composite contexts. Within each context, authoritative Core clusters are defined as connected components of an SNP-threshold graph; K-means assignments and silhouette widths are retained as exploratory diagnostics only. We evaluated the workflow using 172 Klebsiella pneumoniae isolates from six neonatal-surveillance hospitals in South Africa, a focused 36-isolate single-hospital subset from the same surveillance dataset, and 168 Streptococcus pneumoniae carriage isolates from Ghana. In the full K. pneumoniae dataset, ST-only analysis assigned 141 isolates to Core SNP clusters, whereas Facility + ST analysis assigned 134, demonstrating how facility stratification can remove cross-facility genomic connections. In the single-hospital subset, both contexts assigned 30 of 36 isolates to five Core clusters, and Facility analysis retained 23 isolates in four temporally compatible clusters. In the pneumococcal dataset, ST-context analysis assigned 114 isolates to 38 Core clusters, which were characterised across sampling locations and time through Community analysis. SNP2Cluster-Py therefore provides a reproducible framework for adapting genomic clustering to specific surveillance questions while maintaining a clear distinction between genomic relatedness, analytically inferred transmission clusters and confirmed direct transmission. SNP2Cluster-Py v1.1.2 is available under the Apache License 2.0 through GitHub and Zenodo.

title: Transcriptional programs define solid and ascitic dissemination in ovarian cancer
authors: Zhang; K.; Fei; L.; Afenteva; D.; Kahelin; E.; Marchi et al.
abstract: Metastatic cancer cells must survive in distinct anatomical environments, yet how cancer-cell plasticity is organized across these environments remains poorly understood. Here, we integrated RNA and whole-genome sequencing of 600 multiregion and longitudinal specimens from 284 patients with ovarian high-grade serous carcinoma (HGSC), complemented by DNA methylation, single-nucleus multiome profiling and quantitative histomorphology. Among 25 recurrent cancer-cell transcriptional programs, Mes-ECM was associated with solid omental and peritoneal metastases, whereas Mechano-EMP was associated with ascites. Importantly, these compartment-associated transcriptional programs were already present in treatment-naive tubo-ovarian tumors, where their activity was linked to transcriptional compatibility with solid metastatic sites or ascites. Despite their distinct anatomical associations, both states shared a TEAD-AP-1/YAP-TAZ mechanotransductive signature but diverged in their regulatory and microenvironmental relationships. Mes-ECM was linked to extracellular-matrix remodeling, outward stromal signaling and cancer-proximal stromal expansion, whereas Mechano-EMP integrated hybrid epithelial-mesenchymal and stress-inflammatory programs with SDC4-centered inputs from stromal, vascular and myeloid cells. Both programs were associated with altered collagen organization, while chemotherapy-associated remodeling and prognostic associations varied by anatomical site. Our findings reveal a modular organization of metastatic cancer-cell plasticity, linking shared regulatory circuitry to distinct anatomical environments and tumor ecosystems.

title: Comprehensive identification of bacterial and archaeal habitat associations using IndicPiper
authors: Bueno de Mesquita; C. P.; Woodcroft; B. J.; Fierer; N.
abstract: Taxa that are prevalent and abundant in a particular habitat more so than other habitats can be considered indicators of that habitat. In addition to providing basic natural history information, indicator taxa can be used to verify metadata assignments in large public databases, identify potential contamination, and assess contributions of different source populations to a sink population. Despite these potential applications, a comprehensive database of microbial indicator taxa for major habitats of interest does not yet exist. Here we present IndicPiper, a database and methodology that uses the Sandpiper database combined with indicator taxa analysis to identify the habitat associations of bacterial and archaeal genera. IndicPiper includes a clearly defined methodology and set of functions such that any user with a list of habitats of interest could run the functions and generate their own database. IndicPiper uses the Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB) for taxonomy, and the provided database or custom databases can be used to analyze any prokaryotic sample-by-taxa abundance table, including those from shotgun metagenomic and 16S rRNA marker gene sequencing. After presenting the methodology and results, we then present three applications of IndicPiper on actual modern and ancient DNA sequencing datasets. We used IndicPiper to assess the contribution of different source habitats to Lake Tjornin sediments in Iceland over the past 2000 years, to paired indoor and outdoor dust samples from homes across the U.S, and to freshwater samples across the Willamette River watershed in Oregon, USA.

title: Rapid enhancement of antibiotic resistance and divergent remodeling of gene expression in single cells of bacteria
authors: Umetani; M.; Hashimoto; M.; Akiyoshi; S.; Okura; R.; Sakata et al.
abstract: Exposing bacterial cell populations to antibiotics often results in the emergence of descendants with enhanced resistance. Phenotypic heterogeneity and global physiological responses are thought to contribute to resistance evolution. However, identifying the specific stages of drug exposure where phenotypic heterogeneity and physiological responses play critical roles remains elusive. Using long-term single-cell lineage tracking of an Escherichia coli resistance model, here we reveal that resistance-enhanced cells emerge rapidly within a few generations in a clonal bacterial cell population under chloramphenicol (Cp) exposure and stably transmit the enhanced resistance for hundreds of generations in the presence of Cp. High expression of a resistance protein was advantageous during the initial period of drug exposure, but conferred only a marginal fitness advantage during the period of resistance enhancement. Transcriptomic profiles of resistance-enhanced cell populations were lineage-specific, suggesting that multiple gene expression states can support enhanced resistance. Altogether, these results suggest that an interplay between initial phenotypic heterogeneity and divergent remodeling of gene expression drives the rapid acquisition of enhanced antibiotic resistance.

title: Genomic Characterization of a Typical Enteropathogenic Escherichia coli Isolate from an Egyptian Fruit Bat, Rousettus aegyptiacus from Coastal Kenya
authors: Kamau; J.; Kimemia; B. B.; Abuom; D.; Agwanda; B.; Musila et al.
abstract: Enteropathogenic Escherichia coli (EPEC) are responsible for significant morbidity and mortality cases among young children under the age of five, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Atypical EPEC has frequently been reported from animal hosts, however, information on the occurrence and genomic characteristics of typical EPEC in wildlife reservoirs remains limited. This study characterized an Escherichia coli isolated from an Egyptian fruit bat (Rousettus aegyptiacus) sampled in coastal Kenya using whole-genome sequencing. Oral and rectal swabs were collected from 24 bats captured in Kikambala, Kilifi County, Kenya. Bacterial isolates were cultured, sequenced on the Illumina NextSeq 1000 platform, and analyzed using a bioinformatics workflow that included in silico taxonomic classification, serotyping and multilocus sequence typing, virulence gene profiling, antimicrobial resistance gene detection, plasmid identification, and core genome phylogenetic analysis. One isolate, KIKB-471-SWR-A (O128:H6; ST15625), was classified as typical EPEC. Genomic analysis confirmed the characteristic virulence architecture of typical EPEC. Despite numerous antimicrobial resistance-associated genes being detected, the isolate remained phenotypically susceptible to all antimicrobials tested. The isolate clustered within an EPEC lineage, closely associated with a human-derived EPEC strain, and genetically distinct from both commensal and laboratory E. coli reference strains. Despite no evidence of zoonotic transmission, the findings demonstrated that wildlife can harbor E. coli lineages possessing virulence determinants associated with human pathogenic EPEC strains, underscoring the importance of genomic surveillance at wildlife?human interfaces within a One Health framework to improve the understanding of ecology, evolution, and public health significance of diarrheagenic E. coli.

title: Sensory-processing traits generate dietary phenotypes that predict microbiome structure: an agent-based modelling framework
authors: Hunter; W. R.
abstract: Differences in gut microbiome composition are frequently reported across neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions, including autism and depression, and are often interpreted as reflecting underlying neurobiological variation. However, dietary behaviour is both a major determinant of microbiome composition and a downstream consequence of sensory and cognitive processes. To investigate whether microbiome differences can emerge through behavioural pathways alone, I developed a minimal agent-based model linking sensory-processing traits, dietary behaviour, and microbiome structure. Agents were characterised by latent sensory drive, predictability preference, and context sensitivity, which influenced food selection through reinforcement learning and stochastic environmental interactions. Continuous variation in these traits generated a broad spectrum of dietary phenotypes ranging from restrictive to exploratory food-selection strategies. Dietary entropy increased strongly with dietary repertoire size and was associated with reduced microbiome dominance, indicating that more diverse diets produced more even microbial communities. Sensory-processing traits initially appeared to predict microbiome structure directly; however, when dietary entropy was incorporated into the analysis, the direct effects of sensory traits were greatly reduced, while dietary entropy emerged as the dominant predictor of microbiome dominance. Incorporating dietary entropy increased explanatory power from R2 = 0.67 to R2 = 0.99. Sensitivity analyses demonstrated that this dietary filtering mechanism was robust across a wide range of assumptions regarding microbiome persistence, reinforcement learning, and choice stochasticity. These findings suggest that dietary filtering provides a plausible mechanism linking sensory-processing characteristics to microbiome structure and may explain at least some microbiome differences reported across gut-brain studies. Integrating sensory, behavioural, dietary, and microbiome data may therefore be essential for improving causal inference within gut-brain axis research.

title: Deciphering the role of adenosine-related genes in regulating smooth muscle cell phenotypic switch in coronary heart disease via single-cell RNA sequencing
authors: cao; k. k.; Su; K.; Wang; R.; Qu; Y.; Zhang et al.
abstract: Background: Coronary heart disease (CHD) is closely associated with dysregulated lipid metabolism, inflammation, and impaired adenosine signaling. However, the contribution of adenosine-related genes (ARGs) and their relationship with the immune microenvironment remain unclear. Methods: Public transcriptomic datasets were integrated with curated ARGs. Differential expression analysis and weighted gene co-expression network analysis identified candidate genes, and XGBoost, support vector machine-recursive feature elimination, and Boruta were used to select diagnostic features. Gene set enrichment, immune infiltration, regulatory-network, and single-cell RNA-sequencing analyses were performed, followed by reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction validation. Results: We identified 4,884 differentially expressed genes and 243 ARG-associated module genes, yielding 231 candidate genes. DYRK2 and SIGIRR were prioritized as key genes and were consistently downregulated in bulk CHD datasets, including the validation cohort. A two-gene nomogram showed strong diagnostic performance. Functional analyses linked both genes to mitochondrial dysfunction and innate immune regulation, while immune profiling indicated reduced adaptive immune populations and enhanced myeloid-associated inflammation. Single-cell analysis identified smooth muscle cells as a key compartment with altered DYRK2 and SIGIRR expression along pseudotime trajectories and remodeling of vascular endothelial growth factor and pleiotrophin signaling. Reverse transcription-quantitative polymerase chain reaction in clinical samples (n = 5 per group) supported the bioinformatic expression trends (P < 0.05). Conclusions: DYRK2 and SIGIRR emerged as key adenosine-related genes associated with immune-metabolic imbalance and smooth muscle cell dysfunction in CHD. These findings provide a basis for further mechanistic and translational validation.

title: MicroBioAgent: an AI agent for automated microbiome analysis
authors: Li; Z.; WANG; J.; Wang; C.; Ding; Y.; Zhang et al.
abstract: Microbiome data analysis demands customized workflows tailored to specific biological questions, sequencing modalities, and data properties. However, constructing and executing these workflows requires navigating heterogeneous software dependencies, reference databases, and multi-step parameter tuning. Here, we present MicroBioAgent, an autonomous, domain-specific agent framework that translates high-level biological queries into executable, study-specific pipelines across 16S rRNA amplicon, reference-based shotgun, and de novo assembly-based metagenomics. Rather than relying on static pipeline templates, MicroBioAgent employs a closed-loop execution architecture: it dynamically selects and runs bioinformatics tools within user-controlled environments while iteratively inspecting intermediate outputs to adapt downstream analytical decisions. Furthermore, to address the long-running nature of metagenomic computation, we introduce an asynchronous background task-management mechanism that reduces LLM token consumption by over 50% while enabling real-time plan adjustment and automated workflow resumption. We systematically evaluated MicroBioAgent across three benchmarks of increasing complexity: (1) paired amplicon and shotgun profiling of tomato rhizosphere microbiomes, (2) taxonomic and functional profiling coupled with machine-learning classification in a colorectal cancer cohort, and (3) de novo metagenomic assembly, metagenome-assembled genome (MAG) binning, and metabolic pathway reconstruction in a polyethylene degradation study. Across all benchmarks, MicroBioAgent faithfully recapitulated the primary biological findings of the original studies, exhibiting high analytical concordance despite expected tool- and database-dependent variations. In systematic robustness evaluations across 27 independent runs spanning three backbone large language models and three prompt-complexity tiers, MicroBioAgent achieved a 98.8% task completion rate and yielded highly reproducible diversity and differential-abundance estimates. MicroBioAgent establishes a scalable, adaptive paradigm for end-to-end computational microbiome research.

title: RADSuite: Improving Species-Level Identification in Microbiome Research
authors: Christensen; R. N.; Gilliland; M.; Young; J.; Manning-Neal; R.; Fan et al.
abstract: In the last twenty years, the microbiome has become a central focus of biomedical research, with amplicon sequencing of the 16S rRNA gene considered the industry standard for taxon identification of prokaryotes due to its cost-effectiveness. However, common target regions in 16S amplicons often do not uniquely distinguish closely related species, restricting many analyses to the genus level. Additionally, curated databases such as NCBI's 16S curated database often do not contain all intragenomic variants of the 16S gene and lack annotation of the 16S genomic composition and gene structure. To address these limitations, our team created RADSuite, a collection of tools which includes a more robust database of 16S gene copies (RADlib), an application that identifies which V regions will allow for species level identification (RADx), and a step-by-step guide for how to integrate RADlib within existing metagenomic profiling software tools. Here we demonstrate the utility of using RADSuite as a guide for designing 16S amplicon sequencing experiments. For example, RADx can be used to recommend 16S components that enable species-level resolution for most microbes of interest, even when industry-standard default amplicon choices (V3/V4) are insufficient. These findings suggest that targeted variable region selection is critical for reliable species identification. As researchers use RADSuite to improve the quality of their experiments, we anticipate improved experimental accuracy in fields of microbiome research from human health to environmental conservation.

title: A rapid and sensitive Loop-Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP) assay for detection of mecA antibiotic resistance gene in clinical and food bacterial isolates
authors: Baldenweck; L.; Djisalov; M.; Pinamonti; D.; manzano; M.; Gadjanski et al.
abstract: An advanced LAMP assay targeting the mecA gene in methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) was developed and validated using clinical and foodborne S. aureus isolates. Reference strains, including both methicillin-sensitive and methicillin-resistant S. aureus, were used to evaluate and optimize assay performance. With the newly designed ID16 LAMP primer set, the detection limit for mecA was 15 fg/{micro}L of total genomic DNA, equivalent to 5 copies/{micro}L, and the assay turnaround time was only 25 min. All mecA-positive isolates identified by conventional qPCR were successfully detected by the LAMP assay. Overall, the developed LAMP method provides a rapid, highly specific, and sensitive alternative for mecA detection.

title: CONSORTiUM-IO: A Phase 1 Study Evaluating VE800 Plus Nivolumab in Treatment of Select Refractory or Metastatic Cancers
authors: Lyon De Ana; C.; Menon; R.; Bhattarai; S. K.; Prince; A. L.; Buresh et al.
abstract:
Microbiome modulation can augment responses to immunotherapy in advanced cancer. Early studies of anti-PD-1 therapies in combination with fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) reported efficacy in immunotherapy-naive and -refractory settings. However, FMTs are variable in composition, difficult to scale, and risk the transfer of emerging pathogens. VE800 is a consortium of 11 strains of commensal bacteria derived from healthy donors and grown from clonal cell banks. VE800 increased anti-PD-1 efficacy in preclinical models of cancer. CONSORTiUM-IO was a first-in-human, open-label phase 1 study that evaluated safety and efficacy of VE800 with nivolumab in advanced PD-1-refractory melanoma, PD-1-naive gastric/gastroesophageal junction (G/GEJ) adenocarcinoma and PD-1-naive microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer (MSS CRC). VE800 plus nivolumab was well tolerated but offered no improvement over historic response rates. Exploratory analyses in patients with melanoma revealed that VE800 strain engraftment was associated with greater progression-free survival (PFS) and increased immune activation peripherally.

STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCEThe first-in-human study of the safety and efficacy of a defined bacterial consortium in combination with anti-PD-1 treatment in various solid tumors demonstrated the safety of the combination, albeit with low clinical efficacy. The results provide important knowledge and considerations about microbiome modulation in cancer, to help design future trials.

title: Whole-genome sequencing enables improved AML diagnostics and refines assessment of TP53 allelic state and complex karyotype
authors: Stanek; P.; Orsmark-Pietras; C.; Henningsson; R.; Rissler; M.; Landberg et al.
abstract: Accurate genetic characterization is central to modern acute myeloid leukemia (AML) diagnostics, yet current standard-of-care (SoC) testing relies on multiple complementary assays. We compared paired tumor-normal whole-genome sequencing (WGS) with SoC diagnostics in a population-based cohort of 109 adult AML patients, assessing variant detection, disease classification according to ICC 2022 and WHO 2022, and risk stratification according to ELN 2022. WGS showed high concordance with SoC across variant classes. When considering all reported SoC variants together with high-confidence WGS variants as true positives, WGS showed equal to higher sensitivity than SoC for single-nucleotide variants and small insertions/deletions (97% vs 92%), structural variants (SVs; 100% vs 87%), and copy-number alterations (CNAs; 88.5% both). WGS identified clinically important lesions missed by SoC in 16 cases (15%), including FLT3-ITDs and KMT2A, NUP98 and MECOM rearrangements. Classification and risk assignments were 95-96% concordant, with WGS-driven reclassifications in 4-5% of cases, primarily through detection of cryptic SVs and myelodysplasia-related lesions. Integrated analysis of genomic alterations, including copy-neutral loss-of-heterozygosity, refined TP53 allelic state assessment and demonstrated increased genomic complexity in AML with biallelic TP53 alterations. We developed a supervised machine-learning model for complex karyotype (CK) probability, based on WGS-derived copy-number and SV burden, enabling automated identification of CK cases from WGS data. Collectively, these results support paired tumor- normal WGS as a single comprehensive assay well suited for AML diagnostics according to current classification and risk-stratification systems, while refining assessment of TP53 allelic state and karyotypic complexity.
