title: Cervicovaginal metabolites mediate the relationship between vaginal microbiota and risk for Chlamydia trachomatis infection
authors: Dabee; S.; Tsamir-Rimon; M.; Akingba; O.; Kinuthia; J.; MacDonald et al.
abstract:
BackgroundChlamydia trachomatis (CT) remains the most prevalent bacterial sexually transmitted infection and a cause of adverse reproductive outcomes. Epidemiologic studies describe bacterial vaginosis (BV) as a major risk factor for CT infection. Emerging data suggest that BV-associated bacteria and their metabolites contribute to CT susceptibility. Here, we measured the role of specific bacteria in incident CT and evaluated a hypothesized causal role between the vaginal microbiota, its metabolites, and CT risk.

MethodsWe conducted a nested case-control study of Kenyan women who engage in transactional sex from the Mombasa Cohort who acquired CT versus those who did not, and compared their vaginal microbiome and metabolome at the visit preceding CT acquisition. We determined CT infection and total bacterial load using qPCRs. 16S rRNA sequencing was used to characterize the genital microbiome, and BV status was determined using Nugent-Hillier and Amsel scoring criteria. Metabolites were measured using targeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry from a subset of women.

FindingsWomen with BV, high vaginal microbial diversity, and community state types III and IV were significantly more likely to have CT at their next visit. CT infection itself did not alter vaginal microbial diversity. More specifically, both concentrations and relative abundances of Lactobacillus crispatus and several BV-associated bacteria (Sneathia sanguinegens, Umbribacter vaginalis, Prevotella amnii, Hoylesella/Prevotella timonensis, and Ureaplasma urealyticum) were predictive of CT outcomes. Vaginal metabolites differed between cases and controls pre-CT, including Tyramine, reduced and oxidized Glutathione, and sucrose. In a mediation analysis, the vaginal metabolome significantly mediated the relationship between the microbiome and CT infection.

InterpretationWe show for the first time that the association between BV and CT risk is mediated by differences in the metabolome. Identification of the mechanisms underlying increased CT risk with BV can inform interventions to reduce infections in high-risk women.

FundingUS NIH (R01AI13214401-A1)

Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSChlamydia trachomatis (CT) remains the most reported bacterial sexually transmitted infection globally and can lead to serious adverse health outcomes. Previous studies have pointed to an association between the vaginal microbiota composition, particularly the presence of bacterial vaginosis (BV)-associated taxa, and chlamydia susceptibility. However, most studies have been cross-sectional, measuring the microbiome at the time of infection. The few longitudinal studies specifically assessing the microbiome dynamics preceding CT infection have generally been limited by small sample sizes or infrequent sampling. Further, the mechanisms underlying this relationship remain unclear.

Added value of this studyIn this nested case-control study, we evaluated the vaginal microbiome preceding CT acquisition and compared participants who subsequently acquired infection with matched controls who remained uninfected. We found that women who acquired CT had a significantly higher vaginal microbial diversity in the past 1-2 months, while the CT infection itself did not lead to broad changes in the microbiome, suggesting directionality to this relationship. Participants who acquired CT were >2-fold more likely to have BV by Nugent-Hillier or Amsel criteria at the previous visit. Having a diverse community state type IV was associated with the strongest likelihood of CT acquisition. More specifically, women who acquired CT were more likely to have a microbiome characterized by the depletion of Lactobacillus crispatus and higher abundances of Sneathia sanguinegens, Umbribacter vaginalis, Prevotella amnii, Hoylesella (Prevotella) timonensis, and Ureaplasma urealyticum. To assess the possible mechanism through which the microbiome influenced CT risk, we measured the cervicovaginal metabolome in a subset of participants. We found that 70% of the effect of the vaginal microbiome on CT acquisition risk could be explained by the metabolome, highlighting the role of bacterial metabolites in CT susceptibility. Overall, by focusing on samples collected prior to infection acquisition, with a short period between visits, our study contributes robust temporal evidence that the vaginal microbiome impacts CT susceptibility rather than simply being correlated, with the presence of CT, with metabolites potentially playing a key role in this relationship.

Implications of all the available evidenceOur findings support the concept that the vaginal microbiome is a potentially modifiable risk factor for CT acquisition, with specific BV-associated bacteria, alongside L. crispatus depletion, identified as key modulators of risk. This study is a step towards confirming the directionality of the microbiome-CT infection relationship and establishing potential mechanisms through which the microbiome influences CT risk. These findings, along with previous literature, have the potential to lead to microbiome or metabolite-targeted interventions that would reduce the risk of CT acquisition.

title: Genome-resolved metagenomics reveals population-dependent gut microbiome responses to albendazole-ivermectin treatment
authors: Gandasegui; J.; Fleitas; P.; Messa; A.; Gelaye; W.; Shao et al.
abstract: Soil-transmitted helminth control relies on mass anthelmintic treatment, yet helminth-anthelmintic-microbiome interactions and their role on treatment response remain poorly understood. We characterised the microbiome, resistome, and functional profiles of 858 paired stool metagenomes from 429 children treated with albendazole or a fixed-dose albendazole-ivermectin co-formulation in the ALIVE clinical trial in Ethiopia and Mozambique. Baseline microbiome composition differed more by country than infection status and was not associated with albendazole efficacy or adverse events. Co-formulation treatment, particularly three consecutive daily doses, was associated with depletion of Enterobacteriaceae, predominantly Escherichia coli, in Ethiopia, with reductions in E. coli-associated resistance genes and metabolic pathways. Genome-resolved analyses of over 22,000 high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes confirmed this depletion across multiple E. coli strain-level populations, linking taxonomic, resistome, and functional signals to one ecological event. These findings reveal an off-target effect of combination anthelmintic treatment relevant to large-scale deworming programmes and expand genomic resources for African gut microbiota.

title: Knowledge, attitudes and practices regarding antibiotic use and antimicrobial resistance among community pharmacy workers in Bukavu, Eastern Democratic Republic of Congo: a cross-sectional study
authors: Mushobekwa Biringanine; W.; Rugajo; N.; Ntibonera Aganze; J.; Cito Mudekereza; O.; Kabagale Ansima et al.
abstract:
BackgroundCommunity pharmacies are often the first point of care in low- and middle-income countries, yet the knowledge, attitudes and practices (KAP) of their workers regarding antibiotics and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) are undocumented in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

ObjectivesTo assess KAP regarding antibiotic use and AMR, and their determinants, among community pharmacy workers in Bukavu, Eastern DRC.

MethodsA cross-sectional survey was conducted in April-June 2026 among 423 community pharmacy workers, one per pharmacy, selected by multistage sampling across the three health zones of Bukavu, using a structured, interviewer-administered questionnaire. Knowledge (8 items), attitudes (9 items) and dispensing practices (4 items) were scored using modified Blooms cut-offs. Multivariable logistic regression identified determinants.

ResultsGood knowledge was found in 19.4%, favourable attitudes in 17.5% and appropriate dispensing practices in 27.4%. Overall, 96.5% dispensed antibiotics without a prescription and 9.2% knew the WHO AWaRe classification. University education and pharmaceutical qualification were independently associated with good knowledge [adjusted OR (aOR) 4.38 and 2.41] and appropriate practices (aOR 5.74 and 2.01). Good knowledge was associated with favourable attitudes (aOR 4.86, 95% CI 2.68-8.82), which in turn predicted appropriate practices (aOR 6.62, 95% CI 3.50-12.53). In addition, 57.0% knew of "Machange", an informal mixture of medicines: 99.6% of those describing its composition listed at least one antibiotic, and 65.6% of those familiar with it sold it.

ConclusionsCommunity pharmacy workers in Bukavu show substantial gaps in antibiotic-related KAP. Stewardship interventions should combine education with regulation, diagnostic capacity and AMR surveillance within a One Health framework.

title: HLA-Resolve: Four-field HLA typing and MHC variant detection from long-read hybrid capture
authors: Glasenapp; M. R.; Yee; M.-C.; Symons; A. E.; Sheh; J. G.; Garcia et al.
abstract: The major histocompatibility complex (MHC) is among the most polymorphic and difficult-to-genotype regions of the human genome. Accurate typing of its HLA genes, which encode antigen-presenting molecules, is critical for transplantation, pharmacogenomics, and disease-risk prediction. Long-read sequencing is increasingly used in HLA typing because of its ability to phase variants across long distances, but many long-read HLA typing workflows still rely on long-range PCR. Here, we present an end-to-end workflow for MHC genotyping that pairs hybrid capture with long-read sequencing on PacBio or Oxford Nanopore, using single-step enzymatic fragmentation and barcoding to enable automated library preparation. The hybrid capture panel enriches both classical and non-classical HLA Class I and Class II genes, as well as all 69 protein-coding MHC Class III genes. We introduce HLA-Resolve, a bioinformatic tool that types HLA genes from PacBio reads via phased full-gene sequence reconstruction, and we benchmark the capture assay and HLA-Resolve together across 32 geographically diverse samples. With PacBio data, variant calling achieved F1 scores of 99.8% for SNVs and 98.4% for indels against the Genome in a Bottle benchmark. HLA-Resolve showed 99.5% allele concordance with reference typings from the International Histocompatibility Working Group and the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium (HPRC) at three-field resolution and 90.5% at four-field resolution, outperforming three other open-source long-read HLA typers on our HiFi hybrid capture reads. The full-gene sequences reconstructed by HLA-Resolve showed zero edit distance to the corresponding HPRC assemblies in 95% of comparisons. HLA-Resolve also showed high accuracy with whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data, achieving 99.4% two-field concordance across 146 public PacBio WGS libraries and 99.5% three-field concordance across the 52 with full-resolution reference typings. Although developed for the MHC, the workflow is customizable to any gene set, providing a general framework for high-resolution genotyping.

title: Antibiotic prescribing and resistance beyond hospital surveillance networks in India
authors: Kaur; J.; Madaan; V.; Sharma; R.; Agarwal; Z.; Gudi et al.
abstract: Hospital-based networks provide much of the antimicrobial resistance surveillance evidence in India, but community-facing data on both prescribing and resistance remain limited. We analysed 2.78 million prescription-validated antibiotic records and 155,764 microbiology samples from Tata 1mg, a digital healthcare platform, during 2023-2025. We assessed prescribing composition and resistance trends, and explored ecological prescribing-resistance associations using merged monthly series. Access antibiotics accounted for 28.7% of records, compared with 47.0% for Watch and 11.9% for Not Recommended antibiotics. Across 25 eligible states and union territories, Access shares ranged from 16.1% to 38.0%. Urine comprised 93.9% of samples. Among urinary Escherichia coli isolates, resistance was 4.9% to nitrofurantoin and amikacin, compared with 53.6% to ceftriaxone and 57.0% to ciprofloxacin. Exploratory prescribing-resistance associations varied by organism and antibiotic. These findings identify stewardship priorities within a digitally mediated care pathway and illustrate the complementary value of routinely collected pharmacy and laboratory data for surveillance beyond hospital-centred networks. but community-facing data on both prescribing and resistance remain limited. title: Upper respiratory microbiome and host immune signatures associated with SARS-CoV-2 susceptibility and illness in a human challenge model
authors: Hurst; J. H.; Wanchai; V.; Shi; P.; Nookaew; I.; Swain-Lenz et al.
abstract: The upper respiratory tract (URT) microbiome modulates the local mucosal immune environment, with potential implications for respiratory viral infection susceptibility and outcomes. We leveraged a first-in-human SARS-CoV-2 challenge study in 34 healthy young adults, 18 of whom became infected, to characterize host gene expression and microbiome composition and dynamics in nasal and throat samples collected before viral inoculation and over the subsequent 14 days. Compared with participants who remained uninfected, participants who became infected had elevated baseline nasal expression of gene modules related to interferon, innate inflammatory, and neutrophil responses, as well as a delayed transcriptional response to viral challenge. Baseline nasal microbiome composition differed modestly by subsequent infection status, with lower relative abundances of Corynebacterium accolens and higher abundances of Dolosigranulum pigrum and Staphylococcus aureus among participants who became infected. Integrated analyses of microbiome and host gene expression data identified coordinated networks of microbiome features and host immune modules that distinguished infected from uninfected participants, including prior to inoculation. Notably, immune modules associated with infection susceptibility were positively correlated with S. aureus abundance and negatively correlated with the abundances of common nasal commensals, Corynebacterium spp. and Staphylococcus epidermidis, linking altered nasal microbiome community structure with the heightened inflammatory state associated with infection susceptibility. Symptom burden and viral load were similarly linked to distinct networks of microbiome and host gene expression features within nasal samples. Taken together, these findings highlight potential microbiome-host interactions within the nasal mucosa that may contribute to differences in respiratory viral infection outcomes.

title: Shared genetic architecture between digestive infectious diseases and cardiovascular diseases: a genome-wide cross-trait analysis
authors: Ni; J.; Pan; J.; Chen; Y.
abstract: Background Digestive infectious diseases and cardiovascular diseases may share common genetic, inflammatory and immune-related mechanisms. However, the shared genetic architecture between these disease groups, the specific pleiotropic loci involved and the potential contribution of intestinal infectious diseases (IID) to cardiovascular risk remain incompletely understood. Methods We analysed publicly available genome-wide association study summary statistics for 36 binary traits of European ancestry, including 16 digestive infectious disease traits and 20 cardiovascular traits. Univariate linkage disequilibrium score regression was used to estimate SNP-based heritability and prioritise traits. Global and local genetic sharing were evaluated using cross-trait LDSC and SUPERGNOVA. Multi-trait analysis of GWAS, cross-trait sensitivity analyses, FM-summary fine-mapping and Bayesian colocalisation were used to identify and refine pleiotropic loci. Candidate genes and biological functions were investigated using MAGMA, tissue- and cell-type-specific enrichment analyses, transcriptome-wide association analysis and protein-wide association analysis. Bidirectional two-sample Mendelian randomisation and two-step mediation analyses using three independent gut microbiome GWAS resources were subsequently performed. Results Sixteen traits passed heritability quality control, yielding 39 trait pairs with significant global genetic correlations after Bonferroni correction. MTAG identified 41 candidate SNP records and 14 trait-pair-specific lead-SNP records representing eight unique SNPs; 39 candidate records and 12 lead records involved IID. Fine-mapping and colocalisation prioritised eight records representing four unique variants. Locus-based gene prioritisation retained 24 candidate genes across four pairs. Gene-set enrichment identified 43 significant trait-pair-GO term associations, and tissue enrichment identified seven significant associations. Transcriptome-wide analyses implicated 21 candidate genes, and proteome-wide analyses identified four associations involving three proteins. After false discovery rate (FDR) correction, forward MR supported associations of IID liability with cardiac arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, atrial fibrillation and flutter, and ischaemic heart disease; reverse MR supported only cardiac arrhythmias to IID. Five positive exploratory microbiota-IID-cardiovascular mediation patterns were described. Only the Oxalobacter-IID-cardiac arrhythmias indirect effect reached unadjusted P < 0.05. Conclusions Digestive infectious diseases, particularly IID, share substantial genetic architecture with cardiovascular diseases. Integrative genetic analyses identified recurrent pleiotropic loci, candidate genes and putative microbiome-mediated pathways linking IID with cardiovascular outcomes. These findings provide testable hypotheses for further functional validation and clinical investigation.

title: Transcriptomic and Genomic Sequencing of South African Colorectal Cancer Patients Reveal Population-Specific Insights and Variants
authors: Kader; Z.; Abdulla; N.; Bebington; B.; Choudhury; A.; Mpangase et al.
abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) genomic studies have largely underrepresented African populations, limiting understanding of disease biology in these groups. This study addressed this gap by generating integrated genomic and transcriptomic data from South African (SA) CRC patients, establishing a foundation for future cancer studies. Bulk RNA sequencing of 32 samples identified several differentially expressed genes between tumour and normal samples, with AGAP3, AMPD2, ANKRD10, and SALL4 showing strong diagnostic performance (average sensitivity 99.9%, specificity 94.22%, PPV 99.9%, NPV 89.5%). SALL4 performed best and was validated using TCGA data and Kaplan-Meier survival analysis. Consensus Molecular Subtype classification revealed a distinct distribution, with enrichment of metabolic (CMS3, 30%) and mesenchymal (CMS4, 30%) subtypes and under-representation of canonical CMS2 (21%). APC mutation rates were lower than in European patients (~55% vs ~75%). Functional analysis identified inflammatory pathways as primary drivers of carcinogenesis, with viral influences exacerbating the inflammatory tumour microenvironment. Altered neural pathways in tumour samples suggested a consequential gut-brain axis loop as cancer infiltrates enervated tissue, an increasingly relevant field to which these data contribute. Whole-genome sequencing of 12 samples revealed pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants with transcriptomic differential expression; SMPD1, PERM1, PRRT2, and RP1 emerged as potential multi-omics markers, while novel mutations (KDM6A, C2CD2, TAF2, SLC6A16, OR5M10, PITRM1, TRIM64B, CARD11) were identified as previously unrecognised contributors to CRC progression in African samples. These findings expand genomic resources for African cancer research and provide new insights into the molecular landscape and tumourigenesis mechanisms of CRC in SA patients, supporting the development of population-specific precision oncology approaches.

title: Rare miRNA variants in complex neuropsychiatric pedigrees alter synaptic miRNA gene-targets
authors: Mamaladze; L.; Ormond; C.; Hearn; B.; Chang; Y.-C.; Hassan et al.
abstract: Although rare non-coding variants are likely involved in psychiatric disorder susceptibility, their contribution is poorly understood. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) regulate gene expression, and targets in the brain include genes involved in neuronal development and synaptic plasticity. Because single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) can alter miRNA processing and target specificity, this can have disproportionate downstream impact on multiple genes affecting pathways that regulate biological processes, making them compelling candidates for mediating psychiatric disorder risk. We investigated rare miRNA variants in whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from 25 pedigrees with diagnoses including schizophrenia, psychosis, bipolar disorder, depression, OCD, and substance use disorder. Evidence of segregation with schizophrenia and related psychotic disorders was identified for five rare miRNA variants (two seed-region, one mature-region, and two precursor-region variants), including a SNV in the mature-region of miR-4794, segregating strongly in two unrelated pedigrees and identified in a parent-offspring pair with schizophrenia from a third pedigree. One of these two pedigrees also segregates a seed-region SNV in miR-4423-3p, predicted to significantly impact expression-regulation, causing the loss of synaptic gene-targets associated with psychiatric disorders. Collectively, targets of three of the miRNAs are enriched for schizophrenia rare variant risk genes (p-value: 0.00027): six SCHEMA genes were targeted by miR-96 and four genes by miR-4423-3p. While further understanding of miRNA function and validation is required, this study demonstrates the value of integrating structural modelling, target-shift prediction, and pathway enrichment to interpret non-coding variants. This highlights the utility of WGS for identifying and investigating rare non-coding variation in psychiatric disorder susceptibility, supplementing exome-based approaches.

title: Long-term transmission chains fueling the drug-resistant tuberculosis burden in Southern Brazil
authors: Soares; T. d. S.; Pivato; A. F.; Frosi; F.; Pavanelo; D. B.; Godinho et al.
abstract: Background Tuberculosis (TB) remains a leading infectious cause of death, with drug-resistant TB (DR-TB) challenging disease control. Brazil has a high TB burden, and Rio Grande do Sul state reports persistently high incidence and drug-resistance rates. The drivers shaping the regional DR-TB burden remain poorly characterised. Methods We conducted genomic surveillance of confirmed DR-TB cases in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, from January 2023 to September 2024. Clinical isolates underwent genotypic (gDST) and phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (pDST) and whole-genome sequencing (WGS). We analyzed 33 newly sequenced genomes and 267 historical Mycobacterium tuberculosis genomes collected in 2011-2019 to characterize resistance, transmission, and spatiotemporal patterns and estimate the contributions of transmitted and acquired rifampicin resistance. Findings Molecular testing detected rifampicin resistance missed by pDST, including borderline rpoB mutations in 18.2% and emerging resistance-associated variants in 3% of the 33 analyzed isolates. Conversely, pDST detected baseline bedaquiline resistance missed by WGS in one newly diagnosed case. Among 300 genomes, 181 (60.3%) clustered into 32 genomic clusters at a 5-SNP threshold, including 12 with long-term circulation and several spanning prisons and communities. Sublineage frequencies remained stable over time, whereas we observed marked geographic structuring and localized clonal expansion. Among 178 rifampicin-resistant isolates, transmission accounted for an estimated 79.2-88.2% of resistance, corresponding to 11.8-20.8% of cases arising through de novo acquisition during treatment. Interpretation Our findings identify active transmission as the main driver of rifampicin-resistant TB in Rio Grande do Sul, with long-term transmission chains extending across both incarcerated and community settings. These results underscore the urgent need to strengthen timely TB case detection and resistance testing, enhance contact investigations, and implement targeted interventions aiming to interrupt persistent transmission chains.

title: A pilot study of the mutational landscape of colorectal cancer in Black South Africans
authors: Brandenburg; J.-T.; Campbell; L.; Engelbrecht; D.; Mathew; C. G.; Thompson et al.
abstract: **Background:** Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a public health concern in sub-Saharan Africa, where the molecular landscape of the disease remains poorly characterised. In particular, genomic studies of resident Black African populations are limited, and the contribution of population-specific mutational processes and potential infectious exposures remains insufficiently understood. The Molecular, Somatic and Infectious Drivers of Colorectal Cancer in Africa (MOSAIC) collaboration aims to address these gaps by generating population-specific genomic data. This pilot study aimed to assess the feasibility of paired tumour-normal whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and to provide an initial characterisation of somatic mutations and mutational signatures in South African patients with CRC. **Methods:** We recruited five Black South African patients with newly diagnosed, treatment-naive CRC through the CoRecT Cancer study at Chris Hani Baragwanath Academic Hospital and Wits University Donald Gordon Medical Centre, Johannesburg. Fresh-frozen colorectal tumour tissue and matched peripheral blood samples were subjected to paired-end WGS (2 x 151 bp) using the Illumina NovaSeq X Plus platform. Somatic variants were identified using CaVEMan and Strelka2, followed by functional annotation using the Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor (VEP). Protein-altering variants were characterised using the R package maftools. Mutational signature contributions were estimated using SigProfilerAssignment and the COSMIC v3 reference catalogue. **Results:** All ten sequencing samples, comprising five tumour-blood pairs, passed quality control. Estimated sequencing depth ranged from 49.2X to 82.4X for tumour samples and from 22.7X to 40.7X for matched blood samples, with a median of 96.3% well-aligned reads. Following somatic variant calling and filtering, the number of retained mutations ranged from 1,106 to 65,379 per tumour. Three of the five tumours harboured at least one predicted protein-altering variant, comprising seven missense and four splice-site variants across eleven genes. Mutational signature analysis of single base substitutions (SBS) revealed inter-individual heterogeneity. SBS1 and SBS5 were detected across all five tumours, while additional signatures included SBS18, SBS20, SBS26 and SBS44, among others. Several tumours exhibited signatures associated with mismatch repair-related mutational processes. **Conclusions:** This pilot study demonstrates the feasibility of paired tumour-normal WGS and preliminary somatic mutation profiling in Black South African patients with CRC. The findings provide initial insights into the heterogeneous mutational landscape of CRC in this underrepresented population. However, the small sample size and incomplete clinical and molecular characterisation necessitate cautious interpretation. Larger studies incorporating comprehensive mismatch repair assessment, copy-number and structural variant analysis, germline susceptibility profiling and investigation of infectious exposures will be essential to validate these preliminary observations and better understand the molecular and environmental drivers of CRC in African populations.

title: The same practices, year after year: a national observational study of higher-risk antibiotic prescribing in English general practice, 2023-2026
authors: Agarwal; A.; Gill; A.
abstract: Background: There is increasing antibiotic resistance in England. National targets have been set to increase the proportion of antibiotics prescribed in the lower risk Access category. The proportion of higher risk antibiotics within the Watch+Reserve category prescribed in each general practice is publicly available. It is unclear whether a high proportion of Watch+Reserve antibiotics in a practice is due to random variation, patient population or a persistent trend. Methods: Observational study using NHS open prescribing data from 5,791 general practices in England (26.0 million items, September 2025 to August 2026, and the two previous years). Watch+Reserve proportions were compared between practices using over-dispersion adjusted funnel plots with 99.8% control limits. Practices identified as outliers were tested using subsequent data. A quasi-binomial model was fitted adjusting for age, deprivation, practice size and 7 disease registers. Results: 117 practices exceeded the 99.8% control limit (approximately 6 expected by chance). 106 practices were included in a shortlist. Of those in the shortlist in 2024/25, 61% (95% CI 52-70%) exceeded the control limit in 2025/26 compared to 1.0% of all other practices. 36 practices were shortlisted in all 3 years. Adjusting for age, deprivation, practice size and disease registers explained 4.1% of variability. Following adjustment, 101 of 106 practices remained outliers. Overall, shortlisted practices did not prescribe more antibiotics than other practices (median 422 vs 438 items per 1,000 patients per year), but did prescribe fewer Access antibiotics and more Watch+Reserve antibiotics. 10% or fewer of excess Watch+Reserve antibiotics in England were prescribed in shortlisted practices. Conclusions: A small number of practices show persistently high prescribing of higher risk antibiotics, which cannot be explained by recorded need. This provides integrated care boards (ICBs) with a reliable list of practices to review. It was not possible to investigate penicillin allergy. To meet national Access targets, interventions will be needed in all practices, particularly reviewing the use of clarithromycin, co-amoxiclav and azithromycin.

title: Rare copy number variation in alcohol use disorder using whole-genome sequencing in the All of Us Research Program
authors: Farajzadeh Valilou; S.; Kramer; S.; Edizadeh; M.; Singh; M.; Peterson et al.
abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is common, heritable (h2 ~50%) and polygenic, but the contribution of rare structural variation is largely unexamined. Using short-read whole-genome sequencing (srWGS) data from the All of Us Research Program, we tested the association of rare copy number variants (rCNV; minor allele frequency <1%) with AUD in 56,062 participants (5,410 cases, 50,652 controls) defined from electronic health records. Analyses were conducted within European-like (EUR; N=29,392), African-like (AFR; N=8,269) and Admixed American-like (AMR; N=8,049) samples and combined by cross-ancestry meta-analysis. We tested genome-wide rCNV burden, burden within AUD-related, mouse behavioral and neuropsychiatric gene sets, and individual rCNV regions. No genome-wide burden metric or individual rCNV region [≥]10 kb was associated with AUD after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Significant gene-set results were almost exclusively duplications associated with reduced AUD risk across biologically unrelated sets, suggesting a global duplication dosage effect rather than pathway-specific enrichment. In contrast, deletion count within a Neurof_UnionStringent gene set was associated with increased AUD risk (OR=1.04, FDR=0.044), and deletions in xenobiotic-response genes showed nominal associations in multiple ancestry groups. Among rCNV of all sizes, a 58 bp deletion at 16p12.1, a dosage-sensitive neuropsychiatric locus, was significant in the cross-ancestry analysis (OR=2.93, FDR=0.030) without significant heterogeneity. rCNV detectable by srWGS do not appear to contribute substantially to AUD liability at current sample sizes.

title: Genomic Epidemiology of Dengue Virus in Ivory Coast Reveals Five Decades of Viral Circulation with Repeated Introductions from Burkina Faso
authors: Tao; X.; Kadjo; H. A.; Yahaya; S.; Emily; K.; Edgard et al.
abstract: Dengue fever is a rapidly emerging mosquito-borne disease in Africa, yet the continent remains critically underrepresented in genomic surveillance efforts. This disparity is especially pronounced in West Africa, despite phylogenetic studies being concentrated in only a few countries, such as Burkina Faso. Within this broader regional gap, researchers have yet to systematically characterize the dengue virus (DENV) lineages circulating in the Ivory Coast. In this study, we present 24 newly sequenced DENV genomes from Ivory Coast, spanning serotypes DENV-1, DENV-2, and DENV-3, collected between 2017 and 2023. Combined with publicly available sequences, we assembled the most comprehensive dataset to date for the country. We performed maximum-likelihood and Bayesian phylogeographic analyses using global background datasets and reconstructed the spatial and temporal dynamics of dengue virus circulation in Ivory Coast. Our findings reveal multiple independent introductions of DENV into Ivory Coast, predominantly from neighboring Burkina Faso. We identify five introductions of DENV-1 between 2017 and 2019 and four introductions of DENV-2 between 2015 and 2016. DENV-3 showed two separate introductions, one in 2015 and another in 2018. Notably, we also identified an early DENV-1 introduction from India around 1977, suggesting long-distance historical viral movement likely linked to colonial and post-colonial military presence. These results underscore the need for sustained genomic surveillance to monitor viral evolution and inform regional public health responses aimed at controlling dengue outbreaks in West Africa.
